soil.text: A natural mixture of minerals, organic matter, gases, water and organisms that together support the life of plants and soil organisms; all of Earth's soil together is called the pedosphere.

soil science.text: The study of soil as a natural resource: its formation, classification and mapping, its physical, chemical, biological and fertility properties, and how these bear on soil use and management.

pedosphere.text: The outermost layer of Earth's crust, made of soil and subject to soil formation and erosion.

pedology.text: The branch of soil science that studies how soils form and evolve and builds frameworks for describing soil bodies, often in their natural environment.

soil composition.text: The proportions of solids (minerals and organic matter) and of pore space, shared between water and air, that make up a soil.

edaphology.text: The branch of soil science concerned with the influence of soils on living things, especially plants.

uses of soil.text: The many ways people rely on soil, from growing food and fibre to construction, mining and landscape work.

soil reclamation.text: Improving degraded or badly balanced soils by adding materials such as clay, gypsum, sand, organic matter or biochar.

soil health.text: The state of a soil meeting its range of ecosystem functions as appropriate to its environment.

soil as a natural body.text: The view, developed by Dokuchaev, that soil is a natural body with its own genesis and history, distinct from the bedrock beneath it.

soil functions.text: The general capabilities of soils that matter for agriculture, the environment, nature protection, landscape architecture and urban uses.

soil quality.text: The condition of a soil judged by its capacity to perform ecosystem services that meet the needs of human and non-human life.

principles of pedology.text: The working principles pedologists use to explain soil genesis, starting from the idea that external factors drive soil-forming processes and create soil patterns.

soil science in practice.text: The practical work of soil scientists, traditionally mapping soils and increasingly addressing land and environmental problems across disciplines.

vernacular soil classification.text: Folk systems that name soils either with unique names or by obvious traits such as red, hot, fat or sandy.

atmospheric inputs to soil.text: What the pedosphere receives from the air, mainly wind-blown sediment, rainfall and diffusing gases.

forest soils.text: Soils formed under forest, usually well developed with thick humus layers.

grassland and desert soils.text: Soils formed where precipitation equals or falls short of evapotranspiration, so that soil development works under drought.

pioneer organisms in soil formation.text: The first colonisers of bare rock, such as lichens, mosses and microbes, whose acids begin turning rock into soil.

tropical forest soils.text: Soils of tropical forests, which receive more sunlight and rain over longer growing seasons than any other environment.

industrialization and edaphology.text: The ways industrialised production and farming have changed how soils interact with plants.

van helmont's willow experiment.text: An experiment in which Jan Baptist van Helmont (1577–1644) grew a willow tree in a pot of soil for five years, supplying only rainwater.

soil organic matter.text: The organic part of soil: plant and animal remains at various stages of decay, the cells and tissues of soil microbes, and the substances those microbes make.

mineral.text: A naturally occurring solid with a fairly well-defined chemical composition and a specific crystal structure.

earth's critical zone.text: The near-surface environment where rock, soil, water, air and living organisms interact to regulate habitats and the availability of life-sustaining resources.

soil solution.text: The water held in soil pores together with the many organic and mineral substances dissolved or suspended in it.

what counts as soil.text: The unsettled question of where soil ends and other loose surface material begins, in particular whether lifeless regolith can be called soil.

weathering.text: The breakdown of rocks, soils and minerals through contact with water, atmospheric gases, sunlight and living things.

climate and organic matter accumulation.text: The strong control that climate, chiefly temperature and moisture, exerts on how organic matter is produced, built up and broken down in soil.

soil organic matter in the carbon cycle.term: Soil organic matter in the carbon cycle
soil organic matter in the carbon cycle.text: The role of soil organic matter as a large carbon store that can act as either a sink or a source of carbon.

chemical weathering.text: Weathering in which water, oxygen, carbon dioxide and other substances react with rock and change its composition.

biological weathering.text: Weathering started or sped up by living things, such as soil microorganisms, lichens and plant roots.

dissolution weathering.text: Chemical weathering in which a mineral dissolves completely without leaving any new solid; also called simple or congruent dissolution.

oxidation weathering.text: Chemical weathering by oxidation of metals in minerals, most commonly iron changing from Fe2+ to Fe3+.

physical weathering.text: Weathering that breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its chemistry; also called mechanical weathering or disaggregation.

composition of plant residues.text: The water, elements and organic compounds that make up the plant debris from which soil organic matter forms.

soil organic carbon with depth.text: How the amount, age and makeup of soil organic carbon change between the surface layer, roughly the top 20 cm, and the deeper mineral soil.

frost weathering.text: Physical weathering caused by ice forming inside rock outcrops.

mineral hydration.text: Chemical weathering in which water molecules, or H+ and OH− ions, attach rigidly to the atoms of a mineral.

mineral chemistry.text: How the abundance of elements in the Earth's crust, and the swapping of one ion for another, control which minerals exist and how varied they are.

oxide minerals.text: Minerals in which oxygen or hydroxide is the main anion, divided into simple oxides, hydroxides and multiple oxides.

pressure release weathering.text: Physical weathering, also called unloading, that occurs when deeply buried rock is brought to the surface and the weight on it is removed.

salt weathering.text: The breaking up of rock when salty water seeps into cracks and evaporates, leaving salt crystals that grow there; also called haloclasty.

thermal stress weathering.text: Weathering caused by rock expanding and contracting as its temperature changes.

clay.text: A fine-grained natural soil material containing clay minerals, the hydrous aluminium phyllosilicates such as kaolinite.

rock-forming minerals.text: The mineral species and groups that are far more abundant in rocks than the rest.

silicate minerals.text: Minerals built from the silicon–oxygen tetrahedron, [SiO4]4−, grouped by how far those tetrahedra link together.

framework silicates.text: Silicate minerals whose tetrahedra share all four corners, the most polymerized class, including quartz and the feldspars.

phyllosilicates.text: Sheet silicates: minerals made of sheets of linked silica tetrahedra, a class that includes the mica, chlorite and kaolinite–serpentine groups.

soil texture.text: The quality of a soil set by its make-up of sand, silt and clay particles.

clay formation.text: The making of clay minerals, most commonly by long chemical weathering of silicate-bearing rocks, and their gathering into clay deposits.

clay as a building material.text: The use of clay, the defining ingredient of loam, as one of the oldest building materials on Earth.

clay varieties.text: The main kinds of clay, grouped by their dominant clay minerals: kaolinite, montmorillonite–smectite and illite.

uses of clay.text: The shaping and firing of clay into pottery and construction products, and its use in many industrial processes.

hydrolysis and carbonation.text: Chemical weathering in which only part of a mineral dissolves and the rest turns into a new solid such as a clay mineral; carbonation is the form driven by dissolved carbon dioxide.

weathering in soil formation.text: The conversion of rock into soil material as weathering turns its minerals into clay minerals and iron oxides.

mineralogy.text: The branch of geology that studies the chemistry, crystal structure and physical, including optical, properties of minerals.

biogenic minerals debate.text: The dispute among geologists and mineralogists over the International Mineralogical Association's exclusion of crystalline substances made by living things.

carbonate minerals.text: Minerals whose main anionic group is carbonate, [CO3]2−, chiefly calcite, aragonite and dolomite.

calcite.text: A carbonate mineral, the most stable polymorph of calcium carbonate (CaCO3).

mineral identification.text: Telling minerals apart by physical properties such as crystal habit, hardness, lustre, colour, streak, cleavage and specific gravity.

sulfate minerals.text: Minerals that contain the sulfate anion, [SO4]2−, of which gypsum is by far the most common hydrous member.

phytolith.text: A rigid microscopic mineral deposit, usually of silica, formed in plant tissue and often persisting after the plant decays.

soil ph.text: A measure of how acidic or basic (alkaline) a soil is.

soil horizon.text: A layer roughly parallel to the soil surface whose physical, chemical and biological characteristics differ from the layers above and below.

mineral-associated organic matter.text: Soil organic matter chemically stabilized by sticking to clay, iron oxide or other mineral surfaces.

weathering rind.text: A discoloured, chemically altered outer layer of a rock fragment, formed by weathering.

soil buffering capacity.text: A soil's resistance to a change in pH when acid or basic material is added.

soil color.text: The colour of a soil, often its most visually apparent property.

aluminium toxicity.text: Harm to plants from dissolved aluminium, the most widespread problem of acid soils.

factors affecting soil ph.text: The natural and human influences that set a soil's pH, starting with the minerals of its parent material and the weathering they have undergone.

measuring soil ph.text: The field and laboratory methods for determining a soil's pH, from reading the profile and its plants to electronic meters.

soil ph and nutrient availability.text: The control soil pH exerts over which ions are released or held, and so over the availability of plant nutrients.

master horizons.text: The main layers of a soil profile, marked with capital letters, most commonly O, A, E, B, C and R.

lowering soil ph.text: Reducing the pH of an alkaline soil by adding acidifying agents or acidic organic materials.

plant ph preferences.text: The soil pH ranges to which different plant species are adapted.

soil ph and soil organisms.text: The two-way relation between soil pH and the organisms living in the soil.

soil ph and water availability.text: The ways extreme soil pH reduces the water available to plants and organisms.

soil ph classes.text: The named soil pH ranges of the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, from ultra acidic to very strongly alkaline.

munsell soil color charts.text: The standard way soil surveys record soil colour, using the Munsell color system, which specifies a colour by hue, value and chroma.

soil color interpretation.text: Reading what a soil's colours reveal about its organic matter, iron chemistry, aeration and salts.

australian horizon designations.text: The horizon scheme of the Australian Soil and Land Survey Field Handbook (2009), which adds peaty P and D horizons, drops E, and numbers sub-horizons of A and B.

wrb horizon designations.text: The horizon and layer symbols set out in Chapter 10 of the World Reference Base for Soil Resources manual, 4th edition (2022).

bedrock.text: The solid rock beneath the weathered rock and loose surface deposits, together called regolith, in the near-surface crust of Earth or another terrestrial planet.

gleying.text: The development of gray or bluish, low-chroma colours in waterlogged soils as iron is reduced or removed.

core sample.text: A cylindrical section of a material such as sediment, rock or soil, usually obtained by drilling with a hollow tube.

trial pit.text: An excavation dug to study or sample the composition and structure of the subsurface, usually during a site investigation, soil survey or geological survey; also called a test pit.

regolith.text: A blanket of loose, unconsolidated and varied surface deposits covering solid rock.

saprolite.text: Chemically weathered rock, literally 'rotten rock', formed in the lower zones of soil profiles by deep weathering of the bedrock surface.

rock.text: Any naturally occurring solid mass or aggregate of minerals or mineraloid matter.

sedimentary rock.text: Rock formed by the cementation of mineral or organic particles deposited at the Earth's surface.

limestone.text: A carbonate sedimentary rock made mostly of calcite and aragonite, and the main source of lime.

asteroid regolith.text: The loose surface layer of asteroids, produced by impacts and other surface-altering processes.

icy regolith on titan.text: Loose icy material on Saturn's moon Titan, called regolith because it behaves mechanically like regolith on other bodies.

igneous rock.text: One of the three main rock types, formed by the cooling and solidification of magma or lava.

deep weathering.text: Long-continued chemical weathering that builds thick, deeply weathered regolith over bedrock, the product of a region's long weathering history.

primary mineral.text: A mineral that formed during the original crystallization of its host igneous rock and has not been chemically altered since.

metamorphic rock.text: Rock transformed from an existing rock into a new type by heat and pressure, a process called metamorphism.

grus.text: An accumulation of angular, coarse sand and gravel produced by the granular disintegration of crystalline rocks, especially granitoids, through weathering.

lithology.text: The description of a rock unit's physical characteristics visible at outcrop, in hand or core samples, or under low magnification.

feldspar.text: A group of rock-forming aluminium tectosilicate minerals that also contain cations such as sodium, calcium, potassium or barium.

olivine.text: A magnesium iron silicate mineral, (Mg,Fe)2SiO4, of the nesosilicate type.

plagioclase.text: A continuous solid-solution series of framework silicate minerals within the feldspar group.

biotite.text: A common group of dark phyllosilicate minerals in the mica group, approximately K(Mg,Fe)3AlSi3O10(OH,F)2.

mafic.text: Describing silicate minerals, magmas and igneous rocks rich in magnesium and iron and relatively low in silica.

stone stripe.text: An elongated, unvegetated band of mostly talus-like basalt rock along a hillside or at the base of a cliff; also called a lava stringer.

orthoclase.text: A potassium feldspar, KAlSi3O8, an important tectosilicate mineral of igneous rock.

rock cycle.text: The geological concept describing the transitions, through geologic time, among sedimentary, metamorphic and igneous rock.

parent material.text: The underlying geological material, generally bedrock or a superficial (drift) deposit, in which soil horizons form.

transported parent material.text: Loose, uncemented parent material moved by water, wind, ice or gravity, and classified by its last means of transport.

loess.text: A clastic, predominantly silt-sized sediment formed by the accumulation of wind-blown dust.

superficial deposits.text: Geologically recent, mostly unconsolidated deposits, typically of Quaternary age (less than 2.6 million years old).

alluvium.text: Loose clay, silt, sand or gravel deposited by running water in stream beds, on floodplains, in alluvial fans or similar settings.

colluvium.text: Loose, unconsolidated sediment deposited at the base of hillslopes by rainwash, sheetwash, slow downslope creep or a combination of these.

glacial till.text: Unsorted sediment eroded and carried by a glacier and deposited directly from the ice.

loess plateau.text: A plateau of some 640,000 km2 around the upper and middle reaches of China's Yellow River, covered by loess.

residuum.text: Weathered rock that stays in place rather than being moved by erosion, and in time helps form soil.

loess soils and fertility.text: Soils developed on loess, which tend to be very rich and, under suitable climates, among the most agriculturally productive in the world.

loess–paleosol sequences.text: Stacked loess layers separated by buried soils, studied as archives of past climate and environmental change.

non-glacial loess.text: Loess that originates from deserts, dune fields, playa lakes or volcanic ash rather than from glacial outwash.

eluvial deposits.text: In geology, deposits and soils derived from weathering in place, or from weathering plus gravitational movement or accumulation.

river channel migration.text: The lateral shift of an alluvial river channel across its floodplain over time.

volcanic ash.text: Fragments of rock, mineral crystals and volcanic glass under 2 mm across, produced by volcanic eruptions.

cumulose parent material.text: Organic parent material built up in place from plant residues, such as sphagnum moss, preserved by a high water table or other conditions that slow decay.

glaciofluvial deposits.text: Boulders, gravel, sand, silt and clay from ice sheets or glaciers that meltwater streams have transported, sorted and deposited.

periglacial loess.text: Loess blown from the floodplains of glacial braided rivers that carried meltwater and sediment from melting ice sheets and ice caps.

lacustrine parent material.text: Sediment that settled in lakes, forming a well-sorted, fine-textured parent material rich in silt and clay.

glaciolacustrine deposits.text: Parent material formed from glacier-derived sediment carried into lakes, typically lakes at the ice margin.

marine parent material.text: Material carried by rivers to the sea that sank to the ocean floor and later became a parent material.

volcanic tephra parent material.text: Volcanic ash carried by the wind and settled at various distances from a volcano, the most common volcanic parent material.

lichens and soil formation.text: The part lichens, symbiotic colonies of algae or cyanobacteria and fungi, play in breaking down rock and building and stabilizing soil.

desert varnish.text: An orange-yellow to black coating, about one micrometre thick, on exposed rock surfaces in arid environments.

glacial drift.text: All sediment, from clay to boulders, carried by a glacier and deposited by or from the ice or by its meltwater.

topsoil.text: The upper layer of soil, richest in organic matter and microorganisms, where most of the soil's biological activity takes place.

moraine.text: Any accumulation of unconsolidated glacial debris, often till, in currently or formerly glaciated regions.

outwash plain.text: A plain of glaciofluvial deposits built by meltwater outwash at the end of a glacier; also called a sandur.

spheroidal weathering.text: Chemical weathering of jointed bedrock that produces concentric shells of highly decayed rock within saprolite; also called onion-skin weathering.

subsoil.text: The layer of soil beneath the topsoil, a mix of sand, silt and clay with much less organic matter and humus.

soil morphology.text: The branch of soil science that describes soils technically, above all their physical properties such as texture, colour, structure and consistence.

diagnostic horizon.text: A horizon defined by a set of criteria, whose presence or absence at a given depth is used to assign soils to taxonomic units.

o horizon.text: A surface layer of organic material, built from plant residues not mixed into the mineral soil and not waterlogged for long periods.

a horizon.text: The uppermost mineral horizon, at the surface or below an O horizon, where humified organic matter is intimately mixed with mineral material.

eluviation.text: The removal of soil material from upper layers by water percolating down through the profile.

e horizon.text: A mineral horizon that has lost clay, iron, aluminium, organic matter or a mix of these, leaving a concentration of sand and silt, mostly quartz.

hardpan.text: A dense, largely water-impervious soil layer, usually lying just below the topsoil.

soil profile.text: A vertical face of soil showing its horizons, layers roughly parallel to the surface; formally, one face of a pedon.

cryoturbation.text: Frost churning: the mixing of material from different soil horizons, down to bedrock, by repeated freezing and thawing in permafrost soils.

illuviation.text: The deposition in a lower soil layer of material, called illuvium, washed down by rainwater from a layer above.

b horizon.text: A subsurface mineral horizon, formed below an A, E, H or O horizon, where the original rock structure is largely gone and soil formation has altered or enriched the material.

c horizon.text: A layer below the soil horizons, other than hard bedrock, that is little affected by soil formation and lacks the properties of O, A, E or B horizons.

solum.text: The upper part of a soil, its surface and subsoil layers, that has developed under the same soil-forming conditions.

horizon designation.text: The code of letters and numbers that names each soil horizon: a capital master symbol, often followed by lowercase suffixes, with numbers for discontinuities and subdivisions.

h horizon.text: An organic layer, generally peat, that is saturated with water for long periods or has been artificially drained.

r layer.text: Hard, consolidated bedrock underlying the soil at the base of the profile.

horizon suffixes.text: Lowercase letters added to a master horizon symbol to record particular features or processes of soil formation.

lithologic discontinuity.text: A change in parent material within a soil profile, shown in horizon designations by a numerical prefix.

buried soil horizon.text: A genetic horizon that formed at the surface and was later covered by new mineral material, marked with the suffix b.

transitional horizon.text: A horizon combining the properties of two master horizons, written with both capital letters, the dominant one first, as in AB or BA.

fragipan.text: A diagnostic horizon of USDA soil taxonomy: an altered, dense subsurface layer that restricts water flow and root penetration.

commercial topsoil.text: Soil mixtures sold as topsoil, either natural topsoil mined and conditioned for use or manufactured from minerals, biosolids, compost or paper mill sludge.

ice wedge.text: A crack in the ground holding a narrow wedge of ice up to 3–4 metres long at the surface and reaching several metres down.

horizon boundaries.text: The lower border of a soil horizon, described in the field by how sharp it is (distinctness) and how its shape varies sideways (topography).

claypan.text: A dense, compact, slowly permeable subsoil layer with much more clay than the material above, from which a sharp boundary separates it.

duripan.text: A diagnostic horizon of USDA soil taxonomy in which illuvial silica has cemented the subsoil into a hardpan.

petrocalcic horizon.text: A diagnostic horizon of USDA soil taxonomy and the WRB in which secondary carbonates have cemented the subsoil into a hardpan.

silcrete.text: A hard soil duricrust formed when surface soil, sand and gravel are cemented by dissolved silica.

umbric horizon.text: A thick, dark, organic-rich surface horizon that is acid and low in bases; its name comes from Latin umbra, shade.

ferricrete.text: A hard, erosion-resistant layer of sedimentary rock, usually conglomerate or breccia, cemented into a duricrust by iron oxides.

cutans.text: Changes in soil texture or structure at natural surfaces of particles, pores or peds, caused by illuviation.

pedocal.text: A former class of the zonal soil order: soils of semiarid and arid regions rich in calcium carbonate and low in organic matter.

slickensides in soils.text: In pedology, the polished surfaces of cracks that form in soils with a high proportion of swelling clays.

cambic horizon.text: A diagnostic subsurface horizon showing early pedogenic change, recognized when it does not meet the requirements of any other diagnostic horizon.

tepetate.text: A Mexican term, from Nahuatl tepetlatl, for a horizon hardened by compaction or cementation in volcanic regions of Mexico.

albic horizon.text: A bleached, light-coloured subsurface diagnostic horizon left when soil formation moves clay minerals and oxides downward.

calcic horizon.text: A horizon of secondary carbonate accumulation, above 15% calcium carbonate equivalent and at least 5% more carbonate than the layer below.

epipedon.text: In USDA soil taxonomy, a diagnostic surface horizon, the upper part of the soil.

kandic horizon.text: An argillic horizon whose clays are mainly 1:1 silicate clays, giving it a low cation exchange capacity.

mollic epipedon.text: The fertile, dark surface horizon that is the defining diagnostic feature of Mollisols.

natric horizon.text: An argillic horizon in which large amounts of exchangeable sodium have accumulated.

pedon.text: The imaginary three-dimensional unit of soil large enough to show the full range of properties of a particular soil; a soil profile is one face of it.

soil monolith.text: A soil profile dug from the ground in one piece, without disturbing its layers, and preserved for study or display.

spodic horizon.text: An iron-rich diagnostic subsurface horizon of podzols, where iron and aluminium oxides accumulate with humus.

soil formation.text: The development of soil, also called pedogenesis, as shaped by the effects of place, environment and history.

leaching (pedology).text: The removal of soluble materials from one zone of a soil to another by water moving through the profile.

soil-forming factors.text: The five classic, intertwined influences that govern how a soil develops: parent material, climate, topography, organisms and time.

paleosol.text: An ancient soil that formed in the past.

climate as a soil-forming factor.text: The influence of climate on soil formation, chiefly through effective precipitation (precipitation minus evapotranspiration) and temperature, which set the rates of chemical, physical and biological processes.

organisms as a soil-forming factor.text: The influence of plants, animals, fungi, bacteria and humans on how a soil forms.

time as a soil-forming factor.text: The span over which the other soil-forming factors interact, which shapes how far a soil has developed.

topography as a soil-forming factor.text: The influence of relief (slope, elevation and aspect) on soil formation through its control of runoff, erosion and the formation of the surface profile.

dokuchaev's soil-forming equation.text: Vasily Dokuchaev's 1898 equation expressing soil as a function of climate, organisms and parent material over relative time.

jenny's state equation.text: Hans Jenny's 1941 equation treating soil formation as a function of climate, organisms, relief, parent material, time and further open-ended factors: S = f(cl, o, r, p, t, ...).

catena.text: A series of distinct but co-evolving soils arrayed down a slope, all in the same climate and on the same parent material.

pedoturbation.text: The mixing of material between soil horizons, an important factor in soil formation.

leaching model.text: A hydrological model of how irrigation water leaches dissolved substances, notably salt, from soil, depending on the water regime and the soil's properties.

soil biomantle.text: The organic-rich, bioturbated upper part of a soil, including the topsoil, where most soil organisms live, reproduce and die.

chronosequence.text: A set of sites that share similar attributes but differ in age, used to study change over time.

laterite.text: A soil type rich in iron and aluminium that often forms in hot, wet areas, mostly in the tropics.

sesquioxide.text: An oxide with two atoms of an element for every three of oxygen, such as the iron and aluminium oxides Fe2O3 and Al2O3.

podzolisation.text: An extreme form of leaching that eluviates iron and aluminium sesquioxides from the upper soil.

laterization.text: The prolonged chemical weathering of rock under tropical conditions that produces laterite.

stonelayer.text: A subsurface soil layer dominated by particles coarser than 2 mm that generally mimics the surface topography; also called a stone line.

biorhexistasy.text: A theory of the climatic conditions under which periods of soil formation alternate with periods of soil erosion.

paleoatmosphere reconstruction from pale.text: The use of paleosol chemistry to infer the past composition of the atmosphere, with which soils form in near-constant contact.

paleoclimate reconstruction from paleoso.text: The use of paleosols to gauge the climate they formed in, since rates and styles of weathering depend on climate.

paleosol classification.text: The naming of paleosols, which mostly borrows the orders of USDA soil taxonomy because modern systems fit ancient soils poorly.

paleosol identification.text: The recognition of a fossil or buried soil from criteria such as formation in place on bedrock and up-profile changes consistent with weathering.

pedodiversity.text: The variation of soil properties within an area, usually expressed through soil classes.

soil production function.text: The rate at which bedrock weathers into soil, expressed as a function of soil thickness.

laterite aquifers.text: Thick, porous and slightly permeable laterite layers that hold and yield groundwater, especially in rural tropical areas.

laterite building blocks.text: Laterite cut into blocks while moist and soft, which then harden on exposure to air into a durable building material.

laterite for phosphorus removal.text: The use of iron- and aluminium-rich laterite to remove phosphorus and heavy metals from wastewater.

laterite soils in farming.text: The agricultural behaviour of laterite soils, which are clay-rich but heavily leached.

lateritic ores.text: Metal ores concentrated in laterites, including aluminium, iron, manganese, nickel, copper and gold.

periglaciation.text: The geomorphic processes that result from seasonal freezing and thawing, very often in areas of permafrost.

lessivage.text: The washing of fine clay from the upper to the lower part of a soil by water moving down through the soil matrix; also called argilluviation.

ferrallitisation.text: The process by which rock is changed into a soil of kaolinite clay and sesquioxides, the hydrated oxides of iron and aluminium.

ecological succession.text: The change in species composition of an ecological community over time.

leaching efficiency.text: A leaching-model parameter that departs from unity where salt is unevenly distributed in the soil or the soil structure is irregular.

tree throw.text: A bowl-shaped pit in the subsoil made by a tree, through long root growth or when a toppled tree tears out its rootwad.

argillipedoturbation.text: Soil mixing caused by the shrinking and swelling of smectite clays, sometimes called self-mulching.

stone-line origin debate.text: The long controversy over whether stonelayers in soils formed by geological processes or by soil-forming, largely biological, processes.

biomantles and archaeology.text: The finding that most prehistoric cultural materials lie in the soil biomantle, where bioturbation has moved them out of their original context.

biomixing, biotransfer and biosorting.text: The three overlapping sub-processes of soil bioturbation, which together abrade and reduce particles (particle comminution).

dynamic denudation.text: The sum of all processes acting in the soil biomantle, in which bioturbation and other organic effects are commonly dominant.

cheluviation.text: The process in which metal ions in the upper soil bind with organic ligands into chelates that move downward by eluviation and are then deposited.

soil memory.text: The idea that soil keeps a record of past natural changes, environmental conditions and human activity.

microbial soil memory.text: The ability of soil microbial communities to change their structure, diversity and activity in response to natural or human factors and to keep those changes over time.

polygenetic soil.text: A soil, such as a paleosol, that shows evidence of continued soil development under later conditions.

soil geography.text: The branch of physical geography that deals with how soils are distributed across the terrain.

tropical soils.text: The soils of the humid tropics, most of them strongly leached and poor in nutrients, though some areas are fertile.

grain size.text: The diameter of individual grains of sediment, or of the lithified particles in clastic rocks.

lithosequence.text: A set of soils formed under similar conditions on different parent materials, so that their profiles differ because of the parent material.

soils of australia.text: The soils of the Australian continent, many of them extremely ancient and naturally deficient in phosphorus.

sand.text: A granular material of finely divided mineral particles, defined mainly by grain size: coarser than silt and finer than gravel.

silt.text: A granular material finer than sand and coarser than clay, made mostly of broken quartz grains.

soil separates.text: Set ranges of particle size, sand, silt and clay, into which a soil's mineral particles are sorted.

clay size versus clay minerals.text: The difference between clay as a class of very fine particle sizes and clay as material made of clay minerals, two overlapping but distinct definitions.

plasticity of clay.text: Clay's capacity, when wet, to be moulded into a shape that it then keeps, its defining mechanical property.

usda soil texture classes.text: The twelve named categories into which the USDA groups soils by their percentages of sand, silt and clay.

loam.text: Soil made mostly of sand and silt with a smaller amount of clay.

clay soils in agriculture.text: How a high clay content shapes a soil's value for farming, trading poor drainage against greater fertility.

soil texture triangle.text: A triangular chart whose three sides give percent sand, silt and clay, used to read off a soil's texture class.

texture by feel.text: A qualitative field method that judges a soil's texture by moistening and working a small sample by hand.

shrink–swell capacity.text: The degree to which certain clay minerals in a soil expand when wet and contract when dry.

physical properties of soil.text: The measurable physical traits of a soil, which in falling order of importance for crops are texture, structure, bulk density, porosity, consistency, temperature, colour and resistivity.

gravel.text: A loose aggregation of rock fragments coarser than sand.

soil structure.text: The arrangement of a soil's solid particles and of the pore spaces left between them.

ped.text: A natural aggregate of soil particles, formed by soil-forming processes and separated from neighbouring units by pores or voids.

soil structure types.text: The grouping of soil structure by the shape and arrangement of its peds, with five major classes: platy, prismatic, columnar, blocky and granular.

particle-size distribution.text: A list of values or a mathematical function giving the relative amount, usually by mass, of particles of each size in a granular material.

sieve analysis.text: A procedure that measures the particle size distribution of a granular material by passing it through a stack of progressively finer sieves and weighing what each sieve holds.

hydrometer method.text: A laboratory sedimentation test that estimates a soil's percent sand, silt and clay from how fast dispersed particles settle, based on Stokes' law.

expansive clay.text: A clay soil that swells and shrinks greatly as its water content changes.

international soil texture system.text: The first soil particle-size classification, proposed by Albert Atterberg in 1905 from his studies in southern Sweden.

stokes's law.text: A law giving the drag force on a sphere moving through a viscous fluid at very small Reynolds numbers.

soil consistency.text: The ability of soil to stick to itself or to other objects and to resist deformation and rupture.

x-ray sedimentation.text: A hybrid particle-sizing technique that combines sedimentation with X-ray absorption.

soil gradation.text: An engineering classification of a coarse-grained soil according to the range of particle sizes it contains.

hydrophobic soil.text: A soil whose particles repel water.

atterberg limits.text: A set of critical water contents (the shrinkage, plastic and liquid limits) that mark where a fine-grained soil changes from one state of consistency to another.

unified soil classification system.text: An engineering and geological system that classes soils by texture and grain size, giving each a two-letter symbol.

uscs coarse-grained soil groups.text: The USCS groups for soils with more than half their weight retained on the No. 200 sieve: gravels (G) and sands (S), subdivided by grading and fines content.

krumbein phi scale.text: A logarithmic grain-size scale, created by W. C. Krumbein in 1934 from the Wentworth scale, that expresses size as minus the base-2 logarithm of diameter in millimetres.

sediment sorting.text: The removal of a range of particle sizes from a sediment deposit by an agent such as a river or the wind.

grain-size distribution curve.text: A graph of the cumulative percentage of a sample passing each sieve against sieve size on a logarithmic scale.

friability.text: The tendency of a solid material to break into smaller pieces under stress or contact, especially rubbing.

liquid limit.text: The water content at which a clayey soil passes from behaving as a plastic solid to behaving as a liquid.

plastic limit.text: The water content below which a soil stops behaving as a plastic solid and becomes brittle, so it can no longer be rolled into a thin thread.

liquidity index.text: An index that places a soil's natural water content on the scale between its plastic and liquid limits, LI = (W − PL)/(LL − PL).

plasticity index.text: The span of water contents over which a soil behaves plastically, calculated as the liquid limit minus the plastic limit.

uscs fine-grained soil groups.text: The USCS groups for soils with 50% or more passing the No. 200 sieve, classed as silts (M) or clays (C) by plotting plasticity index against liquid limit.

clay activity.text: The ratio of a soil's plasticity index to its clay-size fraction, used to judge how active its clay is.

laser diffraction particle sizing.text: An optical method that measures particle-size distribution from the way particles, dispersed in a liquid or as dry powder, bend light.

soil aggregation.text: The joining of primary soil particles into larger aggregates through rearrangement, flocculation and cementation.

soil aggregate stability.text: A measure of how well soil aggregates resist breaking apart under forces such as water and wind erosion, shrinking and swelling, and tillage.

shrinkage limit.text: The water content below which further drying no longer makes a soil shrink.

flocculation.text: The drawing together of primary soil particles by inter-particle forces into microscopic clumps called floccules.

tilth.text: The physical condition of a soil, especially how well it suits planting and growing a crop.

soil dispersion.text: The breakdown of soil, especially sodium-rich clay, into separate fine particles that water easily washes away.

soil crust.text: A surface layer of soil, often hardened and platy, that differs from the bulk soil beneath it.

improving soil structure.text: Practices that move soil toward a granular, crumb structure by raising its porosity, organic matter and microbial and faunal activity.

hardsetting soil.text: A soil that loses its structure when wet and sets hard into a structureless mass as it dries.

biological soil crust.text: A living community of organisms forming a crust on the soil surface in arid and semi-arid ecosystems.

aggregate hierarchy.text: The idea that soil aggregates form in levels, larger and less dense aggregates being built from smaller, denser ones.

aggregate stability measurement.text: Tests of how well soil aggregates survive stresses like those from water, wind or machinery, made at different aggregate size scales.

slaking.text: The process by which earth materials, such as soil aggregates, disintegrate and crumble when exposed to moisture.

soil resistivity.text: A measure of how strongly a soil resists the flow of an electric current.

coefficients of uniformity and curvature.text: Two values, Cu and Cc, calculated from grain diameters on a soil's size-distribution curve and compared with published limits to grade a coarse soil.

soil water repellency tests.text: Tests that rate how strongly a soil repels water, usually starting with the time one water drop takes to soak in.

specific surface area.text: The surface area of soil particles relative to their amount, defined as surface area per unit mass.

particle size analysis.text: The collective name for laboratory techniques that measure the size range or mean size of particles in a powder or liquid sample.

agrophysics.text: A science on the border of agronomy and physics that studies agroecosystems with the methods of the physical sciences.

clod.text: A mass of soil formed artificially by mechanical disturbance such as cultivation, as opposed to a naturally formed ped.

porosity.text: The share of a material's total volume taken up by empty spaces, given as a fraction from 0 to 1 or as a percentage.

soil physics.text: The study of the physical properties and processes of soil, covering its solid, liquid and gas phases.

gilgai.text: A microrelief of alternating mounds and depressions on the surface of shrink–swell clay soils.

pipette method.text: A laboratory sedimentation method that measures the proportions of coarse and fine silt in a sample from settling rates given by Stokes' law.

bulk density.text: The mass of a soil or other particulate material divided by the whole volume it occupies, including the spaces between and within its particles.

soil mechanics.text: The branch of soil physics and applied mechanics that describes how soils behave.

soil matrix.text: The solid phase of a soil: the mineral particles and organic matter that make it up.

pore space in soil.text: The part of a soil's volume not filled by its solid mineral and organic particles, which holds the soil's water and air.

soil compaction.text: The densification of soil under applied stress as air is pushed out of the pores between its grains.

soil compaction in agriculture.text: The rise in bulk density, or fall in porosity, of farmland soil under externally or internally applied loads, also called soil structure degradation.

pore water pressure.text: The pressure of the groundwater held in the pores between the particles of a soil or rock.

void ratio.text: The ratio of the volume of voids, filled with gas or liquid, to the volume of solids in a soil or other porous material.

effective stress.text: The part of the total stress in a soil that is carried by the solid skeleton rather than by the pore water.

seepage.text: The movement of water through soil.

shear strength (soil).text: The largest shear stress a soil can sustain before it fails.

soil liquefaction.text: The sudden loss of strength and stiffness in a saturated or partly saturated cohesionless soil under stress such as earthquake shaking, so that the solid behaves like a liquid.

cohesion (geology).text: The part of a soil's or rock's shear strength that does not depend on friction between particles.

soil consolidation.text: The gradual change in a soil's volume in response to a change in pressure, as water is slowly squeezed out of or drawn into its pores.

capillary action in soil.text: The rise of water above the water table into the small pores of a soil, held there by surface tension under negative pressure.

geotechnical engineering.text: The branch of civil engineering concerned with the engineering behaviour of earth materials.

quicksand.text: A colloid of fine granular material, such as sand, silt or clay, and water that forms when saturated loose sand is agitated and loses its strength.

angle of repose.text: The steepest angle, measured from the horizontal, at which a granular material can be piled without slumping.

oedometer test.text: A laboratory test that measures a soil's consolidation properties by loading a sample and recording how it deforms.

overburden pressure.text: The pressure at a given depth caused by the weight of the overlying material, also called lithostatic pressure or vertical stress.

specific storage and storativity.text: The volume of water that a unit volume of saturated aquifer releases from storage when the hydraulic head falls by one unit.

specific weight.text: A material's weight per unit volume, also called unit weight, equal to its density multiplied by gravitational acceleration.

relative density.text: A measure of how densely packed a sand or gravel is, comparing its void ratio with its loosest and densest possible states.

soil pore size classes.text: A widely used grouping of soil pores by diameter, after Brewer (1964), from macropores down to cryptopores, each class playing a different part for water and life.

groundwater-related subsidence.text: The sinking of land caused by unsustainable pumping of groundwater.

iupac pore size classification.text: A standard division of pores, set by IUPAC in 1985, into micropores under 2 nm, mesopores of 2 to 50 nm and macropores over 50 nm across.

measuring porosity.text: Laboratory and imaging techniques that find the pore volume of a sample, either directly or from the fluid it takes up.

porosity and hydraulic conductivity.text: The loose link between how much pore space a material has and how easily water flows through it.

effects of soil compaction.text: The on-site and off-site consequences of compaction for soil air and water, plants, soil life, climate, water bodies and food supply.

soil porosity and texture.text: The pattern by which surface-soil porosity falls as particle size rises, because fine-textured soils build aggregates.

types of porosity.text: Categories that distinguish pore systems by their origin and by whether fluids can flow through them, such as primary, secondary, effective and dual porosity.

sand boil.text: A spot where water under pressure wells up through a bed of sand or mud, looking as if it were boiling.

compaction in construction.text: Deliberately densifying soil with heavy equipment so that it can support foundations, roads, walkways and retaining structures.

compaction avoidance and mitigation.text: Biological, chemical and technical measures, backed by policy, that prevent soil compaction or help compacted soil recover.

mechanism of soil compaction.text: How pressure on soil is taken up by closer particle contacts, shrinking the voids and squeezing out water and air, and which soil properties make that easier or harder.

dilatancy.text: The change in volume of a granular material when it is sheared; dense packings expand rather than compress.

thixotropy.text: A time-dependent shear-thinning property: a material that is thick at rest flows more easily when shaken or stressed, then takes time to thicken again.

unsaturated soil conditions.text: The state of a soil whose water content is below its porosity, so that its pores hold air as well as water.

matric suction.text: The negative pore water pressure of unsaturated soil above the water table, caused by surface tension in the pores and defined as pore air pressure minus pore water pressure.

measuring soil bulk density.text: Finding a soil's bulk density from an undisturbed core of known volume, weighed moist and again after oven drying.

porous medium.text: A material containing pores, with a solid skeleton called the matrix and pores usually filled with a liquid or gas.

critical state theory.text: A theory of soil shearing that identifies a distinct strength, the critical state, at which soil keeps shearing at constant volume.

drained shear strength.text: The shear strength of a soil when pore pressures generated by shearing can dissipate as it shears, or when the soil is dry.

factors controlling shear strength.text: The soil properties and conditions that govern a soil's stress–strain behaviour and so its shear strength: composition, initial state, structure and loading.

steady state soil mechanics.text: A refinement of the critical state idea in which soil deforms continuously at constant volume, effective stress, shear stress and velocity, with a statistically steady grain structure.

undrained shear strength.text: The shear strength a soil shows when it is sheared faster than the pore water pressure generated by shearing can dissipate.

particle density.text: The density of the solid particles of a soil or other material alone, not counting the voids between them.

bearing capacity.text: The capacity of soil to support loads applied to the ground, such as a foundation, without failing in shear.

resin-impregnation imaging.text: A way of imaging soil pores by filling an undisturbed core with fluorescent resin, then grinding and photographing it layer by layer.

soil crack modeling.text: Ways of measuring and simulating cracks in soil, which shape infiltration, gas exchange and the effects of compaction.

causes of agricultural compaction.text: The natural and human drivers of compaction on farmland, chiefly heavy machinery, tillage and livestock trampling.

soil mass–volume relations.text: The set of quantities that describe the proportions of air, water and solids in a soil, by volume and by mass.

mohr–coulomb theory.text: A mathematical model of how materials fail under combined shear and normal stress, used to define the shear strength of soils and rocks at different effective stresses.

apparent cohesion.text: Cohesion-like strength in remoulded soft clay that comes from pore water suction and friction rather than from chemical bonds between particles.

compression index.text: The change in a soil's void ratio for each tenfold increase in effective stress, a measure of how compressible it is during consolidation.

origins of consolidation theory.text: The first modern theories of soil consolidation, proposed in the 1920s by Karl Terzaghi and Paul Fillunger along two very different lines.

overconsolidation.text: The state of a soil whose load has been removed, so that it now carries less than the highest stress it has ever borne.

secondary consolidation.text: The slow change in a soil's volume at constant effective stress, also called creep or secondary compression, seen mainly in soils rich in organic matter.

terzaghi's principle.text: The principle that a load on a porous material such as soil is opposed partly by the fluid pressure in its pores, so that its measurable responses follow changes in effective stress.

specific yield.text: The fraction of a material's bulk volume that drains out under gravity, also called drainable porosity.

geotechnical investigation.text: Site exploration that gathers the physical properties of the soil and rock under and beside a site, to design earthworks and foundations.

penetrometer.text: A device that tests the strength of a material, such as soil, by measuring how far a probe sinks into it.

identifying soil compaction.text: Field, laboratory and remote-sensing methods for detecting compacted soil, used in combination because no single method suffices.

pore structure.text: The porosity, pore sizes, pore-size distribution and pore shapes, roughness and tortuosity that together describe the pores of a porous medium.

trampling.text: Repeated walking on the ground by humans or animals.

representative elementary volume.text: The smallest volume over which a measurement gives a value representative of the whole material.

soil strength.text: The resistance a soil offers to deformation, measured in the field as its resistance to a penetrometer.

tortuosity.text: The ratio of a path's actual length to the straight-line distance between its ends, used to predict transport through porous media such as soils.

infiltration.text: The process by which water on the ground surface enters the soil.

soil moisture.text: The water held in a soil, measured by volume or by weight.

permeability (porous media).text: A measure of how readily a fluid, gas or liquid, flows through a porous material such as rock or soil, usually written k.

water content.text: The quantity of water contained in a material such as soil, where it is called soil moisture.

drainage.text: The natural or artificial removal of surface and subsurface water from an area that has too much of it.

hydraulic conductivity.text: A property of soils, rocks and other porous materials that describes how easily a fluid, usually water, moves through their pores or fractures; written K, in metres per second.

water potential.text: The potential energy of water per unit volume, compared with pure water under reference conditions.

darcy's law.text: An equation that describes the flow of a fluid through a porous medium.

soil water retention.text: A soil's ability to take in water and hold much of it against the pull of gravity.

water retention curve.text: The relationship between a soil's water content and its soil water potential.

water table.text: The upper surface of the zone of saturation, the depth below which the ground is saturated with groundwater.

macropore.text: In soil, a cavity larger than 75 μm.

hydraulic head.text: A measure of a liquid's pressure, normalized by its specific weight, plus its elevation above a datum, expressed as a length.

infiltrometer.text: A device that measures the rate at which water infiltrates soil or another porous medium.

factors affecting infiltration.text: The rainfall, soil and surface conditions that control how fast water enters a soil.

depression storage capacity.text: The ability of an area of land to hold water in its pits and depressions so that it does not flow away.

infiltration equations.text: Methods for estimating the volume and rate of water infiltrating a soil.

plant water uptake.text: The ways plants draw soil water into their roots, mainly by the pull of transpiration and partly by osmosis.

permanent wilting point.text: The lowest amount of soil water a plant needs in order not to wilt.

evapotranspiration.text: The combined movement of water from the Earth's surface, open water, ice, bare soil and plants, into the atmosphere by evaporation and transpiration.

saturated and unsaturated flow.text: The two modes of water movement in soil: saturated flow, pushed by gravity and pressure in wet soil, and unsaturated flow, pulled by capillarity toward drier soil.

pedotransfer function.text: A predictive function that estimates soil properties from soil survey data.

transpiration.text: The movement of water through a plant and its evaporation from aerial parts such as leaves, stems and flowers.

soil moisture measurement.text: Estimating soil water content in place, with probes in the soil or by remote sensing, instead of drying samples.

impervious surface.text: Ground covered by water-resistant materials such as asphalt, concrete, brick or stone, mainly pavements and rooftops.

time-domain reflectometry.text: A technique that sends an electrical pulse along a line and reads its reflections; in soil science it is used to measure the water content of soil and other porous media.

soil moisture sensor.text: A device that estimates the volumetric water content of soil, usually indirectly from some other soil property.

waterlogging.text: The saturation of soil with water, so that its air phase is restricted and anaerobic conditions prevail much of the time.

capacitance probe.text: A sensor that uses capacitance to measure the dielectric permittivity of the surrounding soil, and from it the soil's water content.

watertable control.text: The practice of holding the water table at a chosen height by means of drainage.

agricultural land drainage.text: Removing excess water from farmland, such as wetland soils or fields waterlogged for short spells, so that crops are not damaged.

matric potential.text: The part of water potential that comes from water's attraction to solid particles, such as clay or sand in soil, and the menisci it forms between them.

hydrology.text: The scientific study of the movement, distribution and management of water on Earth, including the water cycle and water resources.

horton's equation.text: An empirical formula, named after Robert E. Horton, in which infiltration starts at an initial rate and declines exponentially with time.

agricultural drainage systems.text: Systems that drain water on or in the soil to improve crop production, combining stormwater, erosion and water table control.

kostiakov equation.text: An empirical infiltration equation that assumes the intake rate declines over time as a power function.

geotextile drain filters.text: Synthetic fabrics used in drains to hold back fine soil particles while letting water through, so the drain does not clog.

sustainable urban drainage.text: Drainage designed to imitate the natural flow of water more closely than traditional piped systems.

soil suction and pf.text: Soil suction is the negative of soil water potential, the force needed to pull water out of soil; pF is the common logarithm of suction in centimetres of water.

tile drainage.text: An agricultural drainage system of buried pipes that removes excess subsurface water from fields, leaving air space in the soil and firm ground for machinery.

green–ampt method.text: An infiltration model, named after Green and Ampt, that estimates infiltration from soil suction head, porosity, hydraulic conductivity and time.

transpiration ratio.text: A measure of water use efficiency: the water a plant transpires divided by the dry weight of the harvested plant.

disc permeameter.text: A field instrument that measures water infiltration into soil under tension, giving in situ saturated and unsaturated hydraulic properties.

water balance.text: The principle that inflows to any water system equal its outflows plus the change in storage over a time interval.

bioclogging.text: The blocking of soil pores by microbial cells and their byproducts, such as extracellular polymeric substance.

ecohydrology.text: An interdisciplinary field studying how water and ecological systems interact.

saltmod.text: A computer program that predicts the salinity of soil moisture, groundwater and drainage water, the water table depth and drain discharge in irrigated farmland.

constant-head test.text: A simple, inexpensive laboratory test of hydraulic conductivity in which water flows through a soil specimen under a steady head.

falling-head test.text: A laboratory test of hydraulic conductivity in which a saturated soil sample drains with no water added, so the head declines over time.

field permeability tests.text: Measurements of hydraulic conductivity made in place in the field rather than on samples in a laboratory.

augerhole method.text: A slug test that measures hydraulic conductivity below a shallow water table from the rate at which water refills an auger hole.

hazen's formula.text: Allen Hazen's empirical formula for approximating hydraulic conductivity from a grain-size analysis.

hydraulic anisotropy.text: The condition of a soil layer or aquifer whose horizontal and vertical hydraulic conductivity differ considerably.

transmissivity.text: A measure of how much water a soil layer or aquifer can transmit horizontally, as toward a pumping well.

moisture stress.text: A stress on a plant when the water in its tissues falls below optimal levels, because transpiration outpaces water uptake by the roots.

agricultural drought.text: A condition in which soil is too dry to sustain reliable plant growth.

degree of saturation.text: A measure, used in soil mechanics and petroleum engineering, of how fully a material's pore space is filled with water.

permeability of soils.text: A soil's capacity to let water pass, which depends on particle size, impurities in the water, void ratio, degree of saturation, adsorbed water, entrapped air and organic material.

oven-dry method.text: The direct measurement of water content by drying a sample in an oven and comparing its weight before and after.

satellite soil moisture sensing.text: Estimating surface soil moisture from satellites with microwaves, using the large contrast in dielectric properties between wet and dry soil.

percolation test.text: A field test of how fast soil absorbs water, made before building a septic drain field or infiltration basin.

forchheimer equation.text: An extension of Darcy's law that adds an inertial term for fast flow through porous media, where flow no longer varies linearly with pressure.

drainage equation.text: An equation relating the depth and spacing of parallel subsurface drains to the depth of the water table and the depth and hydraulic conductivity of the soil.

drainage research.text: The study of agricultural drainage systems and their effects, aimed at finding the best system design.

sorptivity.text: A measure of a porous medium's capacity to absorb or release liquid by capillarity, a term introduced by John Philip in 1957.

osmotic potential of soil water.text: The part of water potential lowered by dissolved solutes; with pure water set at zero, it can never be positive.

soil moisture and climate.text: The link between soil water and climate: soil moisture shapes a soil's thermal properties and the persistence of surface temperature and rainfall.

throughflow.text: Lateral, unsaturated flow of water through the soil zone, typically in a permeable layer lying over a less permeable one.

darcy (unit).text: A unit of permeability, with the millidarcy as its thousandth, named after Henry Darcy.

soil moisture active passive.text: A NASA satellite that measures soil moisture and its freeze-thaw state across the planet.

van genuchten model.text: An equation that describes the shape of a soil's water retention curve.

plinthite.text: An iron-rich, humus-poor mixture of clay with quartz and other minerals that forms as a redoximorphic feature in highly weathered soils.

mariotte's bottle.text: A device that delivers a constant rate of flow from a closed bottle or tank.

macropore network.text: The linked system of a soil's macropores, irregular in shape, size and roughness, whose geometry shapes water movement, aeration and root growth.

potential evapotranspiration.text: The water a crop, soil or ecosystem would evaporate and transpire if water were not limited.

soil-plant-atmosphere continuum.text: The unbroken pathway along which water moves from the soil, through plants, into the atmosphere.

hydropedology.text: An emerging field joining soil science and hydrology that studies the interface between the pedosphere and the hydrosphere.

natural impervious area.text: Land usually classed as pervious that can still yield a substantial amount of surface runoff in small and large storms.

total impervious area.text: The share of an area covered by impervious surfaces, given as a fraction from zero to one or as a percentage.

wilting.text: The loss of rigidity of a plant's non-woody parts when turgor pressure in its cells falls towards zero for lack of water.

penman–monteith equation.text: An equation that estimates evapotranspiration from meteorological data in place of direct measurement.

soil inference system.text: A knowledge base, proposed by McBratney et al. (2002), that infers soil properties to fill digital soil databases.

hydraulic gradient.text: The change in hydraulic head between measurement points along a flow path.

double-ring infiltrometer.text: An infiltrometer with an inner ring and a larger outer ring around it, which keeps the flow from the inner ring one-dimensional.

neutron probe.text: A device that measures the quantity of water in soil.

bound water.text: An extremely thin layer of water, a few molecules thick, held on mineral surfaces.

pressure head.text: The height of a liquid column corresponding to the pressure the liquid exerts at its base, expressed as a length.

soil moisture zone.text: The depth of soil from which plant roots draw water, often called the root zone.

frequency domain sensor.text: An instrument for measuring soil moisture in which the operating frequency of an oscillating circuit depends on the dielectric constant of the soil around it.

water retention hysteresis.text: The dependence of a soil's water content at a given matric potential on whether the soil is wetting or drying, that is, on its saturation history.

preferential flow.text: Rapid drainage of water under gravity along connected macropores, crevices, and root and worm channels in soil.

kozeny–carman equation.text: A relation giving the pressure drop of a fluid flowing through a packed bed of solids, and from it the bed's permeability.

eddy covariance.text: A micrometeorological technique that computes vertical turbulent fluxes of gases, heat and water vapour from high-frequency wind and concentration data.

priestley–taylor equation.text: A simplified substitute for the Penman–Monteith equation that needs only radiation observations.

reference evapotranspiration.text: The water a standard, well-watered grass surface would lose under current temperature, humidity, wind and solar radiation, written ET0.

groundwater recharge.text: The downward movement of water from the surface to groundwater, also called deep drainage or deep percolation.

field capacity.text: The water a soil still holds after excess water has drained away and downward movement has slowed.

available water capacity.text: The amount of water a soil profile can store and make available to growing crops.

crop coefficient.text: A plant property used to predict evapotranspiration, most simply the ratio of a crop's evapotranspiration to that of a reference crop, Kc.

artificial groundwater recharge.text: Recharge engineered by people, routing rainwater or reclaimed water into the subsurface.

irrigation scheduling.text: The process irrigation managers use to decide how often and for how long to water.

standard soil water contents.text: Four reference water contents routinely measured in soil science, saturation, field capacity, permanent wilting point and residual water, each tied to a suction.

groundwater.text: Water held beneath the Earth's surface in the pore spaces of soil and rock and in rock fractures.

depression-focused recharge.text: Recharge in which rain falling fairly evenly over an area reaches groundwater mainly beneath surface depressions where runoff gathers.

percolation.text: The downward drainage of water through a soil after the soil has absorbed it.

aquifer.text: An underground layer of permeable, porous or fractured rock, or of unconsolidated gravel, sand or silt, that holds and yields water.

hydrogeology.text: The branch of geology dealing with the distribution and movement of groundwater in soil and rock, mainly in aquifers.

lysimeter.text: A soil-filled container, usually a cylinder, used to study how water and dissolved substances move through soil.

moisture equivalent.text: The percentage of water a soil retains against a centrifugal force 1000 times gravity, proposed in 1910 as a measure of field capacity for fine-textured soils.

confined and unconfined aquifers.text: The division of aquifers by whether an impermeable layer lies directly above them (confined) or their upper boundary is the water table (unconfined).

management allowed depletion.text: The percentage of available soil water that can be used up before plants become stressed.

soil water balance method.text: An irrigation scheduling method, also called the checkbook method, that tracks the water in the soil like a bank account.

groundwater flow equation.text: The equation describing the movement of groundwater through a porous medium, known in mathematics as the diffusion equation.

vadose zone.text: The unsaturated zone between the land surface and the water table, where water in the pores is below atmospheric pressure.

subsurface flow.text: The flow of water beneath the Earth's surface as part of the water cycle.

ecological effects of tile drainage.text: The effects of widespread tile drainage on wetlands, rivers and water quality.

non-limiting water range.text: The range of soil water content within which limits to plant growth from water potential, aeration and soil strength are minimal.

capillary fringe.text: The layer just above a water table into which groundwater rises by capillary action to fill the pores.

tensiometer.text: An instrument that measures the matric potential, or moisture tension, of water in unsaturated soil.

richards equation.text: An equation describing the movement of water in unsaturated soils, published by Lorenzo A. Richards in 1931.

soil moisture velocity equation.text: An equation for the speed at which water moves down through unsaturated soil under the combined pull of gravity and capillarity.

groundwater recharge estimation.text: The methods used to estimate how much water reaches the water table, which no widely applicable method can measure directly and accurately.

finite water-content vadose zone flow me.term: Finite water-content vadose zone flow method
finite water-content vadose zone flow me.text: A one-dimensional alternative to the numerical solution of Richards' equation for simulating water movement in unsaturated soils.

agricultural hydrology.text: The study of the water balance components involved in agricultural water management, especially irrigation and drainage.

phreatic zone.text: The saturated zone below the water table, in which all pores and fractures are filled with water.

interflow.text: Lateral movement of water through the unsaturated zone that returns to the surface or enters a stream.

advection.text: The transport of a substance or quantity by the bulk motion of a fluid.

contaminant transport in groundwater.text: The movement of dissolved contaminants with moving groundwater, studied by contaminant hydrogeology.

irrigation and drainage requirements.text: Calculating how much water a field needs from irrigation, and must lose through drains or wells, from its water balances.

fingered flow.text: Uneven downward flow of water through unsaturated soil in narrow 'gravity fingers'.

unsaturated hydraulic conductivity.text: The hydraulic conductivity of a soil that is not saturated, which depends on its water content.

hydrodynamic dispersion.text: The spreading of dissolved contaminants away from the mean path of the groundwater carrying them, caused by small-scale heterogeneity and uneven velocities in the porous medium.

retardation by adsorption.text: The slowing of a contaminant's average movement relative to groundwater because it adsorbs to the soil, measured by a retardation factor.

convection–diffusion equation.text: A parabolic partial differential equation for a quantity moved by both diffusion and convection (advection).

molecular diffusion of solutes.text: The random thermal movement of molecules that carries solutes from high to low concentration.

soil gas.text: The gases filling the air spaces between soil particles, also called the soil atmosphere.

dye tracing.text: A method of tracking flows by adding dye to a liquid as a tracer.

vadose zone transport models.text: Computer models that simulate water flow and solute transport in unsaturated soil by solving the Richards equation numerically.

colloid-facilitated transport.text: Transport in which colloidal particles carry contaminants through surface water and groundwater.

soil temperature.text: How warm or cold a soil is, set by the balance between the energy it absorbs and the energy it loses.

gas diffusion in soil.text: The net movement of gas molecules through soil pores from higher to lower concentration, the main way soil air exchanges with the atmosphere.

soil aeration.text: The exchange of gases between soil and atmosphere, and the means of improving it.

soil air composition.text: The make-up of the soil atmosphere: similar to the air above, but richer in carbon dioxide and water vapour.

frost line.text: The depth to which groundwater in the soil is expected to freeze, also called frost depth or freezing depth.

frost heaving.text: The upward swelling of soil in freezing weather as ice grows toward the surface from the freezing front.

needle ice.text: Needle-shaped columns of ice that grow from groundwater at the soil surface, usually on cold nights.

soil thermal properties.text: The properties that govern how energy, mostly heat, moves through soil by radiation, conduction and convection, a part of soil physics used in engineering, climatology and agriculture.

permafrost.text: Soil, rock or underwater sediment that stays continuously below 0 °C for two years or more.

ice lens.text: A body of ice that grows where moisture diffusing through soil or rock collects in one zone, usually parallel to the surface.

patterned ground.text: Distinct, often symmetrical geometric patterns formed by the deformation of ground material in periglacial regions.

frost-heave landforms.text: Raised-ground features made by frost heaving in circles, polygons and stripes, called palsas in organic soils such as peat and lithalsas in mineral soils.

frost-susceptible soil.text: Soil whose pore sizes and particle surface area promote capillary flow, so that it can feed ice lenses and heave when it freezes.

premelting and thermal regelation.text: Thin films of liquid water that persist on ice below freezing and let fine soil particles migrate through ice toward warmer soil.

soil gas surveys.text: The use of soil gases in research on microseepage, earthquakes and gas exchange between soil and atmosphere.

lithalsa.text: A frost-raised mound in permafrost areas with mineral-rich soils, where a perennial ice lens has grown within the soil.

albedo.text: The fraction of sunlight a surface reflects, on a scale from 0 (absorbs everything) to 1 (reflects everything).

microclimate.text: Local conditions in the near-surface layer, covering the air just above a surface and the shallow soil and water below, that differ persistently from the surroundings.

fick's laws of diffusion.text: Two laws, posited by Adolf Fick in 1855, that describe diffusion: flux is proportional to the concentration gradient, and concentration changes with time as a result.

core and spike aeration.text: Mechanical aeration that punctures the soil with spikes or removes cores about 1 in × 2 in (25 mm × 51 mm) to improve gas exchange.

soil heat capacity.text: The energy needed to raise the temperature of soil by 1 °C, its specific heat.

frost boil.text: A small circular mound of fresh soil, also called a mud boil or mud circle, formed by frost action and cryoturbation.

linear aeration.text: An aeration method that cuts grooves into soil or turf so that water and amendments penetrate and are retained in the right amounts.

ice segregation.text: The growth of ice lenses where moisture moving through soil or rock collects in one zone, wedging the material apart.

thermal remote sensing of soil.text: Detecting variations in soil thermal properties from satellites and aircraft, mainly with thermal infrared sensors.

seasonal frost.text: Ground that freezes each winter and thaws again, one of three kinds of frozen ground classed by how long they stay frozen, beside permafrost and pereletok.

soil thermal conductivity.text: The ability of soil to conduct heat, measured in W·m−1·K−1.

thermal diffusivity.text: A material's thermal conductivity divided by its density and specific heat capacity, measuring how fast heat spreads through it, in m2/s.

soil heat flux.text: The rate at which heat energy moves through soil in response to a temperature difference between two points.

thermal effusivity.text: A material's ability to exchange heat with its surroundings, the square root of its thermal conductivity times its volumetric heat capacity.

fourier's law.text: The law of heat conduction: the rate of heat flow through a material is proportional to the negative temperature gradient and to the area it crosses.

heat equation.text: A partial differential equation, first developed by Joseph Fourier in 1822, that models how temperature in a body changes through time as heat spreads.

heat probe method.text: In-situ measurement of soil thermal properties with needle probes that heat the soil and record its temperature response.

thermal lag.text: The damping and delay of temperature changes with depth in the ground, so that deeper soil reaches its highs and lows later and less sharply.

bowen's reaction series.text: The sequence in which common silicate minerals crystallize from a cooling basaltic magma, summarized by the petrologist Norman L. Bowen.

ground heat storage.text: Using the ground as a long-term store of heat, carrying solar energy from summer to winter for ground source heat pumps.

ground source heat pump.text: A heating and cooling system for buildings that moves heat to or from the ground, using the near-constant temperature of the earth through the seasons.

zeolite.text: A group of microporous, crystalline aluminosilicate minerals widely used as adsorbents and catalysts.

goldich dissolution series.text: A ranking of how fast common igneous minerals weather at Earth's surface, with minerals formed at higher temperatures and pressures less stable than those formed at lower ones.

volcanic glass.text: The amorphous, non-crystalline product of rapidly cooled magma.

glauconite.text: A green iron potassium phyllosilicate of the mica group, very friable and with very low resistance to weathering.

jarosite.text: A basic hydrous sulfate of potassium and ferric iron, KFe3(SO4)2(OH)6, formed by the oxidation of iron sulfides.

birnessite.text: A hydrous manganese dioxide mineral, nominally MnO2·nH2O, the main manganese mineral at Earth's surface.

pedogenic carbonate.text: Carbonate that forms in place within a soil, as opposed to carbonate inherited from the bedrock or parent material.

soil mineralogy.text: The study of the minerals in soil, one of the branches, with soil physics, chemistry and biology, through which soil processes are studied quantitatively.

powder diffraction.text: A technique that uses X-ray, neutron or electron diffraction on powdered or microcrystalline samples to characterize the structure of materials.

schwertmannite.text: An iron oxyhydroxysulfate mineral, ideally Fe8O8(OH)6(SO4)·nH2O, usually seen as brownish-yellow crusts.

x-ray fluorescence.text: The emission of characteristic X-rays from a material excited by high-energy X-rays or gamma rays, whose energies and intensities reveal which elements are present and in what amounts.

electron probe microanalysis.text: A technique that bombards small volumes of a solid with an electron beam and reads the emitted X-rays to determine its chemical composition non-destructively.
