fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy.text: A technique that records the infrared absorption or emission spectrum of a solid, liquid or gas over a wide range of wavelengths at once.

selective extraction of iron oxides.text: Chemical extractions used in soil analysis to dissolve particular iron- and aluminium-bearing mineral phases selectively so they can be measured.

heavy mineral.text: A mineral denser than 2.9 g/cm3, usually one of the dense minor components of siliciclastic sediments.

environmental magnetism.text: The study of how climate, sediment transport, pollution and other environmental influences affect magnetic minerals, using their magnetic properties as proxies.

soil chemistry.text: The study of the chemical characteristics of soil.

clay mineral.text: A hydrous aluminium phyllosilicate: a sheet-structured silicate that may also carry iron, magnesium, alkali metals and other cations.

mica.text: A group of sheet silicate minerals whose crystals split easily into thin, elastic plates, a property called perfect basal cleavage.

goethite.text: An iron(III) oxide-hydroxide mineral, the α form of FeO(OH), found in soils and other low-temperature settings such as sediment.

colloid.text: A mixture in which microscopically small insoluble particles are dispersed throughout another substance.

tetrahedral and octahedral sheets.text: The two kinds of sheet that build every clay mineral: one of corner-sharing silica tetrahedra, and one of small cations such as aluminium or magnesium each surrounded by six oxygens.

1:1 and 2:1 clay minerals.text: The basic division of clay minerals by how their sheets stack: one tetrahedral and one octahedral sheet per layer in 1:1 clays, an octahedral sheet between two tetrahedral sheets in 2:1 clays.

diatomaceous earth.text: A soft, siliceous sedimentary rock, also called diatomite or kieselgur, that crumbles into a fine white to off-white powder.

vermiculite.text: A hydrous 2:1 phyllosilicate clay mineral that expands greatly when heated.

kaolinite.text: A common 1:1 clay mineral with the composition Al2Si2O5(OH)4, also called kaolin.

illite.text: A group of closely related, non-expanding 2:1 clay minerals, also called hydromica, structurally close to muscovite.

gibbsite.text: A mineral form of aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)3.

hematite.text: A common iron oxide mineral, Fe2O3, widely found in rocks and soils.

soil colloids.text: The microscopically small particles in soil, chiefly clay and humus, whose charged surfaces hold and exchange ions with the soil water.

bauxite.text: A sedimentary rock with a relatively high aluminium content, the world's main source of aluminium.

environmental soil chemistry.text: The part of soil chemistry that studies how contaminants are released into soil and what becomes of them there.

soil chemistry laboratory methods.text: The laboratory techniques soil chemists use to study reactions in samples taken from undisturbed horizons, run with replicated treatments and controls.

chlorite (clay mineral).text: A chemically varied group of 2:1 clay minerals whose layers are bound by a positively charged hydrated magnesium sheet.

zeta potential.text: The electrical potential at the slipping plane around a dispersed particle, the boundary between fluid that moves with the particle and fluid that does not.

ferrihydrite.text: A widespread, poorly crystalline hydrous iron(III) oxyhydroxide mineral that exists only as fine-grained nanoparticles.

clay hypothesis of the origin of life.term: Clay hypothesis of the origin of life
clay hypothesis of the origin of life.text: The idea, proposed by Graham Cairns-Smith in 1985, that complex organic molecules arose on non-organic, replicating silicate crystal surfaces in water.

clay mineral identification.text: Laboratory tests that confirm and quantify clay minerals, using glycol adsorption, cation exchange capacity, X-ray diffraction, differential thermal analysis and chemical analysis.

fougèrite.text: A naturally occurring green rust mineral, a layered double hydroxide of ferrous and ferric iron, described only relatively recently.

colloidal stability.text: The ability of colloidal particles to stay suspended instead of clumping, which depends on the forces between them.

allophane.text: An amorphous to poorly crystalline hydrous aluminium silicate clay mineraloid.

imogolite.text: An aluminium silicate clay mineral, Al2SiO3(OH)4, made of a network of tiny nanotubes.

palygorskite.text: A fibrous magnesium aluminium clay mineral, also called attapulgite, with the formula (Mg,Al)2Si4O10(OH)·4(H2O).

vermiculite in horticulture.text: The use of heat-expanded vermiculite in potting mixes, seed raising and garden soils to hold water, air and nutrients for plants.

particle aggregation.text: The sticking together of particles dispersed in a liquid into irregular flocs or agglomerates, which destabilizes a colloid.

dlvo theory.text: A quantitative theory of colloid stability that sums van der Waals attraction and electrical double-layer repulsion between charged surfaces in a liquid.

kaolinite formation in soils.text: The crystallization of kaolinite from silica and aluminium in solution at ordinary temperature and pressure, as happens in soils.

halloysite.text: An aluminosilicate clay mineral of the kaolinite group, with the formula Al2Si2O5(OH)4.

amorphous clays.text: Young mixtures of silica and alumina in soil that have not yet had time to form regular crystals.

clay mineral x-ray diffraction.text: Identifying clay minerals by passing X-rays through oriented samples and measuring the spacing of their stacked silicate layers.

iron oxides.text: Compounds of iron and oxygen, together with the related ferric oxyhydroxides such as rust.

peptization.text: Turning a settled precipitate back into a colloid by shaking it with a suitable electrolyte, a peptizing agent, so that the solid particles are suspended again.

sepiolite.text: A soft, white, fibrous magnesium silicate clay mineral, Mg4Si6O15(OH)2·6H2O, also known as meerschaum.

hydrous oxides.text: Inorganic compounds of a metal, hydroxide and weakly bound water.

lepidocrocite.text: An iron oxide-hydroxide mineral, γ-FeO(OH), also called esmeraldite or hydrohematite.

maghemite.text: A ferrimagnetic iron oxide, γ-Fe2O3, with the formula of hematite but the spinel structure of magnetite.

limonite.text: An iron ore made of a variable mixture of hydrated iron(III) oxide-hydroxides.

measuring specific surface area.text: Determining a material's surface area per unit mass, most often by gas adsorption with the BET method.

isomorphous substitution.text: The replacement, while a clay forms, of cations in its crystal structure by others of lower valence, which leaves the clay a permanent negative charge.

smectite.text: A group of swelling 2:1 clay minerals, mainly montmorillonite, that take water and cations between their layers.

montmorillonite.text: A soft 2:1 clay mineral of the smectite group, with an alumina sheet between two silica sheets and a water content that varies.

bentonite.text: An absorbent swelling clay made mostly of montmorillonite, in either its sodium or its calcium form.

interlayer cations and clay swelling.text: How the cations held between the layers of 2:1 clays govern how much the clay swells or shrinks as it gains or loses water.

clay mineral weathering sequence.text: The change in a soil's dominant clay minerals as weathering and leaching intensify, from 2:1 clays such as montmorillonite through kaolinite to iron and aluminium oxides.

sesquioxide clays.text: Old, highly leached soil clays made of oxides and hydroxides of iron, aluminium and titanium, left after heavy rainfall removes most of the silica from alumino-silica clays.

fuller's earth.text: Any of various clays used as an absorbent, filter or bleaching agent.

bentonite amendment of degraded soils.text: Adding bentonite clay to degraded farm soils to restore them, as farmers in northeast Thailand have done.

clay–water interaction.text: The umbrella term for the progressive interactions between clay minerals and water, described in five stages: hydration, dispersion, flocculation, deflocculation and aggregation.

layer charge.text: The net negative charge on a clay mineral layer created when ions of lower charge, such as Al3+, replace Si4+, which interlayer cations balance.

beidellite.text: A smectite clay mineral in which more than half of the layer charge comes from aluminium replacing silicon in the tetrahedral sheet.

schulze–hardy rule.text: The rule that the critical coagulation concentration of an electrolyte varies as the inverse sixth power of the charge of its counter-ion.

clay chemistry.text: The applied branch of chemistry that studies the structures, properties and reactions of clays and clay minerals.

humic substance.text: Dark, relatively decay-resistant organic compounds formed during the long-term decomposition and transformation of biomass residues.

chelation.text: The bonding of a metal atom by a molecule that grips it at two or more points, forming a ring structure.

sorption.text: A physical and chemical process by which one substance becomes attached to another.

adsorption.text: The adhesion of atoms, ions or molecules from a gas, liquid or solution to a surface.

variable charge.text: Surface charge on clay edges and organic matter that changes with the pH of the soil solution, because it comes from hydroxyl groups giving up hydrogen ions.

leonardite.text: A soft, waxy, black or brown mineraloid formed by the oxidation of lignite, which dissolves easily in alkaline solutions.

artificial humic substances.text: Humic-like substances produced by people, by composting lignin, adding biochar, or synthesising them industrially from organic feedstocks.

chemistry of humic substances.text: The make-up of humic substances: mixtures of many molecules built from aromatic, aliphatic and carbohydrate units that carry mainly carboxylic and phenolic groups.

humic substances and plant growth.text: The effects of humic substances and other soil organic matter on plant growth and soil fertility.

adsorption isotherm.text: A description of how much substance is adsorbed on a surface as a function of its pressure, or of its concentration in solution, at constant temperature.

desorption.text: The release of adsorbed atoms or molecules from a surface into the surrounding fluid or vacuum; the reverse of adsorption.

chelate effect.text: The greater affinity of a chelating ligand for a metal ion than of similar ligands that bind it at only one point.

chelated micronutrient fertilizers.text: Fertilizers that supply micronutrient metals such as manganese, iron, zinc and copper as metal chelate compounds.

natural chelating agents.text: Molecules made by living things, such as proteins, polysaccharides, organic acids and microbial siderophores, that bind metal ions as chelates.

chemical equivalent.text: The amount of a substance that reacts with, or is equivalent to, a set amount, typically one mole, of another substance in a reaction.

point of zero charge.text: The pH at which the net electrical charge on a particle's surface is zero.

fulvic acid.text: The fraction of humic substances that dissolves in water at any pH.

humic acid.text: The fraction of humic substances that dissolves in water at neutral and alkaline pH but not at acidic pH below 2.

humification debate.text: The dispute over whether humic substances exist in soil as distinct compounds or are products of the alkaline extraction used to isolate them.

humate.text: In economic geology, rock material rich in humic acids, such as weathered coal beds (leonardite), mudrock or pore material in sandstones.

humic acid in drinking water.text: Humic acid in water meant for drinking or industry, where it affects how well the water can be treated and disinfected.

humic substance fractionation.text: The laboratory separation of natural organic matter into humic acid, fulvic acid and humin by alkaline extraction and acidification.

cation-exchange capacity.text: A measure of how many positively charged ions (cations) a soil can hold on the surfaces of its particles.

cation exchange.text: The attraction and release of positively charged ions by negatively charged sites on soil colloids, which swap them with ions in the soil water.

potassium humate.text: The potassium salt of humic acid, made by alkaline extraction of leonardite and used mainly as a soil conditioner.

permanent charge.text: Negative charge built into a clay's crystal structure where lower-charged atoms replace higher-charged ones; it does not change with pH.

anion-exchange capacity.text: A soil's ability to hold negatively charged ions, such as nitrate and phosphate, on positively charged surfaces and release them later by exchange.

base saturation.text: The percentage of a soil's cation-exchange capacity occupied by the base cations Ca2+, Mg2+, K+ and Na+.

base-cation saturation ratio.text: A way of interpreting soil tests that balances soil cations to 'ideal' ratios, either between cations such as calcium and magnesium or as shares of the CEC.

diffuse double layer.text: Two parallel layers of charge around a particle in a fluid: the surface charge itself and a loosely held diffuse layer of attracted ions that screens it.

ionic strength.text: A measure of the concentration of ions in a solution, weighted by their charge.

activity coefficient.text: A factor that corrects a substance's concentration for how far a mixture departs from ideal behaviour.

measuring cation-exchange capacity.text: Finding a soil's CEC by displacing all its bound cations with a concentrated solution of another cation, then measuring the displaced cations or the added cation retained.

base-richness.text: The level of chemical bases, such as calcium, potassium or magnesium ions, in soil or water.

discovery of cation exchange.text: The 19th-century finding, by Thomas Way and John Bennet Lawes at Rothamsted Experimental Station, that soils exchange cations.

debye–hückel theory.text: A theory by Peter Debye and Erich Hückel explaining why electrolyte solutions depart from ideal behaviour.

inner sphere complex.text: A surface complex in which an ion binds directly to a mineral surface with no water molecules between them.

langmuir adsorption model.text: A model of adsorption on a surface of identical sites, each holding at most one adsorbate molecule, with adsorption and desorption reversible.

partition coefficient.text: The ratio of a compound's concentrations in two immiscible phases at equilibrium.

coprecipitation.text: The carrying down by a precipitate of substances that would normally stay dissolved under the same conditions.

redox.text: A chemical reaction in which the oxidation states of the reactants change; short for reduction–oxidation.

freundlich equation.text: An empirical adsorption isotherm relating the amount adsorbed on a solid to the gas pressure or solute concentration.

geochemical modeling.text: Using chemical thermodynamics, kinetics or both, usually by computer, to analyse the chemical reactions in geological systems, including low-temperature aqueous solutions near the Earth's surface.

x-ray absorption fine structure.text: Detailed structure in X-ray absorption spectra whose analysis reveals an atom's local structure and unoccupied electronic states.

chemical speciation.text: A calculation of the concentrations of all the chemical species present in a solution.

redox in soils.text: The electron-transfer reactions that underlie many soil processes and properties.

redoximorphic features.text: Colour patterns in soil from the loss or gain of pigment against the matrix colour, formed by oxidation and reduction of iron or manganese and their movement, or a matrix colour set by ferrous iron.

biological redox reactions.text: The redox reactions on which many essential life processes run, above all respiration and photosynthesis.

oxidizing agent.text: A substance that oxidizes another by taking its electrons, and is itself reduced; also called an oxidant or electron acceptor.

reducing agent.text: A substance that reduces another by giving it electrons, and is itself oxidized; also called a reductant or electron donor.

redox potential (eh).text: The tendency of electrons to pass from an electron donor to an electron acceptor, measured in volts as Eh.

redox couples and half-reactions.text: A redox couple is a reducing species and its oxidized form, such as Fe2+/Fe3+; the oxidation and the reduction taken alone are each a half-reaction.

standard electrode potential.text: The equilibrium voltage of a half-reaction under standard conditions, measured against a standard hydrogen electrode; also called its reduction potential.

in situ chemical oxidation.text: A remediation technique that injects strong chemical oxidizers into contaminated soil or groundwater to destroy contaminants where they lie.

redox gradient.text: A series of redox reactions sorted according to redox potential.

biofilter.text: A pollution control technique in which a bioreactor holding living material captures pollutants and breaks them down biologically.

electron acceptor.text: A chemical species that takes up electrons transferred to it from another compound, and so acts as an oxidizing agent.

oxidation state.text: The hypothetical charge an atom would carry if all its bonds were fully ionic, describing how far it has been oxidized.

redox ladder.text: The order in which redox reactions take place, set by the free energy each redox pair yields.

anaerobic respiration.text: Respiration that uses inorganic electron acceptors other than oxygen, such as nitrate, sulfate or sulfur, at the end of the electron transport chain.

reduction in waterlogged soils.text: The shift of a saturated soil from oxidizing to reducing conditions as oxygen runs out and anaerobic microbes take over.

electron donor.text: A chemical species that transfers electrons to another compound, acting as a reducing agent that is itself oxidized.

isco oxidants.text: The strong oxidizers used in in situ chemical oxidation, most commonly permanganate, Fenton's reagent, persulfate and ozone.

methanogenesis.text: The formation of methane by microbes called methanogens, all of them archaea, as the final step in breaking down organic matter where oxygen is absent.

dissimilatory metal reduction.text: Anaerobic respiration by bacteria and archaea that use a metal, rather than oxygen, as the terminal electron acceptor.

paddy field.text: A flooded field of arable land used to grow semiaquatic crops, above all rice and taro.

standard hydrogen electrode.text: The reference redox electrode that sets the zero of the thermodynamic scale of oxidation–reduction potentials.

obligate anaerobes.text: Microorganisms that are killed by normal atmospheric concentrations of oxygen.

manganese cycle.text: The biogeochemical cycle that moves manganese through the atmosphere, water, living things and rocks and soils.

methanogens.text: Anaerobic archaea that produce methane as a by-product of their energy metabolism.

iron-oxidizing bacteria.text: Chemotrophic bacteria that get their energy by oxidizing dissolved iron.

green rust.text: A family of green layered iron(II)–iron(III) hydroxides that hold another anion, such as carbonate, chloride or sulfate, between their layers.

measuring redox potential.text: Determining Eh by sampling in the field and analysing in the lab, or by placing an electrode in the soil or water for in situ readings.

microbes along redox gradients.text: The layered microbial communities that redox gradients support, and that in turn sharpen those gradients through their respiration.

redox gradients in water and sediments.term: Redox gradients in water and sediments
redox gradients in water and sediments.text: The redox gradients that form in water columns and in the sediments beneath them.

solubility equilibrium.text: The dynamic equilibrium between a solid compound and a solution of that compound, with dissolution and precipitation going on at equal rates.

electron activity (pe).text: A dimensionless measure of redox potential, defined as the negative logarithm of electron activity by analogy with pH.

soil salinity.text: The salt content of a soil; the process by which it increases is called salinization.

soil acidification.text: The build-up of hydrogen cations in a soil, which lowers its pH.

pourbaix diagram.text: A plot of the thermodynamically stable phases of an aqueous system against redox potential (Eh or pe) and pH.

manganese in soil.text: The forms and redox behaviour of manganese in soils, where it is a micronutrient whose solubility is set by redox potential and pH.

hydromorphic soil.text: A soil formed under wetland conditions, waterlogged for long enough to shape its development.

acid rain and soil.text: Rain or other precipitation that is unusually acidic, mainly from sulfuric and nitric acids formed from air pollutants, which acidifies the soils it falls on.

irrigation salinity.text: Salt build-up in irrigated soils, because nearly all water carries dissolved salts that stay behind in the root zone when plants use the water.

soil salinity control.text: Controlling salinization to prevent soil degradation, and reclaiming soils that are already saline.

sodic soil.text: A soil in which sodium (Na+) predominates among the exchangeable and dissolved cations.

fertilizer-induced acidification.text: The lowering of soil pH by chemical fertilizers, above all ammonium-based nitrogen and sulfur fertilizers.

duricrust.text: A hard layer on or near the soil surface where soluble minerals have precipitated and hardened.

acid sulfate soil.text: Soils, sediments or organic substrates such as peat, formed under waterlogged conditions, that contain iron sulfide minerals, mainly pyrite, or their oxidation products.

dryland salinity.text: Salinity in unirrigated landscapes: a rise in the salt of soil, water or the wider environment beyond normal levels, natural but greatly worsened by human activity.

salinity in australia.text: Soil salinity and dryland salinity as problems degrading the environment of Australia.

sodium adsorption ratio.text: An irrigation water quality index, calculated from sodium, calcium and magnesium concentrations, used in managing sodium-affected soils.

environmental impact of irrigation.text: The changes irrigation makes to the quantity and quality of soil and water, and their effects on natural and social conditions in river basins and downstream.

pyrite.text: Iron sulfide, FeS2, the most common sulfide mineral, also known as fool's gold.

measuring soil salinity.text: Determining soil salinity as the salt concentration of the soil solution in g/L, or as its electric conductivity (EC) in dS/m.

acidic parent materials.text: Rocks and sediments whose weathering acidifies the soils formed on them, such as granite and sulfide-rich shale, coal and marine clay.

biological acidification.text: Acidification of soil by living things, as plant roots and decaying plant remains release protons and organic acids.

effects of soil acidification.text: The harm acidification does to plants and soil organisms, from stunted roots to lost biological diversity.

calcareous soil.text: Soil formed from or containing a high proportion of calcium carbonate, as calcite or aragonite.

caliche.text: A soil accumulation of calcium carbonate at depth, where it precipitates and binds other materials such as gravel, sand, clay and silt.

managing soil acidification.text: Ways of preventing or reversing soil acidification, chiefly lime, organic amendments and biochar, with careful fertilizer and irrigation management.

gypcrust.text: A hardened soil layer made of around 95% gypsum (calcium sulfate).

halophyte.text: A salt-tolerant plant that grows in soils or waters of high salinity, such as salt marshes, mangroves and saline semi-deserts.

drainage for salinity control.text: Land drainage, usually by horizontal but also by vertical systems, that carries salty water away and lowers the water table.

leaching requirement.text: The amount of water that must percolate through the root zone to keep soil salinity at a desired level, worked out from the salt balance.

soil salinity models.text: Computer models of water and salt movement in soil used to predict salinity under irrigation and drainage.

sahysmod.text: A computer program that predicts salinity of soil moisture, groundwater and drainage water, water table depth and drain discharge in irrigated land, mapping spatial variation with a network of polygons.

strip cropping for salinity control.text: Irrigating alternate strips of land and leaving those between permanently fallow, so the fallow strips drain and absorb salt from the cropped ones.

alkalinity.text: The capacity of water to resist acidification, set by its buffer of weak acids and their conjugate bases.

chilean caliche.text: Vast deposits in Chile's Atacama Desert, also called caliche, of gypsum, sodium chloride, other salts and sand together with nitrate minerals (salitre).

framboid.text: A raspberry-like microscopic structure common in some sedimentary minerals, especially pyrite: a roughly spherical cluster of tiny crystals.

electrolytic conductivity.text: A measure of how well a solution of ions conducts electricity, used to gauge how much dissolved salt it holds.

pyrite oxidation in acid sulfate soils.term: Pyrite oxidation in acid sulfate soils
pyrite oxidation in acid sulfate soils.text: The oxidation of pyrite in drained soils to sulfuric acid and iron(III) hydroxide, which can make the soil extremely acidic.

acid base accounting.text: The practice of quantifying the sources of acidity and alkalinity in acid sulfate soils so they can be managed.

managing acid sulfate soils.text: Keeping acid sulfate soils wet, restoring their water table or neutralising their acid to prevent or repair acidification.

sulfidic and sulfuric material.text: Diagnostic materials of acid sulfate soils: sulfidic material holds detectable inorganic sulfides, and sulfuric material has a pH below 4 from their oxidation.

managing dryland salinity.text: Reducing dryland salinity by cutting groundwater recharge through soils and vegetation, and coping with salt where groundwater discharges.

primary and secondary salinity.text: The division of salinity into primary salinity, which is natural, and secondary salinity, which human activity induces.

saltwater intrusion.text: The movement of saline water into freshwater aquifers, degrading groundwater quality.

saline seep.text: A seep of saline water where alkali salt crystals form as the salty water reaches the surface and evaporates.

halotolerance.text: The ability of an organism to live in salt concentrations above those it needs for growth.

exchangeable sodium percentage.text: The share of a soil's exchangeable cations, and so of its cation-exchange capacity, that is sodium, expressed as a percentage.

alkali soil.text: A clay soil with a high pH, generally above 8.5, often with poor structure and low infiltration capacity.

maas–hoffman model.text: A mathematical model of how crop yield responds to soil salinity, drawn as a horizontal line that breaks into a downward slope.

road salt and soil.text: The salt spread on roads and walkways to melt ice, and its build-up in roadside soils and waters.

van genuchten–gupta model.text: An inverted S-curve relating crop yield to soil salinity.

man-made soil alkalinity.text: Soil alkalinity caused by people, mainly through sodium salts and lime that reach soil in irrigation water, effluent and industrial emissions.

saline-alkali aquaculture.text: Using fish and seafood farming on saline-alkali land to leach salts, add organic matter and put non-arable land to use.

residual sodium carbonate index.text: An index of the alkalinity hazard that irrigation water or soil water poses to soil.

agricultural gypsum.text: Gypsum (calcium sulfate) applied to soil as a fertilizer and amendment, supplying calcium and sulfur without generally changing soil pH.

reclaiming alkali soils.text: Improving alkali soils by supplying calcium or acidifying material to replace or neutralise excess sodium, and leaching the sodium away.

critical load.text: A quantitative estimate of pollutant exposure below which significant harm to specified sensitive parts of the environment does not occur, as far as is known.

biosaline agriculture.text: Growing plants with saline groundwater or on saline soil, using salt-tolerant plants to farm land too salty for ordinary crops.

manganese toxicity.text: Poisoning of plants by manganese that becomes soluble at low soil pH.

soil biology.text: The study of the activity and ecology of the microbes and animals that live in soil.

soil microbiology.text: The study of the microorganisms in soil, what they do and how they affect soil properties.

biomineralization.text: The process by which living organisms produce or retain inorganic minerals, often hardening or stiffening their tissues.

soil biodiversity.text: The relationship between soil and the variety of life, and the aspects of soil that can be managed with that variety in mind.

soil ecology.text: The study of how soil organisms interact with one another and with their environment.

oligotroph.text: An organism able to live where nutrients are available only at very low levels.

soil animals.text: The animals that live in soil for their whole life or at least as larvae; about 30% of arthropods live in soil.

total organic carbon.text: An analytical measure of the concentration of organic carbon in a sample.

earthworm.text: A soil-dwelling invertebrate of the phylum Annelida; the name covers the largest members of the Oligochaeta.

soil food web.text: The community of organisms living all or part of their lives in the soil, viewed as the network of feeding links that passes energy among them.

detritivore.text: A heterotroph that gets its nutrients by eating detritus: decomposing plant and animal parts and faeces.

soil respiration.text: The production of carbon dioxide by respiring roots, rhizosphere microbes and soil fauna below ground.

earthworm ecological categories.text: The grouping of earthworms by where they live and feed: epigeic, endogeic and anecic.

earthworms and soil fertility.text: The biological, chemical and physical ways earthworm activity improves soil for plants, by fragmenting, mixing, grinding and digesting plant debris.

petrichor.text: The earthy scent often noticed when rain falls on dry soil or rock.

soil enzyme.text: Enzymes in soil, released mainly by microbes, that break down organic matter and free nutrients for plants.

soil bacteria.text: The single-celled prokaryotic organisms of the soil, its most numerous inhabitants.

geosmin.text: A chemical with a distinct earthy or musty smell, made by bacteria common in soil and water.

soil fungi.text: The yeasts, moulds and other fungi of the soil, which lack chlorophyll and spread through the soil as threads called mycelium, feeding on organic matter.

soil actinomycetes.text: Soil bacteria of the phylum Actinomycetota (formerly Actinobacteria), Gram-positive and rich in guanine and cytosine, many of which grow fungus-like branching mycelia.

lumbricus terrestris.text: A large, reddish earthworm, known as the common earthworm, lob worm or nightcrawler, thought to be native to Western Europe and now spread around the world.

soil ecosystem engineers.text: Species that create, significantly modify, maintain or destroy a habitat; in soil, chiefly burrowing animals such as earthworms, ants and termites, and fungi.

bioturbation.text: The reworking of soils and sediments by animals or plants, through burrowing and the swallowing and excreting of grains.

agricultural use of soil microbes.text: Using and managing soil microorganisms to make nutrients available to crops, spur their growth and protect them from disease.

vermicomposting.text: Feeding organic waste to earthworms to turn it into vermicompost.

symbiosis.text: Any close and long-term biological interaction between two organisms of different species.

microbial inoculant.text: An agricultural amendment, also called a soil inoculant or bioinoculant, that uses beneficial rhizosphere or endophytic microbes to promote plant health.

bioturbation in soils.text: The mixing and moving of soil by burrowing animals and by plant roots, which matters for soil production, burial, organic matter content and downslope transport.

lithotroph.text: An organism that takes the electrons it needs for building its cells or making energy from an inorganic substance, usually of mineral origin, rather than from organic matter.

bacterial metabolic types.text: The grouping of bacteria by their source of energy, the electron donors they use and their source of carbon.

microbiologically induced calcite precip.text: A biogeochemical process in which microbes cause calcium carbonate to precipitate within the soil matrix.

chemolithotrophy.text: A way of living in which a cell gets its energy by oxidizing reduced inorganic compounds, such as ammonia, sulfur, ferrous iron or hydrogen.

threats to soil biodiversity.text: Soil changes that reduce the variety of soil life, such as acidification, salinisation, sodicity, structure decline and erosion, many of them driven by how soil is managed.

hypha.text: A long, branching filament of a fungus, oomycete or actinobacterium; in most fungi hyphae are the main mode of growth and together form a mycelium.

mycelium.text: The root-like body of a fungus, a mass of branching, thread-like hyphae.

soil-borne pathogen.text: A disease-causing agent that lives both in soil and in a plant host and tends to infect healthy plants grown in that soil.

soil macrofauna.text: Soil and litter invertebrates between 2 mm and 2 cm, such as earthworms, termites, ants, millipedes, woodlice, beetles, slugs and snails.

thatch (lawn).text: In lawn care, a layer of organic matter that builds up around the base of the grass plants.

termites.text: Eusocial insects that eat decaying plant material, mostly wood, leaf litter and soil humus.

soil mesofauna.text: Soil and litter invertebrates between 0.2 mm and 2 mm, chiefly microarthropods such as mites and springtails, and potworms (enchytraeids).

springtails.text: Springtails (class Collembola) are tiny six-legged arthropods, no longer counted as insects, that live in moist soil and leaf litter almost everywhere on Earth.

enchytraeids.text: Enchytraeids are a family of small, earthworm-like oligochaete worms; the terrestrial species, called potworms, live in highly organic soils.

slime molds and myxobacteria.text: Soil microorganisms whose single cells join into syncytia (slime molds, which are eukaryotes) or swarms (myxobacteria, which are prokaryotes).

soil microbial loop.text: The pathway by which bacteria take up dissolved organic carbon and pass it back up the food web; in soil it concerns soil carbon and the nutrients freed when protozoa and nematodes eat root-fed bacteria.

soil microfauna.text: The smallest soil animals, 20 μm to 200 μm in size: protozoa and tiny multicellular animals such as nematodes, rotifers and tardigrades.

soil algae.text: Photosynthetic microorganisms that live at or near the soil surface and make their own carbon from light.

soil bacteriophages.text: Viruses that infect soil bacteria, among the most abundant yet least studied members of soil microbial communities.

soil protozoa.text: Single-celled eukaryotes of the soil, grouped as flagellates, amoebae and ciliates.

nematode.text: Roundworms or eelworms, the animal phylum Nematoda, most of them free-living microbe feeders but many parasitic.

entomopathogenic nematode.text: Nematodes (thread worms) that infect and kill only insects, living as parasites inside their hosts.

bioturbation and archaeology.text: The disturbance of archaeological layers by burrowing organisms, which blurs the order in which deposits were laid down.

dwarf forest.text: An uncommon ecosystem of miniature trees, also called elfin or pygmy forest, home to small animals such as rodents and lizards.

biogenic mineral controversy.text: The dispute over whether crystalline substances made by living things should count as minerals.

geomycology.text: The study of the part fungi play in geological processes, including forming, transforming and dissolving minerals.

types of biomineralization.text: A scheme that sorts mineral formation by living things according to how much the organism controls it: biomineralization proper, organomineralization and inorganic mineralization.

worm cast.text: A small pile, coil or pellet of soil or sand that burrowing worms expel at the surface.

oribatid mites.text: Oribatid mites, also called moss or beetle mites, are a group of slow-living mites that are the most prevalent arthropods in forest soils.

controls on soil respiration.text: The non-living factors, chiefly temperature, soil moisture and nitrogen, that set how fast soil carbon is respired to CO2.

measuring soil respiration.text: Field and laboratory techniques for measuring how fast CO2 leaves the soil and where it comes from.

soil respiration and global change.text: How rising CO2, warming, changing rainfall and nitrogen fertilization are altering soil respiration around the planet.

sources of soil respiration.text: The organisms and pathways that produce the CO2 leaving soil: roots, rhizosphere microbes, decomposers and soil animals.

millipedes.text: Arthropods of the class Diplopoda, with two pairs of jointed legs on most body segments.

acid mine drainage.text: The acid runoff made when lithotrophic microbes in mining areas oxidize pyrite and other reduced sulfur minerals to sulfate.

lithotrophs in soil formation.text: The part that rock-colonizing lithotrophs, cyanobacteria above all, play in starting soil formation on bare rock.

soil zoology.text: The study of animals that live wholly or partly in the soil, also called pedozoology.

measuring soil biodiversity.text: Ways of counting and identifying soil organisms, increasingly by extracting DNA directly from the soil.

earthworm invasions.text: The spread of a few earthworm species, carried by people, into regions where they are not native.

ammonia fungi.text: Fungi whose fruiting bodies develop quickly and germinate readily when ammonia or other nitrogen-rich material makes the soil alkaline.

global patterns of soil biodiversity.text: The unsettled question of how life in soil is distributed over the globe and whether it follows the same drivers as life above ground.

soil microbial hotspots.text: Small sites in soil, rich in resources such as moisture or nutrients, where microorganisms are concentrated.

invasive earthworms of north america.text: The spread of introduced, mostly European and Asian earthworms into North American forests, especially northern forests that have lacked native worms since the last ice age.

bottom-up control in soil food webs.term: Bottom-up control in soil food webs
bottom-up control in soil food webs.text: Control of a food web from its base, where the biomass, abundance or diversity of higher levels depends on resources from lower levels.

external rumen.text: A partnership in which litter-eating animals such as isopods let microbes enrich their faecal pellets outside the body, then eat the pellets again.

soil fauna extraction methods.text: Techniques for separating organisms from soil samples so they can be counted and identified.

top-down control in soil food webs.term: Top-down control in soil food webs
top-down control in soil food webs.text: Control of a food web from above, where consumers at higher levels set the abundance, diversity or biomass of lower levels.

primary nutritional groups.text: The division of organisms by the sources of energy, electrons and carbon they need to live, grow and reproduce.

stability of soil food webs.text: How well soil food webs resist and recover from disturbance, and why their complexity seems to help.

types of soil food webs.text: The three ways of drawing a food web: topological webs, flow webs and interaction webs.

soil flow webs.text: Food webs that add numbers to the feeding links, tracing how much carbon or other nutrients move from producers to consumers.

plant-parasitic nematodes.text: Pest nematodes that attack crop plants, chiefly their roots, or spread plant viruses between them.

metagenomics.text: The study of all the genetic material from all organisms in an environment, revealing their composition, diversity and functional potential.

chemotroph.text: An organism that gets its energy by oxidizing electron donors from its surroundings, in contrast to phototrophs, which use light.

microbial ecology.text: The study of how microorganisms interact with their environment, also called environmental microbiology.

microbiome.text: The community of microorganisms usually found living together in a given habitat.

oligotrophic soil environments.text: Soils, such as farmed and frozen soils, in which microbes have very few nutrients to live on.

geomicrobiology.text: The field between geology and microbiology that studies the role of microbes in geological and geochemical processes and the effects of minerals and metals on microbes.

plant adaptations to nutrient-poor soils.text: The ways plants of oligotrophic soils take up nutrients more efficiently, use less of them and store them.

drilosphere.text: The part of the soil shaped by earthworm secretions, burrowing and casts: soil that has passed through their gut or lines their burrows.

soil megafauna.text: Soil animals over 2 cm long, mostly burrowing vertebrates, that dig nests and galleries and throw earth up into mounds.

testate amoebae.text: Single-celled amoeboid protists partly enclosed in a shell, or test, with an opening through which their pseudopodia emerge.

streptomyces.text: The largest genus of actinomycete bacteria, found mainly in soil and decaying vegetation.

copiotroph.text: An organism found in environments rich in nutrients, especially carbon.

azotobacter.text: A genus of aerobic, free-living soil bacteria that fix atmospheric nitrogen and release it into the soil as ammonium.

bacterivore.text: An organism that gets its energy and nutrients mainly or entirely by eating bacteria.

fungivory.text: Fungivory or mycophagy is the eating of fungi; organisms that eat nothing else are called fungivores.

fossorial animals.text: Animals adapted to digging that live mainly, though not only, underground.

termite mounds.text: Termite nests that protrude above the soil surface, built of earth and mud and stronger than underground nests.

fungal loop hypothesis.text: The idea that, in arid ecosystems, soil fungi link the activity of plants and biological soil crusts, which respond to different amounts of soil moisture.

detrital food web.text: A food web in which dead plant and animal matter is broken down by decomposers such as bacteria and fungi and passes to detritivores and then carnivores.

organotroph.text: An organism that obtains hydrogen or electrons from organic substrates.

microbial metabolism.text: The means by which a microbe obtains the energy and nutrients, such as carbon, that it needs to live and reproduce.

saprotrophic bacteria.text: Mostly soil-dwelling bacteria that feed on dead organic matter, digesting it outside the cell with enzymes and absorbing the products.

mendocino ecological staircase.text: A flight of uplifted marine terraces on the northern California coast, each about 100,000 years older than the one below and carrying its own soils, microbes, plants and animals.

biocementation of soil.text: The use of microbially induced calcium carbonate precipitation as a cementing technique to strengthen sand that might otherwise liquefy.

ammonia fungi succession.text: The order in which ammonia fungi fruit after ammonia or urea reaches forest soil, divided into early-phase and late-phase groups.

phospholipid fatty acid analysis.text: A technique that uses the fatty acids of membrane phospholipids as chemical markers to estimate the living microbial biomass and community make-up of soil and water.

microarthropods.text: A size group of small arthropods, usually one to several millimetres long, that live mostly in soil.

soil mites.text: Mites are small eight-legged arachnids, and many species live in soil as decomposers.

nematophagous fungi.text: Carnivorous fungi specialised in trapping and digesting nematodes; more than 700 species are known.

enzymatic latch.text: The control of decomposition in peat by phenol oxidases: by breaking down phenolics that inhibit hydrolase enzymes, they release decay, so limits on the microbes limit decomposition.

biofilm.text: A community of microorganisms whose cells stick to each other, and often to a surface, inside a self-made slime of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS).

soil bacterial growth rates.text: How fast soil bacteria produce new biomass and replace their populations, a measure that responds quickly to changing conditions.

plfa biomarkers of soil microbes.text: Signature fatty acids in a PLFA profile that indicate particular groups of soil microorganisms.

birch effect.text: The influence of soil moisture on the cycling of carbon in soil.

microbial biogeography.text: The study of where microorganisms live, at what abundance and why, across space and time.

root.text: The plant organ, usually below the soil surface, that anchors the plant and takes in water and dissolved nutrients.

extracellular polymeric substance.text: High-molecular-weight natural polymers that microorganisms secrete into their surroundings.

biofilm development.text: The microbial developmental process by which a biofilm forms, summarized in five major stages.

legume family (fabaceae).text: The legume or pea family of flowering plants, about 19,000 species, including soybean, beans, pea, chickpea and alfalfa.

fibrous root system.text: A root system of many thin, similar-sized roots growing from the stem base and forming a dense mat near the soil surface, the opposite of a taproot system.

taproot.text: A large, central, dominant root, usually straight, thick and tapering, from which smaller roots branch sideways.

root growth regulation.text: The ways roots sense their surroundings, such as gravity, light, physical barriers and soil conditions, and steer their growth in response.

root system architecture.text: The spatial layout of a plant's whole root system: how its roots branch, spread and angle through the soil.

rooting depth.text: How a plant's roots are spread down through the soil, which depends on the plant's form, where and when water and nutrients are available, and the soil's physical properties.

root hair.text: A thin outgrowth of a single epidermal cell near the root tip that collects water and mineral nutrients from the soil.

plant hormone.text: Signal molecules produced within plants in extremely low concentrations that control growth and development.

specialized root types.text: Root forms adapted to tasks beyond anchorage and uptake, such as aerial, prop, buttress, storage, contractile and cluster roots.

rhizosphere.text: The narrow zone of soil directly influenced by root secretions and by the microorganisms that live with the roots.

mycorrhiza.text: A symbiosis between a fungus and a plant in which fungal hyphae and plant roots interconnect and form an interface at the level of cells.

hydraulic redistribution.text: The passive movement of water by plant roots from moist soil to dry soil.

root exudates.text: The organic compounds, such as sugars, amino acids, proteins, enzymes and DNA, that plant roots release into the surrounding soil.

mutualism.text: An ecological interaction between two or more species in which each gains a net benefit.

root microbiome.text: The changing community of microorganisms, mainly bacteria, fungi and archaea, that lives with plant roots.

bulk soil.text: The soil outside the rhizosphere, not penetrated by plant roots.

mycorrhizal nutrient exchange.text: The trade in which a mycorrhizal fungus gets carbohydrates from its host and in return improves the plant's uptake of water and minerals.

mycorrhizal stress protection.text: The protection mycorrhizal fungi give plants against soil-borne disease, drought, salt and toxic metals.

mycorrhizal types.text: The grouping of mycorrhizas by how the fungus colonises the root, with the main split between ectomycorrhizas and endomycorrhizas.

arbuscular mycorrhiza.text: A type of mycorrhiza in which the fungus enters the cortical cells of a plant's roots and forms tree-like arbuscules inside them.

ectomycorrhiza.text: A mycorrhiza in which the fungus sheathes the root tip and grows between the root's outer cells without entering them.

common mycorrhizal network.text: An underground network formed where the hyphae of mycorrhizal fungi join the roots of two or more plants, of the same or different species, linking them together.

rhizobacteria.text: Bacteria that live with plant roots and can harm, have no effect on, or benefit plant growth.

glomeromycota.text: A group of fungi, with about 230 described species, whose members form arbuscular mycorrhizas with plant roots.

rhizobia.text: Soil bacteria that fix nitrogen once they have settled inside the root nodules of legumes.

endophyte.text: A microbe, often a bacterium or fungus, that lives inside a plant for at least part of its life without causing apparent disease.

arbuscular mycorrhizal nutrient exchange.text: The trade in which arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi take sugars from their host and supply it above all with phosphorus.

glomus (fungus).text: A genus of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi whose species all form mycorrhizae with plant roots.

rhizophagus irregularis.text: An arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus, formerly called Glomus intraradices, used as a soil inoculant in agriculture and horticulture.

arbuscular mycorrhizae in agriculture.text: Managing tillage, fertiliser and cropping so that crops can form working partnerships with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.

siderophore.text: Small iron-binding compounds secreted by microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi, and by some plants, to gather iron.

root nodule.text: A growth on the roots of some plants, chiefly legumes, that houses nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

root mucilage.text: A gelatinous secretion of plant-specific polysaccharides, part of the root exudate, that coats the root cap.

ericoid mycorrhiza.text: A mutualism between plants of the heath family (Ericaceae) and several lineages of mycorrhizal fungi.

spermosphere.text: The zone around a germinating seed where soil, microorganisms and the seed interact.

dual mycorrhiza.text: The ability of a few plant species to host both arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal fungi in the same root system at once.

history of mycorrhizal research.text: The study of root–fungus partnerships from nineteenth-century observations to genome sequencing.

mycorrhizae and climate change.text: How rising carbon dioxide, warming and air pollution affect mycorrhizal fungi and the plants that rely on them.

mycorrhizae on barren soil.text: The part mycorrhizal fungi play in helping plants establish on sterile, barren or degraded soils.

orchid mycorrhiza.text: The symbiosis between orchids and the endomycorrhizal fungi that colonise their roots and seeds.

allelopathy.text: The release by some plants, often from their roots, of chemicals that hold back the growth of other organisms.

rhizosphere research methods.text: Field and laboratory techniques for studying the root zone, from pH measurements to DNA sequencing of its microbes.

rhizosphere signalling.text: The exchange of chemical signals among roots, microbes, fungi and insects in the rhizosphere, which shapes which organisms colonise the root zone.

hartig net.text: The network of fungal hyphae that grows between the epidermal and cortical cells of a root in an ectomycorrhiza.

arbuscular mycorrhizal effects on soil c.term: Arbuscular mycorrhizal effects on soil communities
arbuscular mycorrhizal effects on soil c.text: The ways arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis shapes the bacteria, plants and other organisms living in the soil around roots.

detecting arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.text: Molecular and chemical techniques for finding and measuring arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi in roots and soil.

mycorrhizal inoculation for land restora.text: Adding arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi to soil when replanting degraded land, to rebuild its biological and physical properties.

plant–soil feedback.text: A process in which plants change the biological and physical qualities of their soil, which then changes how well plants can grow in it later.

fungal endophyte defense.text: The use by plants of fungi living inside their tissues as an indirect defence against herbivores.

rhizobium.text: A genus of aerobic, rod-shaped, nitrogen-fixing soil bacteria that live in the root nodules of mainly legumes.

ectomycorrhizae in forestry.text: The use of ectomycorrhizal fungi as inoculum when planting trees and when restoring disturbed ecosystems.

ectomycorrhizal tolerance of polluted so.text: The ability of ectomycorrhizal fungi to survive, and help their hosts survive, soils high in heavy metals, salts, radionuclides and organic pollutants.

ectomycorrhizal extramatrical mycelium.text: The mass of fungal hyphae growing out into the soil from ectomycorrhizas, also called extraradical mycelium.

nod factor.text: Signalling molecules that rhizobia release in response to legume flavonoids and that trigger the formation of root nodules.

root cap.text: The small organ, also called the calyptra, that covers the tip of every growing plant root.

laimosphere.text: The zone of soil, rich in microbes, around the underground parts of plant stems; it is the stem's counterpart of the rhizosphere and spermosphere.

actinorhizal plant.text: A flowering plant that forms a symbiosis with the nitrogen-fixing actinomycete Frankia, which lives in nodules on its roots.

plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria.text: Soil bacteria that colonise plant roots, after being inoculated onto seed, and enhance plant growth.

disease suppressive soils.text: Soils whose microbes keep pathogens from establishing in the rhizosphere of plants.

mycorrhizosphere.text: The zone made up of roots, the hyphae of their mycorrhizal fungi, associated microorganisms and the soil under their direct influence.

frankia.text: A genus of filamentous nitrogen-fixing bacteria that live in root nodules of actinorhizal plants, much as rhizobia do in legumes.

mycorrhiza helper bacteria.text: Soil bacteria that associate with ectomycorrhizal and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and improve the symbiosis.

strigolactones.text: Carotenoid-derived signalling molecules that plant roots secrete into the rhizosphere, where they stimulate arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.

fine root.text: A plant root usually defined as two millimetres or less in diameter.

nitrogen nutrition in the arbuscular myc.term: Nitrogen nutrition in the arbuscular mycorrhizal system
nitrogen nutrition in the arbuscular myc.text: The uptake of soil nitrogen by arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and its transfer to host plants and between plants.

mutualist–parasite continuum.text: The idea that a root microbe can behave anywhere from mutualist to parasite, depending on its host, the environment and the host's health.

root microbiome assembly.text: How individual microbes come together into the communities found on and around roots, a question with two competing explanations.

lateral root.text: A root that grows out sideways from the primary root, arising in the pericycle, and builds up the branching pattern of a root system.

cluster root.text: Cluster roots, also called proteoid roots, are roots that form clusters of closely spaced short lateral rootlets.

deleterious rhizobacteria.text: Root-colonising bacteria that harm plant growth, first described from sugar beet crops.

bradyrhizobium.text: A genus of Gram-negative soil bacteria, many of which fix nitrogen in the root nodules of legumes.

rhizotron.text: An underground laboratory built to study soil and its interactions with plants and animals.

azospirillum.text: A genus of Gram-negative, microaerophilic nitrogen-fixing bacteria that can promote plant growth.

common symbiosis signaling pathway.text: A highly conserved chain of signals in plant root cells that lets plants take in symbiotic microbes such as arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and rhizobia.

ectomycorrhizal exploration types.text: A classification of ectomycorrhizal fungi by the growth pattern and biomass of their extramatrical mycelium and whether they form rhizomorphs.

pneumatophores.text: Specialized aerial roots that let plants breathe air where the soil is waterlogged.

rhizosphere ecology.text: The web of mutualism, predation and competition among the microbes and soil animals that rhizodeposition supports around and inside roots.

farming practices and the mycorrhizosphe.text: The ways the timing, machinery and chemicals of farming help or harm the mycorrhizosphere that crops rely on for nutrients and pathogen resistance.

fine root classification.text: Schemes that divide fine roots by diameter, position in the branching hierarchy or function.

plant-growth promoting fungi.text: Non-pathogenic, filamentous soil fungi that colonise roots, chiefly in the rhizosphere, and benefit plant health and development.

rhizodeposition.text: The addition of organic matter to soil by living roots, which exude compounds and slough off cells, especially at their tips.

plant litter.text: Dead plant material such as leaves, bark, needles and twigs that has fallen onto the soil surface, forming the litter layer or O horizon.

decomposition.text: The process by which dead organic substances are broken down into simpler organic or inorganic matter such as carbon dioxide, water, simple sugars and mineral salts.

humus.text: The stable, well-decomposed form of soil organic matter, derived from the breakdown of plant and animal remains.

organic matter.text: The large pool of carbon-based compounds in natural and engineered environments, derived from the feces and remains of organisms such as plants and animals.

detritus.text: Organic matter made up of the decomposing remains of organisms and plant material, and of feces.

mineralization (soil science).text: The decomposition, or oxidation, of organic compounds by which their nutrients are released in soluble inorganic forms that plants may take up.

particulate organic matter.text: The fraction of organic matter, operationally defined, that does not pass a filter or sieve with openings usually between 0.053 millimetres (53 μm) and 2 millimetres.

humification.text: The transformation of part of the decomposing organic matter into humus, instead of its full mineralization, by soil organisms feeding on litter.

humus and soil fertility.text: The benefits humus brings to farm soils, chiefly better soil structure and a large surface that holds nutrient elements until plants need them.

humus stability.text: The persistence of humus in soil: stable humus resists decomposition for a century or more, while labile humus breaks down within about ten years.

saprotroph.text: An organism that feeds on dead organic matter or waste by secreting chemicals that digest it outside its body, rather than eating it as detritivores do.

litterfall nutrient cycling.text: The return of nutrients from plants to the soil through fallen litter and its decomposition, the main pathway for recycling nitrogen and phosphorus.

forest floor.text: The layer of decaying plant litter and other dead plant matter, also called duff, that mediates between a forest's living vegetation and its mineral and humus-rich soil.

decomposer.text: An organism that breaks down dead organisms and releases the nutrients in the dead matter into its surroundings.

humus form.text: The group of organic and mineral-organic horizons at or near the soil surface, formed from organic residues, that characterizes how litter becomes humus in a given place.

forest litter raking.text: The old practice of raking forest leaf litter to use in place of straw for livestock bedding, widespread in Europe since the seventeenth century.

leaf litter habitat.text: The litter layer as a home and food source for decomposers, plants and larger animals.

litterbag.text: A container or mesh bag set out for a fixed time to collect falling plant litter or to measure how fast confined litter decays.

humus composition.text: The chemical make-up of humus: very large, complex molecules built partly from lignin and other plant polyphenols and partly from similar molecules made by microbes.

mangrove litterfall.text: Litter that reaches coasts from rivers or falls in mangrove forests, which follows a very different path from litter on land.

lignin.text: A class of complex organic polymers, made by cross-linking phenolic precursors, that form key structural materials in plant support tissues, especially wood and bark.

detritus food chain.text: A food chain, also called the detritus cycle, linking detritus, the microorganisms that multiply on it and the detritivores that feed on both.

priming effect.text: A change, positive or negative, in the rate at which soil organic matter decomposes, caused by adding something to soil or compost.

mull humus.text: A humus form in which burrowing soil animals mix organic matter thoroughly into the mineral soil, giving a granular A horizon and no OH horizon.

mor humus.text: A humus form of coniferous forests and ericaceous heaths in which litter decomposes very slowly and accumulates on the soil with little mixing into the mineral soil.

hydrogen cycle.text: The exchange of hydrogen-containing compounds between living and non-living sources and sinks, focused on molecular hydrogen (H2).

glomalin.text: A hypothetical glycoprotein said to be produced abundantly on the hyphae and spores of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi in soil and roots.

moder humus.text: A humus form intermediate between mull and mor, in which litter decomposes slowly and builds up on the mineral soil, mainly as the fecal pellets of litter-dwelling invertebrates.

kerogen.text: Solid, insoluble organic matter in sedimentary rocks, formed from dead plants, algae and microorganisms compressed and heated over geological time.

humin.text: The insoluble, carbon-based macromolecular fraction of soil organic matter, the most resistant of the humic substances.

soil organic matter fractions.text: The grouping of the non-living organic matter in soil into four categories by size, behaviour and persistence, in order of decreasing ease of decomposition.

humus form change.text: The shifting of a site's humus form over time in response to vegetation dynamics, land use, pollution and climate change.

humus form diagnostic horizons.text: The sequence of surface horizons used to identify humus forms, following the stages of litter decomposition and its gradual mixing into mineral matter.

dissolved organic matter.text: Organic matter dissolved in water, operationally the fraction that passes a filter with pores of about 0.22 to 0.7 micrometres; its carbon is called dissolved organic carbon (DOC).

coarse woody debris.text: Fallen dead trees and the remains of large branches lying on the ground in forests, rivers and wetlands.

leaf mold.text: Compost formed as fallen tree and shrub leaves decompose, mainly through slow, cool fungal breakdown rather than bacterial decay.

hemicellulose.text: Any of a group of branched matrix polysaccharides, such as arabinoxylans, found with cellulose in almost all land-plant cell walls.

amphi humus.text: A humus form, also called twin mull or amphimull, that combines moder-like OF and OH horizons with a mull-like granular A horizon.

humusica.text: A worldwide morpho-functional classification of humus forms, created in the 2010s.

tangel humus.text: A mountain humus form on hard limestone or dolomite in cold, humid climates, with a thick accumulated organic layer resting on rock and little or no A horizon.

glomalin controversy.text: The dispute over whether glomalin is a real fungal protein or an artefact of an extraction that also pulls out humic substances and other soil proteins.

photodegradation.text: The alteration of materials by light, often used loosely for the combined action of sunlight and air.

canopy soils.text: Soils, also called arboreal soils, that form where branches, crevices or other features of trees in the forest canopy trap organic matter such as leaves and fine branches.

cutin.text: A waxy polymer that, with cutan, forms the main part of the plant cuticle covering all aerial plant surfaces.

litter quality.text: The chemical make-up of fallen plant material, such as its nutrient, lignin and tannin content, which governs how fast it decomposes and which humus form develops.

microbial necromass.text: The dead biomass of soil microbes, left as cells die and their remains enter the soil organic matter.

humus index.text: An ordinal numerical scale covering all lowland terrestrial humus forms, ranked by the growing share of organic layers in the humus profile.

suberin.text: A lipophilic, complex polyester biopolymer of plants, made of long-chain fatty acids and glycerol.

soil continuum model.text: The view that soil organic matter is a continuum of progressively decomposing organic compounds rather than a set of distinct, persistent humic substances.

canopy soil nitrogen cycling.text: The nitrogen cycle within canopy soils, which feeds epiphytes and also affects the fertility of the forest floor below.

saprophagy.text: Feeding on decomposing dead plant or animal biomass; organisms that do so are saprophages.

white-rot fungi.text: Wood- and litter-decaying fungi that break down lignin, one of the main precursors of humus.

exoenzyme.text: An enzyme that a cell secretes and that works outside it, most often to break down large molecules.

fungal extracellular enzyme activity.text: The secretion by fungi of enzymes that break down complex organic matter outside the cell; most such enzymes in leaf litter and soil come from fungi.

amplicon.text: A piece of DNA that is the source or product of amplification or replication.

metabarcoding.text: DNA or RNA barcoding done so that many taxa in one sample are identified at once.

lignin peroxidase.text: A heme-containing peroxidase enzyme, one of the ligninases, that uses hydrogen peroxide to cleave lignin-like compounds.

michaelis–menten kinetics.text: The simplest model of enzyme kinetics, for reactions that turn one substrate into one product.

manganese peroxidase.text: A heme peroxidase enzyme that uses hydrogen peroxide to oxidise manganese(II) to manganese(III).

amino sugar.text: A sugar molecule in which a hydroxyl group has been replaced by an amine group.

microbial biomass.text: The living microbes of soil and their metabolites, a few percent of soil organic matter with a short residence time.

ecological stoichiometry.text: The study of how the balance of energy and elements affects living systems, and how organisms affect that balance.

acid phosphatase.text: An enzyme that frees attached phosphate groups from other molecules, working best at acidic pH.

β-glucosidase.text: An enzyme that hydrolyses terminal β-D-glucosyl residues, releasing glucose.

soil enzyme assays.text: Laboratory methods that estimate enzyme activity in soil or litter by mixing samples with buffers and a substrate.

microbial carbon use efficiency.text: A measure of how much of the carbon a microbe takes up goes into biomass rather than into maintenance energy.

microbial carbon pump.text: A process in which microorganisms turn dissolved organic carbon into refractory forms that resist further microbial degradation.

stable-isotope probing.text: A microbial ecology technique that traces nutrient uptake by microorganisms by feeding them substrate enriched in a heavy stable isotope.

q10 (temperature coefficient).text: A unitless measure of temperature sensitivity: the factor by which a reaction rate changes for a 10 °C rise.

resistome.text: All the antibiotic resistance genes in communities of pathogenic and non-pathogenic bacteria.

soil classification.text: The systematic grouping of soils by their distinguishing characteristics and by criteria that guide how they are used.

world reference base for soil resources.term: World Reference Base for Soil Resources
world reference base for soil resources.text: An international soil classification system for naming soils and building soil-map legends, edited by a working group of the International Union of Soil Sciences.

usda soil taxonomy.text: The soil classification of the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the National Cooperative Soil Survey, which sorts soils by their properties into six levels from order to series.

soil type.text: A taxonomic unit of soil science: all soils that share a defined set of properties.

fao soil classification.text: A supra-national soil classification developed by the FAO, generalizing how soils form from the interaction of the main soil-forming factors.

canadian system of soil classification.text: Canada's national soil classification, closer to the U.S. system than any other but designed to cover only Canadian soils.

australian soil classification.text: The general-purpose, hierarchical system currently used to describe and classify soils in Australia.

engineering soil classification.text: The grouping of soils by the engineering properties that matter when they support foundations or serve as building material.

natural and technical classification.text: The contrast between natural systems, which group soils by intrinsic properties, behaviour or genesis, and technical systems, which group them by fitness for a particular use.

soil moisture regime.text: A class describing how wet a soil stays through the year, defined by the groundwater table and the water available to plants.

1938 usda soil taxonomy.text: The earlier U.S. soil classification, which divided soils into three orders according to their dominant soil-forming factors.

osha soil classification.text: A U.S. workplace-safety scheme that sorts soils by strength so that excavations and trenches can be protected against collapse.

wrb diagnostics.text: The diagnostic horizons, diagnostic properties and diagnostic materials on which the WRB bases its classification.

reference soil groups.text: The 32 top-level classes of the World Reference Base, each with a two-letter code, listed in the order of its key.

vineyard soils.text: The soils in which grapevines grow, whose make-up is one of the most important considerations in planting a vineyard.

soil temperature regime.text: A class of soil temperature, set by mean annual and seasonal temperatures at 50 cm depth, used to classify soils in USDA soil taxonomy.

soil series.text: The lowest level of USDA soil taxonomy, grouping pedons with similar pedogenesis, soil chemistry and physical properties.

usda suborders and great groups.text: The second and third levels of USDA soil taxonomy: suborders split each order by properties tied to soil moisture and temperature, and great groups split suborders by the kind and sequence of horizons.

usda soil subgroups.text: The fourth level of USDA soil taxonomy, which divides each great group into typic, intergrade and extragrade subgroups.

usda soil family.text: The fifth level of USDA soil taxonomy: a group of soils within a subgroup sharing the physical and chemical properties that govern their response to farming and engineering.

state soil.text: A soil that a U.S. state has chosen as having special significance to it.

udic moisture regime.text: The soil moisture regime of humid climates, where stored moisture plus rainfall roughly equals or exceeds evapotranspiration.

aashto soil classification system.text: An American highway-engineering system that classifies soils and soil–aggregate mixtures for road construction.

naming a soil with the wrb.term: Naming a soil with the WRB
naming a soil with the wrb.text: The WRB procedure that keys a soil out to a Reference Soil Group and then adds every qualifier that applies to it.

argillic.text: The USDA soil taxonomy term for a subsurface horizon enriched in clay.

wrb map legends.text: The WRB rules for naming the units of a soil map, where the number of qualifiers used depends on the map's scale.

ranker (soil).text: A soil developed over non-calcareous material, usually rock.

ustic.text: A soil moisture regime in which water is present but limited at times when conditions suit plant growth, intermediate between aridic and udic.

polish soil classification.text: The system used to describe, classify and organize knowledge about the soils of Poland.

miami (soil).text: A soil series of the Wisconsin Till Plains that is the state soil of Indiana.

pedalfer.text: In the 1938 U.S. classification, a major group of soils rich in aluminium and iron, in which sesquioxides increase relative to silica as the soil forms.

brunisolic order.text: The Canadian order for soils with developed B horizons that meet the requirements of none of the other orders.

canadian organic order.text: The Canadian order of soils made mostly of organic matter, over 30% by weight in the upper half metre, without permafrost near the surface.

chernozemic order.text: The Canadian order of grassland soils whose A horizon is darkened by organic matter, mostly from decaying grass roots.

cryosolic order.text: The Canadian order of soils with permafrost within 1 metre of the surface, or 2 metres if strongly churned by frost.

gleysolic order.text: The Canadian order of soils that are periodically or permanently saturated with water and depleted of oxygen.

luvisolic order.text: The Canadian order of soils with a leached Ae horizon above a Bt horizon in which the washed-down clay has been deposited.

podzolic order.text: The Canadian order of acid soils whose B horizon accumulates amorphous humified organic matter bound to aluminium and iron.

regosolic order.text: The Canadian order of weakly developed soils whose properties are essentially those of their parent material.

solonetzic order.text: The Canadian order of soils whose B horizon is very hard when dry and swells into a sticky, compact mass when wet, because of sodium.

vertisolic order.text: The Canadian order of clay-rich soils that shrink and swell markedly as they dry and wet.

anthroposol.text: A soil profoundly modified or constructed by people, with one or more natural horizons altered, removed or replaced.

kurosol.text: One of the fifteen soil orders of the Australian Soil Classification: soils with a sharp texture contrast between a lighter surface and a strongly acidic, clay-rich subsoil.

référentiel pédologique.text: The French soil reference system, a natural classification based on presumed soil genesis.

greyzem.text: A soil group of the FAO soil classification, named from English 'grey' and Russian zemlja, 'earth'.

handbook of australian soils.text: An earlier soil classification system developed for Australian soils.

aquic conditions.text: A soil moisture regime in which the soil is saturated long enough each year to be virtually free of dissolved oxygen.

aridic moisture regime.text: The soil moisture regime of arid and semi-arid climates, in which soil is dry for at least half the growing season and moist for less than 90 consecutive days.

iso 14688.text: The international standard that sets basic principles for identifying and classifying soils for engineering purposes.

xeric moisture regime.text: The soil moisture regime typical of Mediterranean climates, with cool, moist winters and warm, dry summers.

zonal soil.text: In the 1938 U.S. system, the order of soils whose character reflects the regional climate and vegetation.

usda soil orders.text: The twelve top-level classes of USDA soil taxonomy, whose criteria reflect major differences in how soils formed.

mollisol.text: A USDA soil order of soils with a deep, dark surface horizon rich in organic matter and nutrients, called the mollic epipedon.

azonal soil.text: Immature soils that never get time to develop because their material keeps sliding downslope or is buried by fresh deposits.

intrazonal soil.text: Soils whose profiles reflect a dominant local factor of relief or parent material more than the zonal effects of climate and vegetation.

vertisol.text: A soil rich in expansive clays that crack deeply when dry and swell when wet; an order in USDA soil taxonomy and a WRB Reference Soil Group.

alfisol.text: A USDA soil order of moderately leached soils with a clay-enriched subsoil and relatively high native fertility.

andisol.text: A USDA soil order of soils formed in volcanic ash, rich in glass and in amorphous colloids such as allophane, imogolite and ferrihydrite.

histosol.text: A soil, in both the WRB and USDA soil taxonomy, made primarily of organic materials.

aridisol.text: A USDA soil order of dry soils of arid and semi-arid climates, also called desert soils.

oxisol.text: A USDA soil order of very highly weathered soils rich in iron and aluminium oxides, best known from tropical rainforest within 25 degrees of the Equator.

ultisol.text: A USDA soil order of strongly weathered, acid mineral soils, commonly known as red clay soils.

entisol.text: A USDA soil order of soils with no profile development beyond an A horizon and no diagnostic horizons, little changed from their parent material.

inceptisol.text: A USDA soil order of young soils with little to moderate development and weathering, more developed than Entisols.

gelisol.text: A USDA soil order of very cold climates, defined by permafrost within two metres of the surface.

psamment.text: A USDA suborder of Entisols made of unconsolidated sand, found in shifting dunes or in very coarse parent material weathered for millions of years.

paleopedology.text: The study of soils of past geological eras, from the recent Quaternary back to the earliest periods of Earth's history.

paleopedological record.text: The fossil record of soils, made up chiefly of paleosols buried by flood sediments or volcanic deposits, or preserved at geological unconformities.

orthent.text: A USDA suborder of Entisols that lack horizon development because of steep slopes or parent materials with no lasting weatherable minerals.

sapric.text: Organic soil material, as in a Histosol, so thoroughly decomposed that plant parts and even faecal matter can no longer be identified.

mollisol suborders.text: The seven suborders of Mollisols, set mainly by soil moisture and temperature regimes.

vertisol suborders.text: The six USDA suborders of Vertisols, set by wetness, temperature and how long their cracks stay open.

fossil record of alfisols.text: The record of Alfisol paleosols, which reaches back to woodland and early forest soils of the Late Devonian.

gardening in ultisols.text: Managing the low organic matter and low pH of red clay Ultisols so that garden plants can grow.

ultisol suborders.text: The five suborders of Ultisols in USDA soil taxonomy, set by wetness, organic matter and climate.

soil in the united states.text: The varied soils of the United States, classified in USDA soil taxonomy down to the series, each a unique kind of soil.

gelisol suborders.text: The three suborders of Gelisols: organic Histels, frost-churned Turbels and little-churned Orthels.
