anthrepts.text: A suborder of Inceptisols in USDA soil taxonomy for soils showing evidence of human habitation and farming.

reconstructing paleosol parent material.text: Estimating the vanished parent material of a fossil soil from nearby materials, to measure how much soil formation took place.

spodosol.text: A USDA soil order of acid soils with a spodic horizon, where organic matter complexed with iron and aluminium has accumulated after leaching from the layer above.

soil climate.text: The moisture, temperature and other climatic conditions within a soil's pores, a special kind of microclimate.

trace fossils in paleosols.text: Footprints, burrows, coprolites and root traces preserved in fossil soils as evidence of the activity of past organisms.

muck farming.text: Farming drained swamp soils of sapric organic matter, or muck, mostly for vegetables.

calcid.text: A suborder of Aridisols in USDA soil taxonomy that has accumulated high levels of residual or dust-fall calcium carbonate.

podzol.text: An acid soil with an organic topsoil over a bleached, ash-grey leached layer and an iron-, aluminium- or humus-enriched subsoil; the typical soil of boreal and coniferous forests.

chernozem.text: A black soil, also called black earth or regur, with 4% to 16% humus and plenty of phosphorus and ammonia compounds; a WRB reference soil group.

solonchak.text: A WRB reference soil group of pale or grey, poorly drained soils of arid to subhumid lands with high concentrations of soluble salts.

solonetz.text: A WRB reference soil group with a clay-enriched subsoil high in exchangeable sodium, the natric horizon, within the upper 100 cm.

anthrosol.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils formed or heavily changed by long-term human use, such as irrigation, added organic waste or paddy-field cultivation.

gleysol.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils saturated by groundwater long enough, unless drained, to develop gleyic colours: grey or blue inside, rusty at ped surfaces.

fluvisol.text: A WRB reference soil group of genetically young, stratified soils in river, lake or marine sediments.

acrisol.text: A WRB reference soil group of strongly weathered soils with low-activity clays, in which exchangeable aluminium exceeds the exchangeable base cations.

aridity.text: The condition of regions with low annual precipitation, high temperatures and little available water.

leptosol.text: A WRB reference soil group of very shallow soils over continuous rock, or deeper soils packed with gravel and stones.

cambisol.text: A WRB reference soil group of moderately developed soils at the beginning of soil formation, shown by weak brownish colouring or structure in the profile.

luvisol.text: A WRB reference soil group with a clay-enriched subsoil of high-activity clays, in which base cations equal or exceed exchangeable aluminium.

technosol.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils whose properties and formation are dominated by their technical, human-made origin.

calcisol.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils with a substantial secondary accumulation of lime (calcium carbonate).

andosol.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils formed in volcanic ash and other tephra, rich in allophane or in complexes of aluminium and organic matter.

regosol.text: A WRB reference soil group of very weakly developed mineral soils in unconsolidated material, with no significant profile development.

alisol.text: A WRB reference soil group of acidic soils with high-activity clays, in which exchangeable aluminium exceeds the exchangeable base cations.

stagnosol.text: A WRB reference soil group with strong mottling caused by redox processes under stagnating surface water, without a marked texture change.

planosol.text: A WRB reference soil group with a pale, coarse-textured topsoil showing periodic water stagnation that abruptly overlies a dense, slowly permeable, much more clayey subsoil.

phaeozem.text: A WRB reference soil group of dark soils with a high base status but no secondary carbonates within one metre of the surface.

kastanozem.text: A WRB reference soil group, also called chestnut soil, with a dark, humus-rich topsoil and secondary carbonates.

lixisol.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils with a subsurface build-up of low-activity clays and high base saturation, where base cations equal or exceed exchangeable aluminium.

plaggen soil.text: A deep, humus-rich anthropogenic soil, or plaggic Anthrosol, built up on poor podzols of north-west Europe from the Middle Ages by plaggen farming.

nitisol.text: A WRB reference soil group of deep, red, well-drained tropical soils with at least 30% clay and a strong polyhedral or blocky structure.

umbrisol.text: A WRB reference soil group with a dark, organic-rich mineral topsoil of low base saturation.

retisol.text: A WRB reference soil group in which a pale, clay-poor eluvial horizon tongues in a net-like pattern into the darker, clay-rich argic horizon below.

black dirt region.text: A drained former marsh in Orange County, New York, and Sussex County, New Jersey, named for its dark, extremely fertile sapric muck soil.

plinthosol.text: A WRB reference soil group defined by plinthite, petroplinthite or pisoliths, iron-oxide concretions, in a plinthic horizon starting within 50 cm of the surface.

gypsisol.text: A WRB reference soil group of soils with a substantial secondary accumulation of gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O).

peat.text: An accumulation of partially decayed vegetation or organic matter, found in peatlands, bogs, mires, moors and muskegs.

wrb argic soil groups.text: The five WRB reference soil groups that must have an argic, clay-enriched subsoil horizon: Retisols, Acrisols, Lixisols, Alisols and Luvisols.

theories of chernozem origin.text: The competing explanations, offered since 1763, for how chernozem's thick black topsoil formed.

durisol.text: A WRB reference soil group of free-draining dryland soils whose grains are cemented by secondary silica in the upper metre, as nodules or as a continuous hardpan.

albeluvisols.text: A former WRB reference soil group (1998 and 2006 editions): soils with a thin dark topsoil over a bleached albic horizon that tongues into a clay-enriched Bt horizon.

peat drainage.text: The draining of peat soils, often through canals, for agriculture, forestry and peat extraction.

peat fires.text: Fires in peat deposits, which smoulder underground for long periods and are not put out by light rain.

peat formation.text: The build-up of peat where plant material fails to decay fully under acidic, oxygen-poor, waterlogged conditions.

serpentine soil.text: An uncommon soil formed from weathered ultramafic rock, such as peridotite and serpentinite, that contains minerals of the serpentine group.

charcoal.text: A lightweight black carbon residue made by strongly heating wood or other plant and animal material in minimal oxygen, driving off water and volatile compounds.

terra preta.text: A very dark, fertile, human-made soil (an anthrosol) of the Amazon Basin, also called Amazonian dark earth.

brown earth.text: A well-drained, fertile type of soil found mainly in humid temperate climates.

peat archives.text: The record of past vegetation, pollen, spores, animals and archaeological remains preserved layer by layer in a peat profile.

peat fuel.text: Dried peat burned for heat and power, traditionally cut by hand and left to dry in the sun.

peat hags.text: A form of erosion at the sides of gullies cut into peat, leaving overhanging banks of peat and vegetation.

rendzina.text: A shallow, humus-rich soil formed on carbonate-rich, or occasionally sulfate-rich, parent rock, recognized in British, German and some obsolete classifications.

peat in horticulture.text: The use of peat as a raw material for gardening and horticulture, now being restricted in some places.

peat material types.text: The division of peat material into fibric, hemic and sapric kinds by how far it has decomposed.

peatland permafrost.text: Permanently frozen peat ground, which makes up around half the area of northern peatlands.

peatland restoration.text: Repairing damaged peatlands, usually by blocking drainage channels so they rewet and native vegetation recovers.

terra rossa.text: A well-drained, reddish, clayey to silty soil of neutral pH, typical of the Mediterranean region.

dark earth.text: A dark, organic-rich layer up to 1 m thick that, in geology and archaeology, marks long-lasting human settlement.

charcoal in terra preta.text: The low-temperature charcoal, a form of pyrogenic or black carbon, that indigenous farmers added to poor soils to make terra preta.

tropical peat.text: A histosol of tropical latitudes, found in South East Asia, Africa and Central and South America.

red soil.text: A reddish, clay-rich soil that typically develops in warm, temperate and humid climates and makes up about 13% of Earth's soil.

brown podzolic.text: A class of the British soil classification, grouped with the podzolic soils but intermediate between podzols and brown earths.

bay mud.text: Thick deposits of soft, water-saturated, unconsolidated silty clay on the floors of certain estuaries, mostly in temperate regions shaped by glacial cycles.

origin of terra preta.text: The question of how Amazonian dark earths came to exist: made on purpose, built up from settlement refuse, or improved from naturally fertile patches.

synthetic terra preta.text: A fertilizer made from materials meant to replicate those of terra preta, such as crushed clay, blood and bone meal, manure and biochar.

subaqueous soil.text: Soil formed in sediment of shallow, permanently flooded environments, or in any area under water too deep for rooted plants to grow.

brickearth.text: A superficial deposit of homogeneous loam or silt, first named in southern England, that is periglacial wind-blown loess.

fill dirt.text: Earthy material used to fill a depression or hole, build mounds or otherwise artificially change the level of land.

stagnogley.text: A non-alluvial, non-calcareous loamy or clayey soil with a dense, impervious subsurface horizon, classed among the gleyic soils.

calcareous grassland.text: A grassland ecosystem on thin, basic soils such as those of chalk and limestone downland, also called alkaline grassland.

takir.text: A smooth, bare clay flat in the deserts of Central Asia, similar to a salt flat; the Turkic name means 'smooth, even, or bare'.

serpentine barrens.text: Grassland or savanna on serpentine outcrops where the climate would otherwise support forest, found as an ecoregion in parts of the United States.

serpentine plant communities.text: The distinctive flora of serpentine soils, marked by poor productivity, high endemism and tolerance of drought, heavy metals and scarce nutrients.

blue goo.text: A sticky, plastic, bluish-grey clay soil formed from highly weathered serpentinite mélange.

duplex soil.text: An Australian term for a soil with a sharp contrast in texture between its horizons, also called a texture contrast soil.

constructed soil.text: A mixture of organic and mineral materials, often including repurposed organic waste, designed to approximate natural soil and grow plants.

origin of terra rossa.text: The long-running dispute among geologists, geomorphologists and soil scientists over what terra rossa formed from and how it relates to the carbonate rock beneath it.

latosol.text: A tropical rainforest soil, also called tropical red earth, with a relatively high content of iron and aluminium oxides.

gumbo soil.text: A soil dominated by very fine clay particles, often with small amounts of sand or organic material.

mesotrophic soil.text: A soil of moderate inherent fertility, between eutrophic and oligotrophic soils.

acrotelm.text: The upper of the two layers of an undisturbed peat bog, holding living plants, which overlies the catotelm.

subaqueous soil mapping.text: Surveying underwater soils much as land soils are mapped, except that the mapper works from the water.

machair.text: A fertile, low-lying grassy plain of dune grassland on parts of the north-western coasts of Ireland and Scotland, especially the Outer Hebrides.

black cotton soil.text: The black, clayey soil of India's Deccan Plateau, also called regur, named for its suitability for growing cotton.

paddy soil.text: The soil of flooded rice paddies, counted among the anthropogenic soils.

soil fertility.text: The ability of a soil to sustain agricultural plant growth, giving plants a habitat and steady, high-quality yields.

plant nutrition.text: The study of the chemical elements and compounds plants need for growth, reproduction and metabolism, and of how they are supplied.

nutrient.text: A substance an organism uses to survive, grow and reproduce.

soil depletion.text: The decline of a soil's fertility when the components that make it fertile are removed and not replaced, and the conditions that support fertility are not maintained.

essential plant nutrients.text: The chemical elements a plant must have to complete its life cycle; sixteen are usually listed as essential for growth and reproduction.

soil test.text: A laboratory or in-situ analysis to determine the chemical, physical or biological characteristics of a soil.

colonial soil depletion.text: The loss of soil fertility caused by colonial settlers' land practices, such as free-ranging livestock, unmanured fields and heavy burning in colonial New England.

irrigation effects on soil fertility.text: How the quality of irrigation water, and how well it drains away, maintains, degrades or improves a soil's fertility and tilth.

liebig's law of the minimum.text: The principle that growth is set not by the total resources available but by the scarcest one, the limiting factor.

nutrient management.text: The science and practice of linking soil, crop, weather and water conditions with farming and conservation practices to use nutrients efficiently for yield, quality and profit while limiting their loss to the environment.

macronutrients and micronutrients.text: The division of plant nutrients into macronutrients, taken up in relatively large amounts, and micronutrients, needed only in small amounts.

soil depletion under plantation slavery.text: The exhaustion and abandonment of land on Southern slave plantations, whose owners sought to maximize the labour extracted rather than the output per acre.

soil fertility and human health.text: The idea, championed by Albert Howard, that the health of crops, livestock and people begins with a fertile, well-kept soil.

plant micronutrients.text: Essential elements that plants and other organisms need only in very small amounts, mostly as required parts of enzyme systems.

nutrient mobility in plants.text: How readily a nutrient can be moved within a plant from older tissues to where it is most needed.

nutrient deficiency in plants.text: The effects on a plant of too little of an essential nutrient, ranging from slightly slower growth to stunting, deformity, discoloration and death.

soil fertilization.text: Adding the nutrients a soil most often lacks for crops, above all phosphorus, nitrogen and potassium, the three elements every commercial fertilizer analysis lists.

nitrogen as a plant nutrient.text: Nitrogen, the most critical element plants draw from the soil, taken up as the ammonium cation or the nitrate anion.

molybdenum deficiency.text: Limited plant growth because a plant cannot take up enough of the essential micronutrient molybdenum from its growing medium.

engineering soil tests.text: Soil tests in geotechnical engineering that measure physical characteristics such as water content, void ratio and bulk density.

grid soil sampling.text: Collecting GPS-located soil samples on a regular grid to estimate how nutrients vary across a field.

testing soil for lead.text: Soil testing for lead, a particularly dangerous soil contaminant, to judge the health risk of garden soil.

carbon-to-nitrogen ratio.text: The ratio of the mass of carbon to the mass of nitrogen in organic residues.

nutrient movement to roots.text: The movement of dissolved nutrient ions through the soil to root surfaces by mass flow, diffusion and root interception.

root nutrient uptake.text: How plants take essential elements in through their roots, above all the root hairs, and pass them to the conducting tissues.

phosphorus as a plant nutrient.text: Phosphorus, a primary plant nutrient and, after nitrogen, probably the element most likely to be deficient in soils.

potassium as a plant nutrient.text: Potassium, a primary nutrient present in all plant parts that activates enzymes, though it is not built into any major plant constituent.

boron as a plant nutrient.text: Boron, a micronutrient that affects flowering, fruiting, pollen germination, cell division and the forming of cell walls.

hydroponics.text: Growing plants in a water-nutrient solution instead of nutrient-rich soil or substrate.

iron as a plant nutrient.text: Iron, a micronutrient plants need to make chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.

nutrient interactions.text: The ways the supply of one nutrient affects the uptake, movement or action of another in plants.

plant nutrient toxicity.text: Harm to a plant from a nutrient present at too high a level.

plant tissue analysis.text: Chemical analysis of plant tissue to describe a plant's nutrient status, also called its ionome or nutrient profile.

zinc as a plant nutrient.text: Zinc, a micronutrient required by a large number of plant enzymes and essential to DNA transcription.

compost feedstock c:n balance.text: Balancing the carbon and nitrogen in compost feedstocks, which matters for compost much as for soil feedstock.

sediment c/n ratio.text: Use of the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of sediments as a proxy for the sources of their organic matter and for past climate.

nutrient depletion.text: The loss of nutrients and micronutrients from a habitat, most often the soil; a form of resource depletion.

iron deficiency chlorosis.text: A plant disorder, also called lime-induced chlorosis, in which a plant gets too little iron to make enough chlorophyll, so its leaves turn yellow.

chlorosis.text: A condition in which leaves make too little chlorophyll and turn pale, yellow or yellow-white.

nitrogen deficiency.text: A plant disorder in which a plant cannot obtain enough nitrogen from the soil, causing stunting, poor flowering and fruiting, and chlorosis.

nutrient management plan.text: A farm plan that makes all the nutrient sources a crop uses more efficient while lowering production and environmental risk.

beneficial plant elements.text: Elements that improve plant health but whose absence does not stop the life cycle, such as cobalt, strontium, vanadium, silicon and nickel.

calcium as a plant nutrient.text: Calcium, a secondary macronutrient that forms part of plant cell walls and reaches plants as exchangeable ions and moderately soluble minerals.

nitrogen management.text: Managing applied nitrogen so crops use it as efficiently as possible and as little as possible is lost from the soil.

carbon in plant nutrition.text: The supply of carbon to plants, taken mainly as carbon dioxide from the air through photosynthesis.

magnesium as a plant nutrient.text: Magnesium, a secondary macronutrient best known as a constituent of the chlorophyll molecule.

nitrogen losses from soil.text: The escape of usable nitrogen from soil through leaching of nitrate, denitrification and ammonia volatilization.

soil and crop nitrogen tests.text: Tests of soil and plants used to judge whether, and how much, nitrogen a crop needs.

sulfur as a plant nutrient.text: Sulfur, a secondary macronutrient that is part of some amino acids and vitamins and is essential for chloroplasts.

mitscherlich's law of physiological rela.text: Alexander Mitscherlich's 1909 law relating crop yield to the quantity of plant food by a logarithmic function.

barren vegetation.text: Land where plant growth is sparse or stunted and biodiversity may be limited.

illinois soil nitrogen test.text: A method, introduced in 2007, that measures the soil nitrogen available to plants by estimating amino sugar nitrogen.

manganese deficiency.text: A plant disorder from too little available manganese, often confused with and occurring alongside iron deficiency.

boron deficiency.text: A shortage of the micronutrient boron in plants, the most widespread micronutrient deficiency, which stops cell expansion, kills growing points and reduces fertility.

liebig's barrel.text: A picture of the law of the minimum: a barrel with staves of unequal length holds water only up to its shortest stave.

phosphorus deficiency.text: A plant disorder caused by an insufficient supply of phosphorus, taken up as phosphate ions.

potassium deficiency.text: A plant disorder caused by depletion of potassium ions in the soil, also called potash deficiency.

zinc deficiency.text: Limited plant growth because the plant cannot take up enough of the essential micronutrient zinc from its growing medium.

nitrogen use efficiency.text: The proportion of the nitrogen present that a plant absorbs and uses.

law of the maximum.text: A principle developed by Arthur Wallace that total crop growth is proportional to about 70 growth factors and cannot exceed their aggregate value.

biogeochemical cycle.text: The movement and transformation of chemical elements and compounds between living things, the atmosphere, water and Earth's crust, including the soil.

calcium deficiency.text: A plant disorder caused by too little available calcium in the growing medium or, more often, by low transpiration of the plant or the affected tissue.

hoagland solution.text: A standard hydroponic nutrient solution that supplies every essential plant element, devised by Hoagland and Snyder in 1933.

non-destructive plant tissue tests.text: Field tests that estimate a crop's nitrogen status from leaf chlorophyll without destroying the sample, faster than laboratory analysis.

luxury consumption.text: Uptake by a plant of more of a nutrient than healthy growth needs, as happens with potassium when soil levels are high.

nitrogen cycle.text: The biogeochemical cycle in which nitrogen changes between chemical forms as it moves among the air, land and sea.

nitrogen fixation.text: The conversion of the abundant but unreactive nitrogen gas of the air into usable nitrogen compounds such as ammonia and nitrate.

phosphorus cycle.text: The biogeochemical cycle that moves phosphorus through rocks, water and living things.

sulfur cycle.text: The biogeochemical cycle in which sulfur moves between rocks, waters and living things, changing its oxidation state as it goes.

nutrient cycle.text: The movement and exchange of inorganic and organic matter back into the production of living matter, also called ecological recycling.

immobilization (soil science).text: The conversion of inorganic nutrients into organic compounds by microbes or plants, which makes them unavailable to plants; the opposite of mineralization.

calcium cycle.text: The transfer of calcium between dissolved and solid forms as it moves through rocks, soils, waters and living things.

ammonification.text: The conversion by bacteria and fungi of organic nitrogen in dead organisms and wastes into ammonia or ammonium.

nitrification.text: The biological oxidation of ammonia to nitrate, by way of nitrite.

nitrifying bacteria.text: Chemolithotrophic bacteria that get their energy by oxidizing ammonia or nitrite, including the genera Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter and Nitrospira.

reactive nitrogen.text: All forms of nitrogen in the environment except unreactive nitrogen gas, also called fixed nitrogen.

haber–bosch process.text: The main industrial method of making ammonia, combining nitrogen from the air with hydrogen over an iron catalyst.

nitrosomonas.text: A genus of Gram-negative bacteria that oxidize ammonia to nitrite, one of five genera of ammonia-oxidizing bacteria.

nitrification inhibitor.text: A chemical added with ammonia, ammonium or urea fertilizers to slow their conversion to nitrate in the soil.

denitrification.text: The microbial reduction of nitrate, through a series of gaseous nitrogen oxides, to nitrogen gas.

iron cycle.text: The biogeochemical cycle of iron, chiefly its cycling between the +2 (ferrous) and +3 (ferric) oxidation states.

discovery of biological nitrogen fixatio.text: The nineteenth-century research showing that living organisms, above all bacteria, fix nitrogen from the air.

oxygen cycle.text: The movement of oxygen through the Earth's atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and crust.

denitrifying bacteria.text: A diverse group of bacteria from many phyla that carry out denitrification, reducing nitrate to nitrogen gases.

human impact on the nitrogen cycle.term: Human impact on the nitrogen cycle
human impact on the nitrogen cycle.text: The large changes people have made to the global nitrogen cycle, chiefly through synthetic fertilizer and fossil fuel burning.

nitrogen assimilation.text: The uptake of nitrate or ammonium by plants and microbes and its incorporation into their own organic compounds.

mercury cycle.text: The biogeochemical cycle in which natural and human processes move mercury between chemical forms and environments.

reservoirs and residence time.text: The places where elements are held during a cycle: long-term reservoirs and short-term exchange pools, with residence time measuring how long an element stays.

biogeochemistry.text: The science of the chemical, physical, geological and biological processes that govern the make-up of the natural environment, the pedosphere included.

diazotroph.text: An organism, usually a bacterium or archaeon, that can fix atmospheric nitrogen gas into usable compounds such as ammonia.

phosphorus release by weathering.text: The slow freeing of phosphate from minerals such as apatite as rocks weather, the main natural source of phosphorus on land.

soil phosphorus retention.text: The binding of phosphate by soil minerals, by adsorption or precipitation, which keeps dissolved phosphorus low and limits what plants can take up.

silica cycle.text: The biogeochemical cycle that moves silica, including silica made by living things, between the Earth's systems.

ammonia-oxidizing archaea.text: Archaea, mainly of the group Nitrososphaerota, that carry out the first step of nitrification by oxidizing ammonia to nitrite.

discovery of nitrification.text: The late nineteenth-century work that proved nitrification is carried out by microbes in two steps.

bioavailability (soil).text: The amount of an element or compound in soil that an organism can actually take up across its cell membranes.

nitrobacter.text: A genus of rod-shaped, gram-negative, chemoautotrophic bacteria that oxidize nitrite to nitrate in soil and marine systems.

dissimilatory sulfate reduction.text: The reduction of sulfate to hydrogen sulfide by sulfate-reducing microbes, which use sulfate in place of oxygen to oxidize organic compounds.

sulfate-reducing microorganisms.text: Bacteria and archaea that respire anaerobically using sulfate as the terminal electron acceptor, reducing it to hydrogen sulfide.

human impact on the sulfur cycle.term: Human impact on the sulfur cycle
human impact on the sulfur cycle.text: The large rise in sulfur flowing through air, water and soil since people began burning coal and other fossil fuels.

human impact on the phosphorus cycle.term: Human impact on the phosphorus cycle
human impact on the phosphorus cycle.text: The changes people have made to the phosphorus cycle, chiefly by mining phosphate rock for fertilizer.

organic phosphorus mineralization.text: The breakdown of organic phosphorus compounds by enzymes into free phosphate that plants and microbes can use.

urease.text: A nickel-containing enzyme that breaks urea down into carbon dioxide and ammonia.

potassium cycle.text: The biogeochemical cycle that moves potassium through Earth's rocks, soils, living things, air and waters.

soil nitrous oxide emissions.text: The release of nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas, from soils as a by-product of microbial nitrification and denitrification.

nitrogenase.text: The enzyme complex that catalyses the reduction of nitrogen gas to ammonia in nitrogen-fixing microbes.

denitrification-coupled methane oxidatio.text: The anaerobic oxidation of methane by denitrifying bacteria that use the electrons to reduce nitrate, removing both methane and fixed nitrogen.

nitrospira.text: A genus of bacteria that oxidises nitrite to nitrate, the second step of nitrification.

comammox.text: Complete ammonia oxidation: nitrification carried out entirely by one organism, which turns ammonia into nitrite and then nitrate.

anammox.text: Anaerobic ammonium oxidation: a microbial process that turns ammonium and nitrite directly into nitrogen gas and water.

leghemoglobin.text: An oxygen-carrying plant globin found in the nitrogen-fixing root nodules of legumes.

nitrogen cascade.text: The sequential passage of the same reactive nitrogen from one ecosystem to the next, causing effects at each step.

nitrogen deposition.text: The fall of reactive nitrogen from the atmosphere onto land and water, in rain, as gases or as aerosols.

nitrogen saturation.text: The state in which available nitrogen exceeds what vegetation, soil and microbes can take up, so the excess is lost to water and air.

dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammon.text: An anaerobic respiration in which microbes oxidize organic matter using nitrate instead of oxygen, reducing it to nitrite and then to ammonium; also called nitrate ammonification.

microbial sulfur oxidation.text: The oxidation of reduced sulfur compounds, such as sulfide and elemental sulfur, by microorganisms that gain energy from it, often to fix carbon.

selenium cycle.text: The biological cycle of selenium, in which some organisms reduce its oxidised forms and others oxidise the reduced element back again.

soil potassium pools.text: The three forms in which soil holds potassium: fixed in minerals, exchangeable on particle surfaces, and dissolved in soil solution.

phosphate solubilizing bacteria.text: Beneficial soil bacteria that dissolve inorganic phosphate from insoluble compounds, making it available to plants.

sulfur assimilation.text: The process by which living organisms build sulfur into their biological molecules.

nitrous oxide reductase.text: The enzyme that performs the last step of bacterial denitrification, reducing nitrous oxide to nitrogen gas.

nitrogen-15 tracing.text: A technique that uses the heavy stable isotope nitrogen-15 to follow and measure conversions within the nitrogen cycle.

fertilizer.text: Any natural or synthetic material applied to soil or to plant tissues to supply plant nutrients.

compost.text: A mixture of decomposed organic materials used as plant fertilizer and to improve the soil's physical, chemical and biological properties.

soil conditioner.text: A material added to soil to improve its physical qualities, usually its fertility and sometimes its mechanics.

mulch.text: A layer of material applied to the surface of soil.

biochar.text: A form of charcoal, sometimes modified, made by heating biomass with little oxygen and intended for use in soil.

environmental effects of fertilizers.text: The direct and indirect harm that producing and using fertilizers does to water, soil, air and ecosystems.

fertilizer application timing.text: Matching when and how much fertilizer is applied to crop needs, weather and the type of farming.

macronutrients in fertilizers.text: The nutrients fertilizers supply in varying proportions: chiefly nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (NPK), plus micronutrients.

fertilizer classification.text: The grouping of fertilizers by how many nutrients they supply, straight or multinutrient, and by origin, inorganic or organic.

nitrogen fertilizers.text: Fertilizers that supply nitrogen, made from ammonia produced by the Haber–Bosch process.

urea.text: A simple organic nitrogen compound, CO(NH2)2, found in mammal urine and widely used as a nitrogen fertilizer.

agricultural lime.text: A soil additive of pulverized limestone or chalk whose main active component is calcium carbonate.

leachate.text: Any liquid that passes through a material and carries away dissolved or suspended components of it.

liming (soil).text: Adding calcium- and magnesium-rich materials such as marl, chalk, limestone, burnt lime or hydrated lime to soil.

carbon farming.text: A set of farming methods that aim to store carbon in soil and biomass, for a net removal of carbon from the atmosphere.

compost application.text: The use of finished compost on fields, in beds and in growing mixes to add organic matter and nutrients.

perlite.text: An amorphous volcanic glass, usually formed by hydration of obsidian, that expands greatly when heated.

composting.text: The aerobic decomposition of organic solid wastes into a humus-like material, compost.

fertilizer effects on soil biology.text: The changes heavy fertilizer use brings to soil organisms, from root symbioses to soil animals and microbes.

fertilizers and greenhouse gases.text: The carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide released in making and using nitrogen fertilizer, estimated at around 5% of human greenhouse gas emissions.

micronutrient fertilizers.text: Fertilizers that supply elements plants need only in tiny amounts, typically boron, zinc, molybdenum, iron and manganese.

biofertilizer.text: A substance containing living microorganisms that colonize the rhizosphere or plant interior and promote growth by increasing the supply or availability of nutrients.

solid and liquid fertilizers.text: The two physical forms in which fertilizers reach crops: granules, powders or prills, or water-based solutions.

trace mineral depletion.text: The question of why concentrations of micronutrients such as iron, zinc, copper and magnesium in many foods have fallen over the last 50–60 years.

rock flour.text: Fine, silt-sized rock particles made by glaciers grinding bedrock, or by artificial grinding to a similar size.

vermicompost.text: The product of composting with worms: a mix of decomposing food or plant waste, bedding and worm castings (vermicast).

biochar as a soil amendment.text: Mixing biochar into or spreading it on soil to raise fertility, hold water and nutrients and store carbon over the medium to long term.

biochar carbon removal.text: Carbon sequestration by turning biomass into biochar, whose stable carbon then stays locked in soil or other materials.

marl.text: An earthy material rich in carbonate minerals, clay and silt, which becomes marlstone when hardened into rock.

compost organisms.text: The chemical decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi, and physical decomposers, such as worms and insects, that break down compost.

compost tea.text: A liquid of fermented water extracts leached from composted materials, applied to crops.

industrial composting.text: Large-scale composting methods, chiefly in-vessel, aerated static-pile and windrow composting.

phases of composting.text: The sequence of temperature stages that composting passes through under ideal conditions, from mesophilic to thermophilic to cooling and maturation.

controlled-release fertiliser.text: A granulated fertilizer that releases its nutrients into the soil gradually, over a controlled period.

ammonia volatilization from urea.text: The loss of fertilizer nitrogen to the air as ammonia gas when urea breaks down at the soil surface.

hot and cold composting.text: Two ways of composting that differ in pile size and temperature, and so in how long they take.

pathogen removal in composting.text: The killing of pathogens and weed seeds by the heat of composting, and the suppression of plant pathogens by finished compost.

potassium fertilizers.text: Fertilizers that supply potassium, made from potash, a mixture of potassium minerals.

fertilizer burn.text: Damage to a plant caused by too much fertilizer, the wrong type of fertilizer, or too little water applied with it.

raised-bed gardening.text: Gardening in soil raised above ground level and usually enclosed in a frame.

hügelkultur.text: A horticultural technique in which a mound of decaying wood and other compostable plant matter is planted as a raised bed.

manure.text: Organic matter, mostly animal feces, used as organic fertilizer in agriculture.

organic fertilizers.text: Fertilizers of biological origin, derived from living or formerly living materials.

foliar feeding.text: Feeding plants by applying liquid fertilizer directly to their leaves.

hydroabsorbent polymers.text: Polymers such as polyacrylamides and polymethacrylates that absorb several hundred times their own weight in water, tested as soil conditioners.

polyacrylamide soil conditioners.text: Synthetic polyacrylamide polymers added to soil to improve its structure and how it handles water.

green manure.text: A crop grown specifically to be worked into the soil while still green.

animal manure.text: Manure made from livestock dung and urine, handled either as farmyard manure mixed with bedding or as liquid slurry.

bone meal.text: Ground animal bones and slaughterhouse waste, used as a livestock supplement and as a slow-release organic fertilizer.

seaweed fertiliser.text: Organic fertilizer made from seaweed and used to raise soil fertility and plant growth.

guano.text: The accumulated excrement of seabirds or bats, used as fertilizer.

manure management.text: The capture, storage, treatment and use of animal manure in an environmentally sustainable way.

hazards of animal manure.text: The health and environmental risks of animal manure, from pathogens and nitrogen losses to drug residues taken up by crops.

living mulch.text: Low groundcover plants grown under a main crop to slow weeds and give the other benefits of mulch.

organic mulch.text: Mulch of plant or animal residues, such as leaves, straw, bark, wood chips or manure, which decays over time.

plastic mulch.text: Thin plastic sheeting laid over soil, with crops growing through slits or holes in it.

sour mulch.text: Organic mulch that has turned anaerobic and smells of vinegar, ammonia, sulfur or silage.

biochar production.text: Biochar is made mainly by pyrolysis, the heating of biomass without oxygen so that it decomposes instead of burning.

reuse of human excreta.text: The use of treated human excreta for the plant nutrients, organic matter and energy it contains, most often as fertilizer and soil conditioner.

slash-and-char.text: An alternative to slash-and-burn in which cleared vegetation is charred instead of burned, leaving biochar for the soil.

biochar properties.text: The physical and chemical makeup of a biochar, set by its feedstock and production method, which explains how it performs in a given use.

night soil.text: A historical euphemism for human excreta collected, usually at night, from cesspools, privies, pail closets and pit latrines.

biosolids.text: Treated sewage sludge: solid organic matter recovered from sewage treatment and used as fertilizer or soil conditioner.

urine as fertilizer.text: The use of human urine, rich in nitrogen (mostly as urea) and potassium, as a crop fertilizer.

humanure.text: Human excreta used as a nutrient-rich input to composting.

composting toilet.text: A dry toilet that treats human waste by composting, turning it into a compost-like material.

azolla.text: A genus of seven small floating aquatic ferns, the mosquito ferns, that host a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium.

digestate.text: The material left after anaerobic digestion of a biodegradable feedstock, the other main product besides biogas.

isobutylidenediurea.text: An organic compound derived from urea (IBDU) that acts as a controlled-release nitrogen fertilizer.

bokashi.text: An anaerobic, fermentation-based composting method that turns food waste and other organic matter into a soil amendment using specialized bran.

lime requirement.text: The amount of lime needed to neutralize an acid soil, which soil-testing laboratories work out from the soil's base saturation.

liming and soil organic carbon.text: The net change in soil organic carbon after liming, the outcome of three processes pulling in different directions.

structure liming.text: Liming aimed at improving aggregate stability in clay soils, usually with calcium oxide or hydroxide mixed with calcium carbonate.

marling.text: Spreading marl, or raw chalk and lime debris, on fields to improve the soil, one of the oldest soil amendments in agriculture.

aglime and strontium isotope studies.text: The distortion that agricultural lime introduces into strontium-based studies of where prehistoric people lived.

calcium carbonate equivalent.text: A rating that compares a liming material's neutralizing power with that of pure calcium carbonate.

liming of the brazilian cerrado.text: The large-scale liming that turned Brazil's acidic, nutrient-poor cerrado into farmland from the 1960s on.

nutrient release from green manure.text: The breakdown of incorporated green manure by heterotrophic bacteria into nutrients available to the following crop.

compost for soil carbon.text: Spreading compost over the soil surface without tilling so that it stores carbon in a stable form.

grazing management and soil carbon.text: The dispute over whether rotating livestock through small paddocks builds carbon in grassland soils.

feces as fertilizer.text: The use of treated human feces, dried, composted or as fecal sludge, to fertilize crops and add organic carbon to soil.

multiple barrier approach.text: A series of treatment steps and other precautions that together prevent pathogens spreading when excreta are reused in farming.

wood ash.text: The powdery residue left when wood burns, made up largely of calcium compounds.

biofertilizer microorganisms.text: The organisms used in biofertilizers, longest among them the nitrogen fixers Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum and blue-green algae.

fertilizer salt index.text: A measure of how much a fertilizer raises the osmotic pressure of water, compared with sodium nitrate set at 100.

coated urea.text: Controlled-release fertilizers made of urea prills coated in less-soluble materials such as sulfur or polymers.

urease inhibitors.text: Additives that block the urease enzyme so that urea fertilizer stays in its non-volatile form for longer.

nitrification and urease inhibitors.text: Chemicals added to nitrogen fertilizers to slow their conversion in the soil and so make them more efficient.

npk rating.text: A label of three numbers giving a fertilizer's content of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

ammonium nitrate.text: A salt of ammonium and nitrate ions that is an important nitrogen fertilizer, with an NPK rating of 34-0-0.

uan.text: A liquid fertilizer made of urea and ammonium nitrate dissolved in water.

biostimulant.text: A substance, microbial culture or mixture used to promote crop growth that is neither a pesticide nor a fertilizer.

history of fertilizers.text: The development of fertilizer use from ancient manuring and minerals to the synthetic fertilizer industry that grew from the 19th century.

guano age.text: The 19th-century era of large-scale guano export, from Humboldt's investigations at Callao in 1802 to the War of the Pacific.

liquid manure.text: A mixture of animal waste and organic matter, sometimes thinned with water, used as farm fertilizer.

landfill leachate.text: Contaminated liquid formed when rain or other water percolates through landfill waste, which can pollute groundwater if not managed.

converting npk labels to elemental conte.term: Converting NPK labels to elemental content
converting npk labels to elemental conte.text: Calculating a fertilizer's elemental phosphorus and potassium from the P2O5 and K2O values on its NPK label.

phosphate fertilizers.text: Fertilizers that supply phosphorus, extracted from phosphate rock whose main minerals are fluorapatite and hydroxyapatite.

ecological sanitation.text: An approach to sanitation that aims to reuse human excreta safely in agriculture, closing the nutrient loop between sanitation and farming.

polyhalite.text: An evaporite mineral, a hydrated sulfate of potassium, calcium and magnesium, used as fertilizer.

nutrient budgeting.text: A comparison of all the nutrients applied to a farm's soil with all those removed from the land.

fertilizer placement.text: Where fertilizer is put relative to the crop, such as broadcast over the field or banded with the seed, a choice that can strongly affect how efficiently crops take it up.

toxic elements in fertilizers.text: Contaminants such as cadmium, fluoride, uranium and other heavy metals that some fertilizers, especially phosphate and slag-based ones, add to soils.

phosphorite.text: Phosphate rock: a non-detrital sedimentary rock rich in phosphate minerals.

superphosphate.text: A chemical phosphate fertilizer made by treating phosphate-rich material, first bones and later phosphate rock, with acid.

fertilizer runoff and water pollution.text: The movement of nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilized land into surface water with rain and snowmelt, and into groundwater by leaching.

phosphate rich organic manure.text: An organic fertilizer made by co-composting rock phosphate, used as an alternative to diammonium phosphate and single superphosphate.

diammonium phosphate.text: A water-soluble ammonium phosphate salt, (NH4)2HPO4, made by reacting ammonia with phosphoric acid and used as fertilizer.

struvite.text: Magnesium ammonium phosphate, a phosphate mineral with formula NH4MgPO4·6H2O.

peak phosphorus.text: The potential shortage of economically mineable phosphorus, a limited resource used up by fertilizer production.

phosphogypsum.text: The calcium sulfate hydrate, mainly gypsum, left as a by-product when phosphoric acid for fertilizer is made from phosphate rock.

water cycle.text: The continuous movement of water, changing form as it goes, between reservoirs on, above and below the Earth's surface.

surface runoff.text: The unconfined flow of water over the ground surface, as opposed to flow in stream channels; also called overland flow.

subsidence.text: The downward vertical movement of the Earth's surface, caused by natural processes or by human activity.

stormwater.text: Water that comes from precipitation, including heavy rain and meltwater from hail and snow.

runoff.text: The flow of water across the land, a major part of the water cycle.

straw.text: The dry stalks of cereal plants left after the grain and chaff have been removed, an agricultural byproduct.

retention basin.text: An artificial pond with a permanent pool of water and vegetation around its edge, built to manage stormwater runoff.

bioswale.text: A channel built to gather and carry stormwater runoff while removing debris and pollution from it.

land development.text: The alteration of a landscape, for example turning natural land over to farming or housing, or dividing it into building lots.

land use and the water cycle.term: Land use and the water cycle
land use and the water cycle.text: The local and regional changes to the water cycle that follow changes in land use and land cover.

infiltration-excess overland flow.text: Runoff that forms when rain falls faster than the ground can absorb it and surface hollows are already full.

runoff mitigation.text: Measures that limit the harm done by surface runoff: land-use controls, erosion controls, flood control and controls on chemical use.

saturation-excess overland flow.text: Runoff produced at once when rain keeps falling on soil that is already saturated and whose surface hollows are full.

subsurface return flow.text: Water that soaks into a hillside upslope, flows sideways through the soil and seeps back out near a channel; also called throughflow.

urban runoff.text: Surface runoff from rain, landscape irrigation and car washing created by urbanization.

seasonal subsidence and heave.text: The sinking of the ground as clay-rich soils dry and shrink with the seasons, and its rise again when they rewet.

stormwater management.text: The control of both the quantity and the quality of stormwater.

stormwater sinkholes.text: Sinkhole collapses caused when urban stormwater drains down through karst ground and carries soil and rock fragments away.

rainfall-runoff model.text: A model of how rainfall on a drainage basin is converted into runoff.

hydrological transport model.text: A mathematical model that simulates the flow of rivers, streams, groundwater or drainage fronts and calculates water quality.

electrical double layer.text: The cloud of balancing cations that surrounds every negatively charged clay platelet, whose thickness depends on the salinity of the water.

hydrologic soil group.text: One of four classes, A to D, into which the NRCS sorts soils by how readily they take in water, used to choose a runoff curve number.

soil erosion.text: The wearing away of the upper layer of soil, a form of soil degradation.

runoff curve number.text: An empirical number, CN, used in hydrology to predict direct runoff or infiltration from rainfall excess.

water erosion.text: The removal of soil by rainfall and by the surface runoff it produces.

soil and water assessment tool.text: A free, open-source hydrology model and GIS simulation sponsored by the USDA, known as SWAT.

rainfall erosivity.text: The power of rainfall to cause soil erosion, set mainly by how much rain falls and how intensely.

wind erosion.text: Erosion by wind, which lifts and carries away loose particles (deflation) and wears down surfaces with windborne grains (abrasion).

erosion control.text: The practice of preventing or controlling wind and water erosion in farming, land development, coastal areas, river banks and construction.

dust.text: Fine particles of solid matter; on Earth, mostly particles in the air from soil lifted by wind, volcanic eruptions and pollution.

vegetation cover and erosion.text: The protection that living plants and the litter they leave give the soil against wind and water erosion.

agriculture and soil erosion.text: The acceleration of soil erosion by farming practices that loosen, bare or compact the soil.

erodibility.text: The inherent lack of resistance of a soil or rock to erosion.

climate change and soil erosion.text: The expected rise in soil erosion as warming brings heavier rainfall and alters vegetation, litter, soil moisture and frozen ground.

deforestation and soil erosion.text: The rise in soil erosion that follows removal of forest cover and its protective forest floor.

slope and erosion.text: The influence of a slope's steepness and length on how fast runoff flows and how much soil it erodes.

rill erosion.text: Erosion in rills, shallow channels no more than a few centimetres deep cut into soil by flowing surface water.

gully erosion.text: Erosion that cuts gullies, steep-sided channels formed in soil by running water, mass movement or both, usually on hillsides or in floodplains.

universal soil loss equation.text: A widely used empirical model (USLE) that estimates long-term average annual soil loss from water erosion as the product of six factors.

splash erosion.text: Erosion caused when falling raindrops strike bare soil and knock particles loose.

urbanization and erosion.text: The increase in erosion and polluted runoff caused by construction, roads and paved urban land.

erosion prediction.text: Using data and models to predict where, and how fast, erosion may happen in the future.

soil loss tolerance.text: The maximum average yearly soil loss, in tons per acre per year, that still lets a soil sustain current production economically and indefinitely; also called the T value.

riparian buffer.text: A vegetated strip beside a stream, usually forested, that shades it and partly shields it from the effects of neighbouring land use.

geotextile.text: A permeable fabric laid with soil to separate, filter, reinforce, protect or drain it.

jet erosion test.text: A geotechnical test, done in the field or the laboratory, that measures a soil's resistance to erosion with a jet of water.

mineral dust.text: An atmospheric aerosol of suspended soil minerals, mainly oxides and carbonates.

tillage erosion.text: Soil erosion in cultivated fields caused by the movement of soil during tillage.

dust control.text: The suppression of airborne solid particles smaller than 500 micrometres.

grassed waterway.text: A strip of native grassland 2 to 48 meters (6.6 to 157.5 feet) wide, laid along the lowest line of a cultivated dry valley to control erosion.

revegetation.text: The replanting and rebuilding of the soil of disturbed land.

prairie restoration.text: The work of restoring prairie destroyed by industrial, agricultural, commercial or residential development to its earlier state.

wepp.text: The Water Erosion Prediction Project model, a physically based erosion simulation built on hydrology, plant science, hydraulics and erosion mechanics.

rill initiation.text: The start of a rill, when the shear stress of runoff exceeds the soil's shear strength and water begins to tear particles loose.

sheet erosion.text: The even erosion of soil or other material across a wide area by a thin, unchannelled layer of flowing water.

support practice factor.text: The P factor of the Universal Soil Loss Equation, a soil loss ratio expressing how much conservation practices reduce erosion.

rainfall simulator.text: A device used in soil science and hydrology to study how soil reacts to rainfall.

post-fire hillslope stabilization.text: Treatments that steady burned slopes by offsetting fire's damage to vegetation and soil, to cut the risk of damaging runoff and erosion downhill.

tillage erosion measurement.text: Ways of quantifying tillage erosion, either by tracking soil moved by tillage or by measuring where soil is lost and gained.

tillage erosion models.text: Computer models that simulate how tillage moves soil along a hillslope or across a field.

sediment.text: Solid material made of loose particles that is carried to a new place and deposited there.

erosion.text: The removal of soil, rock or dissolved material from one place on the Earth's surface by processes such as flowing water or wind, and its transport to another place where it is deposited.

erosion index.text: Potential erosion from all sources except gullies divided by the soil's T value, the erosion rate above which long-term productivity may suffer; also called the erodibility index.

revised universal soil loss equation.text: A revised form of the Universal Soil Loss Equation, known as RUSLE, still used to estimate soil erosion.

wind erosion equation.text: A model that estimates a field's potential average annual soil loss to wind, used to design wind erosion control.

aeolian processes.text: The erosion, transport and deposition of sediment by wind at or near the Earth's surface.

sediment control.text: A practice or device that keeps eroded soil on a construction site so it does not wash off and pollute nearby waters.

sediment pollution of waterways.text: The harm done to rivers, lakes, coasts and their life by excess sediment washed in from eroding soil.

mass wasting.text: The movement of rock or soil down slopes under the force of gravity; also called mass movement.

downhill creep.text: The slow downward movement of soil and rock on a gentle slope; also called soil creep.

slope stability.text: The ability of a soil or rock slope to withstand movement; the opposite condition is slope instability or slope failure.

landslide.text: Any of several forms of mass wasting with relatively rapid ground movement, such as rockfalls, mudflows, slope failures and debris flows.

sediment transport.text: The movement of solid particles, from clay to boulders, by gravity together with the water, air or ice in which they are carried.

sediment grain shape.text: The description of sediment particles by three parameters: overall form (sphericity), roundness of corners and surface texture.

sediment delivery ratio.text: The fraction of gross erosion on a catchment (interrill, rill, gully and stream erosion) expected to reach the river outlet.

chemical erosion.text: The loss of material from a landscape in dissolved form, as solutes.

coastal erosion.text: The wearing away of shorelines, mainly by currents and waves, with changes in sea level also playing a part.

glacial erosion.text: Erosion by moving glacier ice, mainly through abrasion, plucking and ice thrusting.

landslide classification.text: A scheme sorting landslides into six types of movement (fall, topple, slide, spread, flow and slope deformation), each found in both rock and soil.

internal erosion.text: The formation of voids inside a soil as seeping water removes material.

river and stream erosion.text: Erosion by water flowing continuously along a linear channel, which deepens valleys and wears away river banks.

solifluction.text: Gradual downslope mass movement of soil linked to freezing and thawing.

quick clay.text: A highly sensitive glaciomarine clay, also called Leda or Champlain Sea clay, that can change from a solid into a watery fluid when disturbed.

debris flow.text: A water-laden mass of soil and broken rock that flows down mountainsides, funnels into channels and leaves thick muddy deposits on valley floors.

deposition (geology).text: The geological process by which sediment, soil and rock are added to a landform or landmass.

aeolian transport.text: The movement of sediment by wind through suspension, saltation (skipping) and creep (rolling or sliding).

deflation.text: The lifting and removal of loose surface material by turbulent wind.

sand dune.text: A mound or ridge of sediment heaped up by the wind, independent of any obstacle.

wind abrasion.text: The wearing of rock and landforms by wind-driven grains, also called corrasion.

climate change and landslides.text: The effects of changing temperature, rainfall and evapotranspiration on where, how often and how strongly landslides occur.

landslide hazard mapping.text: Analysing the factors behind past landslides to map where future ones are likely, to reduce losses and guide land-use planning.

dust bowl.text: A decade of severe dust storms and drought, 1930–1940, that badly damaged the farming and ecology of the High Plains and North American prairies.

dust storm.text: A storm in which strong wind blows loose sand and dirt off dry ground, common in arid and semi-arid regions; also called a sandstorm.

landslide monitoring.text: Tracking slope movement to judge danger, issue timely alerts and plan protective measures.

shallow and deep-seated landslides.text: Landslides grouped by the depth of their sliding surface: within the soil mantle or weathered bedrock (shallow), or well below tree rooting depth (deep-seated).

silt fence.text: A temporary fabric fence used on construction sites to keep sediment carried by stormwater runoff out of nearby waters.

denudation.text: The sum of processes by which moving water, ice, wind and waves wear down the Earth's surface, lowering its elevation and relief.

dust bowl government response.text: The US federal programmes of the 1930s that answered the Dust Bowl with soil conservation, tree planting and farm relief.

economic legacy of the dust bowl.term: Economic legacy of the Dust Bowl
economic legacy of the dust bowl.text: The lasting fall in farmland value and population that followed the Dust Bowl's loss of topsoil.

earthflow.text: A viscous downslope flow of water-saturated fine-grained material moving under gravity.

sedimentation.text: The settling of suspended particles out of a fluid until they come to rest against a barrier.

siltation.text: Water pollution by fine silt and clay particles, both as raised suspended sediment and as unwanted fine deposits on the bottom.

river bank failure.text: The sudden mass wasting of a stream bank, when gravity on its rock and soil exceeds the cohesive and adhesive forces holding them together.

sediment basin.text: A temporary pond on a construction site that captures soil washed off in rain storms and protects the water quality of nearby waters.

mudflow.text: A fast-moving flow of debris and soil that has been liquefied by added water; also called a mudslide.

gelifluction.text: The downslope movement of waterlogged topsoil driven by seasonal freezing and thawing, closely related to solifluction.

fluvial sediment processes.text: The movement of sediment by rivers and streams, with the erosion, deposition and landforms it creates.

fiber roll.text: A temporary tube of straw, coconut fibre or similar material laid on construction slopes to control erosion and trap sediment.

sediment treatment systems.text: Systems that clear sediment-laden construction runoff by adding flocculants and then filtering or settling the water.

saltation.text: A mode of transport in which wind or water lifts loose grains from a bed and carries them in short hops back to the surface.

hole erosion test.text: A geotechnical laboratory test of a soil's resistance to erosion, used above all for internal erosion in embankment dams.

vegetation and slope stability.text: The two-way link between slopes and the plants growing on them, which can either strengthen or weaken a slope.

gully stabilisation.text: Altering water flow through a gully to reduce scouring, let sediment build up and allow plants to return.

slope stability analysis.text: Static or dynamic, analytical or empirical methods for evaluating the stability of natural slopes and of dams, embankments and excavations in soil and rock.

slope stabilization.text: Engineering work on slopes that raises their stability and lessens the effect of landslides.

mass wasting landforms.text: The deposits and landforms left by mass wasting, usually subtle but occasionally spectacular.

baer–babinet law.text: The idea that the Earth's rotation influences how rivers form, making them erode one bank more than the other.

soil sloughing.text: The falling of soil off banks and slopes when it loses cohesion.

fluvio-thermal erosion.text: The combined mechanical and thermal erosion of ice-rich soils and sediments by an unfrozen river or stream.

tdr in geotechnical monitoring.text: The use of time-domain reflectometry to watch for slope movement at highway cuts, rail beds and open-pit mines.

suspended load.text: The part of a flow's sediment that is lifted off the bed and held up in the fluid by turbulence.

stream power.text: The energy that flowing water in a river or stream expends on its bed and banks, first derived by R. A. Bagnold in the 1960s.

bed load and suspended load.text: The two main ways a flow carries sediment: rolling and sliding along the bed as bed load, or held up in the water as suspended load.

hjulström curve.text: A graph, drawn by Filip Hjulström in 1935, of the flow velocity needed to erode, transport or deposit sediment of each grain size.

fech fech.text: A very fine powder formed by the erosion of clay-limestone terrain, found mostly in deserts.

bank erosion.text: The wearing away of the banks of a stream or river, as distinct from scour of its bed.

desert pavement.text: A desert surface covered with closely packed, interlocking pebble- and cobble-sized rock fragments.

shear strength of discontinuities.text: The shear strength along a discontinuity, such as a joint, in a soil or rock mass, which strongly shapes how the mass behaves.

quick clay formation.text: The sequence by which glacial rock flour, laid down loosely in the sea and later raised above it, became a weak and water-rich clay.

quick clay landslides.text: Landslides in quick clay, which are retrogressive: they usually start at water and work their way upslope.

legacy sediment.text: Bodies of sediment laid down as a result of human activity since the Neolithic.

river bank protection.text: The structural and vegetative measures used to keep river banks from eroding and failing.

headward erosion.text: Erosion at the head of a stream channel that moves its origin upslope, lengthening the stream, valley or gully and enlarging its drainage basin.

aggradation.text: The rise in land elevation, usually in a river system, as sediment is deposited; also called alluviation.

entrainment.text: The incorporation of surface sediment into a moving fluid such as air, water or ice, as part of erosion.

shear velocity.text: A shear stress rewritten in units of velocity, also called friction velocity.

badlands.text: Dry terrain in which soft sedimentary rocks and clay-rich soils have been deeply eroded into steep, bare ground.

measuring denudation rates.text: The estimation of how fast a landscape is being lowered, usually expressed in centimetres or inches per 1000 years.

shields parameter.text: A dimensionless number used to calculate when sediment begins to move in a fluid flow.

corrasion.text: Mechanical erosion of the land surface by material dragged across it by running water, waves, glaciers, wind or downslope movement.

root reinforcement of soil.text: The strengthening of soil by roots that grow across potential failure planes, act as piles and limit surface erosion.

root pull-out resistance.text: The force a root resists before being pulled out of the ground, usually only a little less than its laboratory tensile strength.

transpiration and slope stability.text: The stabilising of slopes by plants that draw water out of the soil and transpire it, lowering soil pore water pressure.

landslide causes and triggers.text: The distinction between the conditions that make a slope vulnerable to failure (causes) and the single event that finally sets it moving (trigger).

rainfall-triggered landslides.text: Landslides set off by heavy or prolonged rain, the main trigger in most cases.

sediment yield.text: The quantity of sediment per unit area of a watershed that a river removes over a period of time.

soil piping.text: The progressive internal erosion of soil by seeping water, which carves subsurface pipes that discharge water downstream.

vegetative filter strip.text: A strip of grass or other permanent vegetation that shields riparian areas from runoff carrying sediment, pesticides, pathogens and nutrients.

wetland.text: A semi-aquatic ecosystem whose ground is flooded or saturated, permanently or seasonally, so that oxygen-poor processes take place in its soils.

peatland.text: A wetland whose soils consist of organic matter from decaying plants, forming layers of peat.

hydric soil.text: Soil that is permanently or seasonally saturated with water, so that it turns anaerobic, as in wetlands.

landscape ecology.text: The science of how ecological processes relate to particular ecosystems across a range of landscape scales and spatial patterns.

marsh.text: A wetland dominated by herbaceous rather than woody plants.

swamp.text: A forested wetland, with saturated soils or standing water dominated by water-tolerant woody plants.

floodplain.text: Land beside a river, from the channel banks to the valley sides, that floods when discharge is high.

ombrotrophic.text: Describing soils or vegetation that receive all their water and nutrients from precipitation rather than from streams or springs.

salt marsh.text: A tidal wetland in the upper intertidal zone, regularly flooded by seawater or brackish water and dominated by salt-tolerant plants.

bog.text: A wetland that accumulates peat, a deposit of dead plant material, often sphagnum moss.

muskeg.text: A peat-forming ecosystem of northern, mostly Arctic and boreal, climates, roughly synonymous with bog or peatland.

slump (geology).text: A form of mass wasting in which a coherent mass of loosely consolidated material or rock moves a short distance down a slope.

polder.text: A low-lying tract of land enclosed by dikes that forms an artificial hydrological unit.

riparian zone.text: The strip of land where a river or stream meets the land around it.

minerotrophic.text: Describing environments that get their nutrients mainly from groundwater flowing through mineral-rich soil or rock, or from surface water flowing over land.

fen.text: A peat-accumulating wetland fed by mineral-rich ground or surface water.

geomorphology.text: The scientific study of the origin and evolution of landforms created by physical, chemical or biological processes at or near Earth's surface.

bog–rich-fen gradient.text: The arrangement of bogs and fens along a gradient from poor to rich, with bogs at the poor end, extremely rich fens at the rich end and poor fens between.

wetland nutrient cycling.text: The cycling of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and other elements in wetland soils, which sit at the interface of oxygenated and oxygen-free environments.

peatland carbon storage.text: The accumulation of carbon in peatland soils, which makes peatlands the largest natural carbon store on land.

raised bog.text: An acidic, mineral-poor bog fed only by precipitation, whose peat has risen into a dome above the groundwater.

freshwater marsh.text: A non-forested marsh with shallow fresh water that is continuously or frequently flooded.

alluvial fan.text: A cone-shaped spread of sediment that fans out from a concentrated source, such as a narrow canyon opening onto a plain.

paludification.text: The most common way boreal peatlands form, as peat builds up on previously drier, vegetated mineral soils and turns forest, grassland or bare land into peatland.

prairie pothole.text: A marsh in one of the many shallow depressions left by glaciers across northern North America.

vernal pool.text: A seasonal marsh in a shallow depression that holds shallow water in winter and spring and may be completely dry by summer and fall.

wet meadow.text: A freshwater marsh that is regularly flooded but often dry in summer.

slope aspect.text: The compass direction that a land surface faces, also called exposure.

palsa.text: A peat mound with a permanently frozen core of peat and mineral soil, typical of mires in the zone of discontinuous permafrost.

land loss.text: The conversion of coastal land to open water by natural processes and human activities.

ramsar convention.text: An international treaty for the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands, also called the Convention on Wetlands.

landscape patch and mosaic.text: A patch is a relatively uniform area that differs from its surroundings; the mosaic is the whole pattern of patches, corridors and matrix that makes up a landscape.

ecotone.text: A transitional zone between two communities, one kind of boundary between landscape patches.

spatial heterogeneity.text: The uneven distribution of objects across a landscape, a measure of how its parts differ from one another.

blanket bog.text: Peatland that forms where high rainfall and low evapotranspiration let peat cover broad stretches of rolling ground, not just wet hollows.

börde.text: A region of highly fertile, loess-covered lowland in North Germany, a 'fertile plain'.

peat swamp forest.text: A tropical moist forest whose waterlogged soil keeps dead leaves and wood from fully decaying, building a thick layer of acidic peat.

constructed wetland.text: An artificial wetland built to treat sewage, greywater, stormwater runoff or industrial wastewater.

wetland ecosystem services.text: The benefits wetlands give society, such as carbon storage, water purification, flood control and wildlife habitat.

wetland greenhouse gas emissions.text: The release of methane, nitrous oxide and carbon dioxide from wetland soils, which makes wetlands the largest natural source of atmospheric methane.

wetland hydrology.text: The flow, storage and chemistry of surface and ground water in a wetland, the main factor that produces wetlands.

wetland loss.text: The draining, filling and conversion of wetlands for agriculture, building and other uses.

mire.text: A peatland that is still actively forming peat.

shrub swamp.text: A freshwater wetland dominated by shrubs, too wet to become swamp forest but too dry or shallow to become marsh.

hillslope evolution.text: The change over time in the erosion rates, erosion styles and shape of the slopes of hills and mountains.

flark.text: A depression or hollow within a bog, typically one of a series of parallel hollows separated by ridges called strings.

floodplain soils.text: The soils of floodplains, which vary with small changes in elevation and swing between aerated and flooded states.

palustrine wetland.text: Any inland, non-tidal wetland whose ocean-derived salts stay below 0.5 parts per thousand.

us legal hydric soil definition.text: In US federal law, a soil that, undrained, is saturated, flooded or ponded long enough in the growing season to become anaerobic and support water-loving vegetation.

suffosion.text: The washing of loose soil or sediment down through fissures in the rock beneath, one of the two processes that form subsidence sinkholes.

string bog.text: A bog of slightly raised ridges and islands carrying woody plants, alternating with flat, wet sedge mats.

hummock.text: A small knoll or mound above the surrounding ground, usually under 15 metres high and found in groups or fields.

soil-surface roughness.text: The vertical variations in the micro- and macro-relief of a soil surface, together with their statistical distribution.

hydrosere.text: The plant succession by which an area of open fresh water fills in and becomes land, ultimately woodland.

pedotope.text: The total soil component of the non-living matrix of an ecotope.

mima mounds.text: Low, flattened, circular to oval natural mounds of loose, unstratified, often gravelly sediment forming an overthickened A horizon.

hillslope sediment flux models.text: Numerical models of hillslope erosion that describe the sediment flux on a slope at a given time rather than how its form changes.

soil-mantled parabolic hills.text: Convex, soil-covered hills long held to reflect a steady-state balance between soil production and soil erosion.

irrigation.text: Applying controlled amounts of water to land to help grow crops, landscape plants and lawns.

crop rotation.text: Growing a series of different crops on the same land over successive growing seasons.

leaching (agriculture).text: The loss of water-soluble plant nutrients from soil, carried away by rain and irrigation water.

land reclamation.text: Creating new land from oceans, seas, riverbeds or lake beds; the result is called reclaimed land or land fill.

agricultural soil science.text: The branch of soil science that studies soil conditions as they bear on growing food and fibre.

herbicide.text: A substance, commonly called a weed killer, used to control unwanted plants.

potting soil.text: A substrate, also called growing medium or potting mix, used to grow plants in containers.

organic farming.text: A farming system that relies on natural, non-synthetic inputs such as compost, manure and green manure, with techniques such as crop rotation and mixed cropping.

surface irrigation.text: Irrigation in which water is spread over the soil surface by gravity.

monocropping.text: Growing a single crop year after year on the same land, also called continuous cropping.

fallow.text: Leaving arable land unsown for one or more growing cycles.

irrigation efficiency.text: The share of water applied to a field that the crop actually uses: field water efficiency is the water transpired by the crop divided by the water applied, times 100.

regenerative agriculture.text: A conservation and rehabilitation approach to farming that aims to regenerate topsoil, raise biodiversity and strengthen the health of farm soil.

sprinkler irrigation.text: Irrigation in which water is piped to points in the field and sprayed overhead by high-pressure sprinklers or guns.

subirrigation.text: Irrigation by artificially raising the water table so that the soil is moistened from below the plants' root zone.

wastewater irrigation.text: Watering crops with recycled or untreated municipal wastewater, whose nutrients can also fertilize them.

crop choice in rotations.text: Choosing the crops of a rotation by what each adds to or takes from the field: organic matter, nutrients, pest control and protection from erosion.

intercropping.text: Growing two or more crops at the same time in the same field, a form of polyculture.

sustainable agriculture.text: Farming that reduces environmental harm, sustains and expands natural resources and uses non-renewable resources productively.

crop rotation and erosion control.text: The use of crop sequences, residue and fallow management within a rotation to cut soil lost to erosion, often alongside zero or reduced tillage.

mixed farming.text: Farming that combines growing crops with keeping livestock, which helps manage rotations and cycle nutrients.

polyculture.text: Growing two or more crops in the same place at the same time.

nitrate leaching.text: The loss of nitrate from soil as drainage water carries the excess ions, which soils do not hold, down to groundwater, streams and the sea.

drip irrigation.text: A micro-irrigation method that lets water drip slowly to plant roots, from above or below the soil surface, placing it in the root zone to minimize evaporation.

soil solarization.text: A non-chemical pest control method that traps the sun's heat in soil until many soil-borne plant pathogens are killed or badly weakened.

integrated pest management.text: Pest control that combines non-chemical and chemical methods to keep pests in economic check while relying less on chemicals.

crop yield.text: The amount of a crop, or of a product such as milk or wool, produced per unit area of land.

precision agriculture.text: A farm management strategy that gathers and analyses data on time, place and individual plants or animals to fit decisions to variation across fields, for better efficiency, yield and sustainability.

green revolution.text: A period in which technology transfer initiatives produced a large increase in crop yields.

rotation effect.text: Agronomists' name for the yield benefit that crops gain from being grown in rotation.

agricultural land reclamation.text: Reclaiming land from the sea or from wetlands to make farmland, the main driver of reclamation before industrialisation.

soil steam sterilization.text: A farming technique that fully or partly sterilizes soil with steam, in open fields or greenhouses.

shifting cultivation.text: A farming system in which a plot is cropped for a while and then abandoned to fallow regrowth while the cultivator moves to another plot.

herbicide persistence.text: How long a herbicide stays active in soil: low residual activity if rain or soil reactions neutralize it within weeks or months, high if it stays potent for the long term.

soil-applied herbicides.text: Herbicides applied to the soil before planting or crop emergence, taken up by the roots or shoots of emerging seedlings.

phosphorus leaching.text: The loss of phosphorus from fields by downward movement through the soil, an important pathway on flat, sandy land or soils prone to preferential flow.

slash-and-burn agriculture.text: A form of shifting cultivation in which forest or woodland plants are cut and burned to create a field called a swidden.

salt tolerance of crops.text: The highest salt level a crop can withstand without losing productivity, beyond which it is harmed.

coir.text: Coconut husk fibre, whose processed form, coco peat, is used in potting mixes and as a substitute for peat.
