land restoration.text: Returning land to a different or earlier state for an intended purpose, which may include renaturalisation or rewilding.

within-field variability.text: Differences in growing conditions within and between fields, which precision agriculture measures and manages.

dryland farming.text: Growing crops without irrigation, typically in regions where a cool wet season charges the soil with the moisture crops will use in the following dry season.

saturated media extract.text: The main test of a potting mix's chemistry, which analyses a water extract of the mix.

specialty potting mixes.text: Growing media adapted to a plant's, or a growth stage's, needs for aeration, drainage, nutrition and pH.

monoculture.text: Growing a single crop species in a field at one time.

agrominerals.text: Minerals, sometimes called stone bread, that matter to farming and horticulture because they can supply essential plant nutrients.

agrogeology.text: The study of agrominerals, the minerals that matter to farming, their origins and uses; more broadly, geology applied to farm soil productivity and health.

soil remineralization.text: Replenishing a soil's mineral nutrients by working crushed rock powder into it.

organic farming and soil quality.text: The dispute over whether organically managed soils end up better or worse than conventionally farmed ones.

organic soil fertility management.text: In organic farming, replacing the nutrients crops remove through the natural breakdown of organic matter, using green manure and composting.

basin irrigation.text: Surface irrigation in which a level area enclosed by earth banks is flooded quickly and the water left to soak in.

furrow irrigation.text: Surface irrigation through small parallel channels running down the field's main slope, with water flowing by gravity from the top end.

spate irrigation.text: Irrigation that diverts seasonal floods from normally dry river beds onto fields or into storage basins.

fallow syndrome.text: Poor nutrient uptake by a crop after a fallow period because the soil lacks arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.

fertigation.text: The injection of fertilizers and other water-soluble products into an irrigation system.

holistic planned grazing.text: Grazing that keeps rotating livestock herds between fields to mimic how natural herds graze.

alley cropping.text: Growing strips of crops between rows of closely spaced trees or hedges.

biofumigation.text: Pest control in which a fumigant gas comes from fresh plant material chopped and buried in the soil to decompose.

rock phosphate fertilizer.text: Phosphorite, a phosphorus-bearing sedimentary rock used as a sustainable, low-cost source of phosphorus for crops.

zaï.text: A farming technique of digging pits in poorly permeable soil to catch water and concentrate compost.

biosolarization.text: An alternative to soil fumigation that adds organic amendments or compost before solarizing, so that microbial activity shortens the treatment.

natural farming.text: An ecological farming approach set out by Masanobu Fukuoka, also called the Fukuoka method or do-nothing farming.

deficit irrigation.text: An irrigation strategy that waters a crop during its drought-sensitive growth stages and limits water at other times.

soilless growing substrates.text: Inert or organic materials such as perlite or gravel that mechanically support plant roots in hydroponics, where plants grow without soil.

expanded clay aggregate.text: A lightweight, porous aggregate made by heating clay to about 1,200 °C in a rotary kiln, often called LECA.

soil steaming methods.text: The ways of applying steam to soil, grouped as substrate, surface and deep soil steaming, chosen by soil structure, crop and area to treat.

center-pivot irrigation.text: Sprinkler irrigation from equipment that rotates around a central pivot, watering a circular area of crop.

multiple cropping.text: Growing two or more crops on the same land within one year instead of just one.

variable rate application.text: Applying a material such as fertilizer at a rate that changes with the location or qualities of each part of a field, instead of uniformly.

soil salinity classes for crops.text: Bernstein's grouping of soils by the electrical conductivity of a saturated soil-paste extract (ECe), matched to the crops each class can still grow well.

methyl bromide.text: An organobromine gas, CH3Br, long used as a fumigant and soil sterilant.

crop tolerance to seawater.text: The ability of a crop to withstand the high salinity of irrigation with seawater or a mix of fresh water and seawater.

tillage.text: The preparation of soil for farming by mechanically agitating it, for example by digging, stirring or overturning it.

agroecology.text: An academic discipline that studies ecological processes as they apply to agricultural production systems.

agroecosystem.text: An ecological system that people manage and shape in order to farm.

soil sickness.text: A decline in soil fertility and crop yield, often after long-term monoculture, marked by a shift in harmful and beneficial soil microbes.

plough.text: A farm tool for loosening or turning over soil before sowing seed or planting.

arable land.text: Land that can be ploughed and used to grow crops.

effects of tillage.text: The consequences of tilling for a soil: it loosens and aerates the topsoil for planting, but it also degrades structure, speeds erosion and compacts the soil.

primary and secondary tillage.text: The division of tillage into deeper, more thorough primary operations and shallower, often more selective secondary ones.

harrow.text: A farm implement for surface tillage, used after ploughing to break up and smooth the soil surface.

contour plowing.text: Ploughing or planting across a slope along its elevation contour lines, also called contour farming.

crop residue.text: The stalks, stubble, leaves and other plant material left in a field after harvest.

conservation tillage.text: A group of practices that reduce tillage and leave at least 30% of crop residue, or at least 1,000 lb/ac (1,100 kg/ha) of small grain residue, on the surface during the critical erosion period.

no-till farming.text: A way of growing crops or pasture without disturbing the soil by tillage, also called zero tillage or direct drilling.

forest site preparation.text: Any of the treatments applied to a forest site to ready it for seeding or planting.

intensive tillage.text: Tillage that leaves less than 15% crop residue cover, or less than 500 pounds per acre (560 kg/ha) of small grain residue, on the soil.

mounding.text: A forest site-preparation treatment that builds raised planting spots, which have improved seedling performance on cold, wet sites.

no-till and soil carbon.text: The dispute over whether no-till farming really increases the organic carbon stored in soil.

reduced tillage.text: Tillage that leaves 15 to 30% crop residue cover, or 500 to 1000 pounds per acre (560 to 1100 kg/ha) of small grain residue, during the critical erosion period.

slash burning for site preparation.text: Broadcast or prescribed burning of logging slash on cleared forest sites to prepare them for planting or seeding.

tillage and archaeology.text: The damage tilling does to buried ancient remains such as long barrows.

mouldboard plough.text: A plough whose curved mould board lifts the slice of soil cut by the share and turns it over into the previous furrow.

weed management in no-till.text: Controlling weeds without tillage, using herbicides, cover crops, mowing or crimping in place of cultivation.

three-field system.text: A crop rotation in which a field grows one set of crops in the first year, a different set in the second and lies fallow in the third.

conversion to arable land.text: Making land that cannot grow crops capable of cultivation.

stubble burning.text: Deliberately setting fire to the straw stubble left after harvesting grains such as rice and wheat.

keyline design.text: P. A. Yeomans' system of planning farm landscapes around the natural flow of water to make the best use of their water resources.

ard.text: The early animal-drawn scratch plough, which drags a share through the topsoil to cut a shallow furrow.

chisel plough.text: A plough for deep tillage that loosens and aerates soil while leaving crop residue on the surface.

heavy plough.text: A wheeled plough heavy enough to carry a large metal-faced mould board and so to work the heavy soils of northern Europe.

hoe cultivation.text: Turning soil with hand-held digging sticks and hoes, the way soil was worked when agriculture began.

mole plough.text: A deep plough with a torpedo-shaped tip that leaves a drainage channel underground, or breaks up deep impermeable layers, without digging trenches.

cultivator.text: A farm implement for secondary tillage, either a frame with teeth dragged through the soil or a machine with rotating disks or teeth such as a rotary tiller.

vertical tillage.text: A set of tillage principles that, like conservation agriculture, aims to improve soil health, raise infiltration and reduce erosion and compaction.

optimum water content for tillage.text: The soil moisture content at which tillage breaks the soil into the largest number of small aggregates.

disc harrow.text: A harrow whose cutting edges are rows of concave metal discs set at an angle, used to till soil and chop weeds or crop residue.

seedbed.text: The local soil environment into which seeds are planted.

deep ploughing.text: Ploughing deeper than 50 cm, compared with ordinary ploughing that rarely goes below 20 cm.

minimum tillage.text: A soil conservation system that keeps soil manipulation to the minimum a crop needs, without turning the soil over.

strip-till.text: A minimum-tillage conservation system that tills only the narrow strip of soil that will hold the seed row, leaving the soil between rows untilled.

stubble mulching.text: Leaving stubble or crop residue in place on the land as a surface cover during a fallow period.

controlled traffic farming.text: A management system that confines all machinery loads to the smallest possible area of permanent traffic lanes, to limit soil damage from heavy or repeated passes.

mulch tillage.text: A seeding method in which the whole soil surface is tilled and crop residue mixed in, while some residue stays on the surface.

plough pan.text: A compacted layer of soil created by tillage, also called a tillage pan.

soil conservation.text: Preventing the loss of topsoil to erosion, and the loss of fertility through overuse, acidification, salinization or chemical contamination.

cover crop.text: A crop planted to cover the soil rather than to be harvested.

subsoiling.text: Deep tillage with a subsoiler, an implement whose heavy shanks loosen and break up soil below the depth reached by ploughs, harrows or rototillers.

terrace (earthworks).text: A flat surface cut into a hill or mountainside for growing crops, usually built as a series of steps like a staircase.

ridge tillage.text: A form of conservation tillage that keeps the cultivated part of the soil profile at a distance from the water table, so that it is better aerated.

soil management.text: Applying operations, practices and treatments to protect soil and improve its performance, such as its fertility or mechanical behaviour.

windbreak.text: One or more rows of trees or shrubs, also called a shelterbelt, planted to shelter land from the wind and protect soil from erosion.

agroforestry.text: A land use system that integrates trees with crops or pasture.

strip farming.text: Farming a field divided into long, narrow strips that alternate in a crop rotation, also called strip cropping.

soil stabilization.text: Any physical, chemical, mechanical or biological method, alone or combined, of altering a natural soil to meet an engineering purpose.

cover crops for soil fertility.text: Growing cover crops, often legumes, to raise soil fertility, chiefly by supplying or conserving nitrogen.

conservation agriculture.text: A farming system, as defined by the FAO, that prevents loss of arable land and regenerates degraded land through minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and diverse plant species.

soil management and greenhouse gases.text: The effect of how soils are managed on greenhouse gases: management can emit nitrous oxide and carbon, or store carbon dioxide as soil organic carbon.

reducing pesticide use.text: Cutting pesticide use to protect soil, since pesticides can contaminate soil, nearby vegetation and water for a long time.

soil-conservation farming.text: Farming that combines no-till, green manures and other soil-enhancing practices to protect and rebuild the soil.

lynchet.text: An earth terrace on a hillside, typical of the ancient field systems of the British Isles.

cover crops and soil water.text: The ways cover crops change how water enters, moves through and leaves a field's soil.

cover crops in pest and disease control.term: Cover crops in pest and disease control
cover crops in pest and disease control.text: Using cover crops to break pest and disease cycles, lure pests away as trap crops and attract their natural enemies.

weed suppression by cover crops.text: The control of weeds by cover crops, through competition while they grow and smothering or chemical inhibition after they die.

contour trenching.text: Digging continuous trenches along the contour of a slope to conserve water and soil and raise crop yields, an easily applied technique in arid sub-Saharan areas.

buffer strip.text: A strip of land kept under permanent vegetation, mostly on farmland, to protect soil, water and air quality.

soil conservation and domestic allotment.term: Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Act of 1936
soil conservation and domestic allotment.text: A US federal law of 1936 that let the government pay farmers to cut production in order to conserve soil and prevent erosion.

terracette.text: A landform of roughly parallel, step-like ridges on a steep hillside.

great plains shelterbelt.text: A US project, begun in 1934, to plant windbreaks across the Great Plains states.

check dam.text: A small, sometimes temporary dam built across a swale, ditch or waterway to counter erosion by slowing the water.

catch crop.text: A fast-growing crop, a type of cover crop, grown between two successive main crops.

magnesium chloride dust control.text: Spreading magnesium chloride on unpaved roads and dusty sites, where its moisture-absorbing nature keeps fine particles from becoming airborne.

mechanical soil stabilization.text: Strengthening a soil layer by confining the movement of its particles, for example with geogrids or three-dimensional geocells.

prairie strips.text: Strips of native perennial vegetation placed within row-crop fields to protect soil and water and support biodiversity.

bioretention.text: Removing sediment and contaminants from stormwater runoff by passing it through planted soil, where plants and microbes hold and break down pollutants.

soil survey.text: The process of classifying the soil types and other soil properties of an area and recording them geographically; also called soil mapping.

soil map.text: A geographical representation of the soil types, or of soil properties such as pH, texture, organic matter or horizon depth, across an area.

contour buffer strip.text: Strips of perennial vegetation alternating with wider cultivated strips of cropland across a slope.

filter strip.text: A band of grass or other permanent vegetation at a field's edge that shields riparian areas from sediment, pesticides, pathogens and nutrients in runoff.

vetiver system.text: A soil and water conservation system built on hedgerows of the vetiver grass.

prime farmland.text: A US Department of Agriculture designation for land with the best combination of physical and chemical characteristics for producing food, feed, forage, fibre and oilseed crops, and available for those uses.

remote sensing.text: Gathering information about an object or area from a distance, usually with sensors on satellites or aircraft, instead of measuring it on site.

geographic information system.text: Integrated computer hardware and software that store, manage, analyse, edit and display geographic data.

digital soil mapping.text: The computer-assisted production of digital maps of soil types and soil properties, also called predictive soil mapping.

soil value.text: Germany's comparative rating of soil quality (Bodenwertzahl), scored from soil sampling data on a scale from 0 (very low) to 100 (very high).

soil survey interpretation.text: The use of soil survey information to predict the potentials and limitations of soils for particular uses, such as crops, building or gardens.

digital elevation model.text: A computer representation of elevation data that depicts terrain, or the objects on top of it.

european soil database.text: The only harmonized soil database in Europe, the source of many other soil data, information and services.

ssurgo.text: The Soil Survey Geographic database, digital soil data produced and distributed in the United States by the Natural Resources Conservation Service.

pedometrics.text: The application of mathematical and statistical methods to the study of the distribution and genesis of soils.

pedometric mapping.text: Data-driven production of soil property and soil class maps by statistical methods, also called statistical soil mapping.

land suitability classification.text: An FAO method of land evaluation that appraises and groups areas of land by their fitness for a defined use.

universal model of soil variation.text: A model that splits a soil variable at any place into a deterministic trend, a spatially autocorrelated random part and leftover noise: Z(s) = m(s) + ε′(s) + ε″.

aerial photography.text: Taking photographs of landscapes and surface features from aircraft or other airborne platforms.

site index.text: A forestry measure of a site's potential for tree growth, given as the height of dominant and co-dominant trees at a base age.

storie index.text: A soil rating method based on the soil characteristics that govern a land's potential use and productive capacity.

scorpan model.text: A mnemonic model, S = f(s,c,o,r,p,a,n), that predicts a soil class or attribute from soil, climate, organisms, relief, parent material, age and position.

land use capability map.text: A map showing the potential uses, usually for farming, of each unit of land.

fao land suitability classes.text: The numbered degrees of suitability within each FAO land suitability order, in decreasing order of suitability.

soil information system.text: A systematic, consistent collection of gridded or vector soil property and class maps, with attached report, manual or metadata, covering a whole area of interest.

web soil survey.text: An online service run by the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service that gives access to soil data from the National Cooperative Soil Survey.

site index curves and equations.text: Graphs or equations that convert a stand's measured dominant height and age into its site index.

inductively coupled plasma atomic emissi.term: Inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy
inductively coupled plasma atomic emissi.text: An analytical technique (ICP-AES or ICP-OES) that detects chemical elements from the light emitted by atoms and ions excited in an argon plasma.

gas chromatography.text: Chromatography that separates and analyses compounds that can be vaporized without decomposing.

elemental analysis.text: Analysis of a material such as soil for its elemental, and sometimes isotopic, composition.

atomic absorption spectroscopy.text: An elemental analysis method that measures the concentration of metals in a sample from the light their atoms absorb.

loss on ignition.text: A test that strongly heats a soil or mineral sample at a set temperature until its mass stops changing, so the weight lost measures the volatile components driven off.

kjeldahl method.text: A wet-chemistry method that measures the organic nitrogen plus ammonia and ammonium in a sample.

inductively coupled plasma mass spectrom.text: Mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) that ionizes a sample in an inductively coupled plasma and counts the resulting ions to detect metals and some non-metals at very low concentrations.

ion chromatography.text: Chromatography that separates ions and ionizable molecules by their affinity for an ion exchanger.

fine earth fraction.text: The part of a soil made of particles 2 mm across or smaller.

ion-selective electrode.text: A membrane-based potentiometric sensor that converts the activity of a specific ion in solution into an electrical potential.

ammonium acetate extraction.text: The use of ammonium acetate solution in soil analysis to displace exchangeable cations, for measuring CEC and available potassium.

molybdenum blue phosphate test.text: A colorimetric test in which phosphate forms a blue molybdenum complex whose depth of colour is proportional to phosphorus concentration.

soil thin section.text: A slice of rock, mineral or soil ground to about 30 μm and mounted on glass for study under a polarizing microscope.

soil micromorphology.text: The description, measurement and interpretation of soil features too small to see with the unaided eye.

soil biofabric.text: Soil fabric made by organisms, typically small, often pelleted micro- and mesobiofabric left by ants, worms and termites and seen with a hand lens or in soil thin sections.

mineral alteration in thin section.text: The changes natural processes make to a mineral's chemical composition or crystal structure, as they appear under the microscope.

geomorphometry.text: The science of measuring the shape of the land surface and the effects of that shape on human and natural processes.

ground-penetrating radar.text: A geophysical method that images the subsurface with radar pulses, recording reflections from buried boundaries.

electrical resistivity tomography.text: A geophysical technique that images subsurface structure from electrical resistivity measured with electrodes at the surface or in boreholes.

multispectral imaging.text: Imaging that captures data in a small number of separate wavelength bands, typically 3 to 15, including bands beyond visible light.

spatial variability.text: The way a quantity measured at different places takes different values from place to place.

geostatistics.text: A branch of statistics that deals with spatial or spatio-temporal data sets.

hyperspectral imaging.text: Imaging that records a full, finely resolved spectrum across many continuous bands for each pixel, to identify materials or detect processes.

normalized difference vegetation index.text: A widely used remote-sensing measure of the health and density of vegetation, calculated from the red and near-infrared bands.

variogram.text: A graph or function describing how much pairs of observations differ according to the distance separating them, the key tool of geostatistics.

kriging.text: A geostatistical interpolation method that predicts a value at an unsampled point as a weighted average of nearby known values, based on a model of their covariance.

regression-kriging.text: A spatial prediction technique that regresses the target variable on auxiliary variables, such as terrain and remote-sensing layers, and then kriges the regression residuals.

spatial interpolation.text: Estimating the values of a quantity at arbitrary places from values known at a set of points, when the variables are spatial coordinates.

inverse distance weighting.text: A deterministic interpolation method that estimates unknown values as a weighted average of known points, each weighted by the inverse of its distance.

topographic wetness index.text: A steady-state wetness index, computed from slope and upslope contributing area, that quantifies topographic control on hydrological processes.

soilgrids.text: A system for automated global soil mapping based on models fitted to soil profiles and environmental covariate data.

planetary gamma-ray spectrometry.text: The use of orbiting gamma-ray spectrometers to map the elements of planetary surfaces, especially the Moon and Mars.

near-infrared spectroscopy.text: A spectroscopic method using the near-infrared part of the spectrum, from 780 nm to 2500 nm.

carbon cycle.text: The part of Earth's biogeochemical cycles in which carbon moves among living things, soils, rocks, water and the atmosphere.

soil carbon.text: The solid carbon stored in soils, both as organic matter from plants, animals and microbes and as inorganic carbonate minerals.

carbon sink.text: A natural or artificial process that removes a greenhouse gas, or a substance that forms one, from the atmosphere, taking up more carbon than it releases.

climate change mitigation.text: Action to limit the greenhouse gases in the atmosphere that cause climate change, also called decarbonisation.

carbon sequestration.text: The storing of carbon in a carbon pool, which limits climate change by reducing carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

soil carbon and climate change.text: The two-way link between climate and soil carbon: climate change alters soils and their carbon, and soil carbon losses or gains alter the climate.

effects of climate change on agriculture.term: Effects of climate change on agriculture
effects of climate change on agriculture.text: The many ways a changing climate alters farming, most of them making it harder for agriculture to provide global food security.

soil inorganic carbon.text: Carbon held in soil as minerals, mainly carbonates, formed by weathering of parent material or by soil minerals reacting with atmospheric CO2.

soil organic carbon.text: The carbon held in soil organic matter, which is about 50% carbon by dry weight.

managing soil carbon.text: Choosing land and farm practices to avoid losses of soil organic carbon and to build it up.

permafrost carbon cycle.text: The Arctic part of the global carbon cycle, in which carbon moves from permafrost soils to plants, microbes and the air and back into frozen soil by burial.

active layer.text: The top layer of soil in permafrost regions that thaws each summer and freezes again in autumn.

soils as carbon sinks.text: The role of soils as a short- to long-term carbon store holding more carbon than all land vegetation and the atmosphere combined.

pingo.text: An ice-cored hill, 3–70 m high and 30–1,000 m across, that grows only in permafrost.

soil carbon sequestration.text: Drawing carbon dioxide from the air into soil, where plants fix it as organic carbon; it is a major soil property and an ecosystem service.

permafrost thaw.text: The warming and thawing of permafrost under climate change, seen as a thickening active layer and shrinking frozen ground.

permafrost zones.text: The division of permafrost regions by how much of the land is underlain by permafrost: continuous, discontinuous, sporadic and isolated.

fast and slow carbon cycles.text: The split of the carbon cycle into a fast biological cycle that turns over in years and a slow geological cycle that takes millions of years.

methane emissions.text: The release of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, to the atmosphere from human activities and natural sources such as wetlands.

carbon catchment health.text: The wider benefits to soil and catchment health that come from raising soil carbon, beyond its role as a carbon sink.

soil carbon monitoring.text: Estimating soil organic carbon stocks and their changes by field survey and modelling, as climate reporting requires.

soil organic carbon and soil function.term: Soil organic carbon and soil function
soil organic carbon and soil function.text: The way organic carbon sustains a soil's ability to provide services, a capacity known as soil health.

climate change feedbacks.text: Natural processes that change how much the planet warms for a given amount of greenhouse gas emissions; positive feedbacks amplify warming and negative ones damp it.

terrestrial carbon pool.text: The carbon held on land, in all living and dead land organisms and in soils.

carbon pool.text: Any reservoir in the Earth system where carbon resides in some chemical form for a period of time.

land-use change and carbon loss.text: The release of land carbon to the atmosphere when people clear or convert vegetation, chiefly by turning forest into farmland or towns.

soil carbon feedback.text: The release of carbon from soils in response to global warming, which in turn adds to warming.

alpine permafrost.text: Permafrost found at high elevations, in mountains cold enough to keep the ground frozen year after year.

construction on permafrost.text: Engineering methods for building on permafrost without thawing the frozen ground that supports the structure.

history of permafrost research.text: The development of permafrost science from early Siberian reports to modern international collaboration.

massive ground ice.text: Permafrost so rich in ice that ice exceeds 250 percent of the dry soil by mass.

yedoma.text: Ice-rich, organic-rich permafrost of Pleistocene age, about 2% carbon by mass with 50–90% ice by volume.

past extent of permafrost.text: The much larger area that permafrost covered during the Last Glacial Maximum.

permafrost base depth.text: The depth at which Earth's geothermal heat balances the mean surface temperature at 0 °C, marking the bottom of permafrost.

permafrost ecology.text: How permanently frozen ground shapes the plants, animals and microbes that live with it.

permafrost landforms.text: The surface features built by freezing, cracking and thawing of permafrost ground.

permafrost thaw and infrastructure.text: The threat that thawing permafrost poses to settlements, roads, pipelines and buildings built on frozen ground.

pollutants released by permafrost thaw.text: Toxic waste and natural mercury held in frozen ground that thaw could release into the environment.

revival of ancient organisms from permaf.term: Revival of ancient organisms from permafrost
revival of ancient organisms from permaf.text: The survival of ancient microbes and plant tissue in frozen ground, and their possible revival when permafrost thaws.

methanotroph.text: Bacteria or archaea that use methane as their source of carbon and energy.

mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storag.term: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage
mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storag.text: The part that root-associated mycorrhizal fungi play in building, keeping and losing the soil carbon pool.

subsea permafrost.text: Permafrost beneath the seabed of polar continental shelves, on land exposed during the Last Glacial Maximum and since flooded.

thaw-induced ground instability.text: The weakening and movement of ground as its permafrost ice thaws and drains.

wetland restoration.text: Restoring wetlands and peatlands so that they keep sequestering carbon and storing water.

thermokarst.text: Irregular terrain of marshy hollows and small hummocks formed when ice-rich permafrost thaws.

permafrost carbon release.text: The escape of long-stored carbon from thawing permafrost soils to the atmosphere as microbes decompose it.

climate change and soil fertility.text: The decline in soil quality expected as warming brings heavier rain and faster decay of soil organic matter.

sea level rise and farmland.text: The loss of low-lying farmland to flooding, erosion and salt as sea levels rise.

thawing of potentially arable land.text: The prospect that climate change will open new farmland as frozen ground in the far north thaws.

permafrost carbon feedback.text: The warming caused when thawing permafrost releases its stored carbon as carbon dioxide and methane, which in turn drives more thaw.

permafrost carbon stocks.text: The amount of organic carbon held in permafrost-region soils and deposits, more than twice the carbon in the atmosphere.

agricultural greenhouse gas emissions.text: The greenhouse gases released by farming, including from agricultural soils and from clearing land for crops.

talik.text: A zone of ground that stays unfrozen all year within a permafrost area.

land use, land-use change, and forestry.term: Land use, land-use change, and forestry
land use, land-use change, and forestry.text: The greenhouse gas inventory sector covering emissions and removals that result from human land use, land-use change and forestry.

soil carbon sponge.text: Porous, well-aggregated, healthy soil that absorbs and holds water well.

thaw depth.text: The level down to which soil has warmed to zero degrees Celsius at a given moment, separating thawed soil from frozen soil below.

syngenetic permafrost growth.text: Growth of permafrost upward as new material is deposited on a site under freezing conditions.

abrupt permafrost thaw.text: Rapid thaw by hillside collapse (retrogressive thaw slumps) and thermokarst lake formation, which can expose deep soil to microbes within days.

arctic methane emissions.text: Methane released in the Arctic, mainly from thawing permafrost, melting sea ice, clathrate breakdown and the melting Greenland ice sheet, which adds to atmospheric methane.

permafrost carbon dioxide emissions.text: The carbon dioxide released by aerobic microbial respiration in thawed permafrost soils, the bulk of permafrost emissions.

permafrost carbon storage processes.text: The two processes, syngenetic permafrost growth and cryoturbation, that carry plant-derived carbon down into permafrost for storage.

permafrost methane emissions.text: The methane produced by anaerobic microbes in waterlogged thawed permafrost, especially under thermokarst lakes.

permafrost emission estimates.text: Projections of the total greenhouse gases that thawing permafrost will release over this century and beyond.

pereletok.text: A layer of frozen ground that stays frozen through several summers but eventually thaws.

soil formation in the active layer.term: Soil formation in the active layer
soil formation in the active layer.text: The cold-climate soil-forming processes, dominated by frost churning, that act in the seasonally thawed layer above permafrost.

black carbon in soils.text: Fire-derived carbon, from vegetation fires or deposited from the air, held in soil as charcoal particles and soot.

biochar permanence.text: How long the carbon locked in biochar stays stored before returning to the atmosphere, the key measure of its durability as carbon removal.

biochar carbon credits.text: Certified credits sold for carbon dioxide removed by producing biochar and storing it durably, traded on voluntary carbon markets.

carbon cycle feedbacks.text: The positive and negative climate feedbacks that come from Earth's carbon cycle, mostly negative so far.

supra-permafrost talik.text: An unfrozen layer that forms between the seasonally frozen surface and the permafrost when summer-thawed ground fails to refreeze in winter.

compost-bomb instability.text: A proposed tipping point at which warming triggers runaway, explosive releases of soil carbon from peatlands.

silicate weathering and carbon dioxide.text: The natural removal of atmospheric CO2 when carbonic acid in rain and groundwater dissolves silicate and carbonate minerals.

enhanced weathering.text: A carbon dioxide removal method that speeds up natural weathering by spreading finely ground silicate rock, such as basalt, so that it reacts with water and air.

mineral carbonation.text: The deliberate dissolution and carbonation of silicate minerals to lock CO2 into carbonate.

terrestrial enhanced weathering.text: Enhanced weathering done on land by spreading crushed silicate minerals over the ground surface.

mycorrhizal fungi and soil aggregation.text: The way mycorrhizal fungi help bind soil into aggregates that physically shield organic carbon from microbial decay.

mycorrhizal inhibition of decomposition.text: The slowing of soil carbon decomposition when ectomycorrhizal fungi compete with free-living decomposers for nutrients or water.

mycorrhizal priming.text: The speeding-up of soil carbon decomposition when mycorrhizal fungi feed free-living decomposers with easily used carbon compounds.

recalcitrance of mycorrhizal tissues.text: The idea that how slowly mycorrhizal fungal tissue decays helps set how long its carbon stays in soil.

alternate wetting and drying.text: A controlled, intermittent irrigation method for lowland rice in which fields are allowed to dry for a few days before being re-flooded, instead of being kept under standing water.

pathways of wetland methane emission.text: The three routes by which methane made in wetland soils reaches the air: molecular diffusion, transport through plant aerenchyma, and ebullition.

controls on wetland methane flux.text: The factors, chiefly water table, temperature, substrate and ecosystem production, that set how much wetland methane reaches the atmosphere.

wetland drainage and methane.text: The mixed effect on methane emissions of draining wetlands for development, housing and farming.

wetland nitrous oxide fluxes.text: The exchange of nitrous oxide between wetland soils and the air, which can run in either direction.

earth system and land surface models.term: Earth system and land surface models
earth system and land surface models.text: Computer models that represent the land surface, including vegetation, soil and terrain, within simulations of climate and the carbon and water cycles.

soil degradation.text: A regressive change in which a stable soil loses its equilibrium; more broadly, any disturbance to a soil judged harmful or undesirable.

land degradation.text: A process in which land becomes less healthy and productive through human activities or natural conditions.

soil methane uptake.text: The consumption of methane, including atmospheric methane, by methanotrophic microbes in soils, which makes soils a natural methane sink.

peatland rewetting.text: Returning a drained peatland to its original waterlogged state so peat-forming vegetation recovers and peat can accumulate again.

paludiculture.text: Rewetting drained peatlands while continuing to farm them with crops suited to wet conditions.

deforestation.text: The clearing of a forest or stand of trees and conversion of the land to non-forest uses such as farms, ranches or towns.

causes of land degradation.text: The many interrelated human and natural drivers of land degradation, both proximate and underlying.

global extent of land degradation.text: How much of the world's land is degraded and how many people live on it, as estimated by the UN, the IPCC and others.

impacts of land degradation.text: The harm degraded land and soil cause: lost productivity, food insecurity, water pollution, biodiversity loss, natural hazards and economic costs.

desertification.text: The gradual degradation of fertile land into arid desert through a combination of natural processes and human activities.

sustainable land management.text: Managing land in ways that prevent and reverse its degradation while conserving soil and water.

soil sealing.text: The loss of soil resources when land is covered over for housing, roads or other construction.

land consumption.text: The conversion of land with healthy soil and intact habitats into industrial farmland, roads and especially urban settlements.

drylands.text: Zones defined by scarce water, where precipitation is balanced by evaporation and plant evapotranspiration; UNEP counts tropical and temperate areas with an aridity index below 0.65.

united nations convention to combat dese.term: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification
united nations convention to combat dese.text: An international convention (UNCCD) to combat desertification and ease the effects of drought through national action programmes backed by international cooperation.

climate change and desertification.text: The role of a warming climate in expanding the world's drylands and driving desertification.

reversing desertification.text: Techniques and countermeasures that mitigate or reverse desertification.

desert greening.text: Reclaiming deserts and desertified land, with methods matched to each kind of desert.

soil improvement against desertification.text: Techniques that supply water to dryland soils and fix and enrich them to halt desertification.

climate change and land degradation.text: The worsening of land degradation by climate change, especially in low-lying coasts, river deltas, drylands and permafrost areas.

overgrazing.text: Grazing in which animals eat grass faster than it can grow back, as when pastures are stocked above the livestock carrying capacity.

causes of desertification.text: The natural and human factors that strip land of most of its vegetation and turn it into desert.

human role in desertification.text: The dispute over how far local human overexploitation, rather than natural climate variability, drives desertification.

soil retrogression.text: The reversion of a soil toward pioneer conditions, mainly through erosion of its upper horizons after its vegetation is destroyed.

soil climax and succession.text: The steady balance that a soil and its vegetation reach after evolving together, the highest development its environment can produce.

soil enhancement and rebuilding.text: Practices that counter erosion and rebuild a degraded soil, chiefly by improving its structure, adding organic matter and limiting runoff.

agrivoltaics in deserts.text: Pairing solar panels with planted vegetation in deserts to support ecosystem function even where rain is scarce.

definitions of desertification.text: The competing formal definitions of desertification, of which more than 100 existed by 2005.

desertification and dust storms.text: Storms of wind-blown sand and dust that become more frequent as desertification leaves more loose material for the wind to pick up.

desertification and food insecurity.text: The threat desertification poses to global food security by shrinking the land that can be farmed sustainably.

desertification and poverty.text: The deepening poverty of dryland communities as desertification lowers land productivity and pushes people off the land.

desertification in south america.text: Desertification across South America, where 25% of the land is drylands and over 68% has suffered soil erosion from deforestation and overgrazing.

desertification in the gobi and mongolia.term: Desertification in the Gobi and Mongolia
desertification in the gobi and mongolia.text: The spread of the Gobi Desert across northern China and southern Mongolia, the fastest-expanding desert on Earth.

desertification in the sahel.text: Desertification in Africa's Sahel, a hot dry belt with 100–600 mm of rain a year, where climate change and human activity combine.

history of desertification.text: The long natural history of deserts, which grew and shrank mostly independently of people, and the later study of human-driven land deterioration.

grassland degradation.text: A biotic disturbance, also called vegetation or steppe degradation, in which grass struggles to grow or disappears from land through overgrazing, burrowing small mammals or climate change.

managed grazing.text: Grazing that moves herds through many small fenced paddocks every day or two, mimicking natural grazers so the grass can regrow.

land degradation on farms.text: The degradation of agricultural land, shaped by farmers' local choices and by global drivers such as trade, climate change and demographic change.

land sensitivity and resilience.text: Two measures that together describe how vulnerable a landscape is to degradation.

types of land degradation.text: The forms land degradation takes, from long-known erosion and physical, chemical and biological decline to newer forms such as pollution and land loss.

woody plant encroachment.text: The spread and thickening of native woody plants, bushes and shrubs at the expense of grasses and forbs.

three-north shelter forest program.text: China's Great Green Wall: planted windbreak forest strips (shelterbelts), begun in 1978, meant to hold back the Gobi Desert and supply timber.

great green wall (africa).text: An African Union project adopted in 2007, first conceived as a belt of trees across the Sahel from Djibouti to Dakar to combat desertification and hold back the Sahara.

farmer-managed natural regeneration.text: A low-cost land restoration technique in which farmers regrow and manage trees and shrubs from living stumps, roots and seeds.

rangeland management.text: The science and practice of conserving and sustainably managing rangelands, manipulating their components to yield the best mix of goods and services over time.

aridity index.text: A numerical indicator of how dry the climate is at a given place.

soil unsealing.text: Removing asphalt, cement and other human-made covers so that a sealed soil can again perform its natural functions.

dryland restoration.text: Work to return degraded drylands to their former function, or to manage them so they degrade no further.

bush control.text: Action to manage the density and composition of bushes and shrubs in an area, also called brush management.

causes of woody plant encroachment.text: Local land-use drivers such as overgrazing, fire suppression and the loss of wild herbivores, together with global drivers such as rising CO2, that favour woody plants over grasses.

woody encroachment and soil carbon.text: The change in ecosystem carbon when woody plants invade grassland: a sink if only above-ground biomass is counted, but uncertain once grass and soil organic carbon losses are included.

woody encroachment and soil water.text: The link between woody encroachment and reduced groundwater recharge, because bushes use far more rainwater than grasses and alter streamflow.

degrees of grassland degradation.text: The three sequential stages of grassland degradation: light, moderate and high.

grassland restoration.text: Restoring degraded grassland with methods matched to how severely it is degraded.

rain garden.text: A designed planted site, also called a bioretention facility, that lets runoff from roofs, roads and other hard urban surfaces soak into the soil and be cleaned.

urban soil.text: Soil in cities and towns, often stripped of its topsoil, compacted and contaminated by human activity.

small mammals in grassland degradation.text: Damage to grassland blamed on growing populations of burrowing small mammals such as marmots, voles, pikas and zokors.

land abandonment.text: The giving up of farmed land, after which, for example, woody plants may re-establish on it.

land degradation neutrality.text: A policy goal, set in UN Sustainable Development Goal 15, of restoring degraded land and soil so that the world becomes land degradation-neutral by 2030.

spoil tip.text: A pile of spoil, the waste earth material removed during mining or large excavations.

urban forestry.text: The care and management of single trees and tree populations in towns and cities to improve the urban environment.

bioretention soil mix.text: The engineered growing soil, or substrate, through which a rain garden filters collected water.

artefacts in soil.text: Objects in soil recognizably made or extracted from the earth by humans, a defining feature of human-made soils.

soil stockpile.text: A pile of topsoil excavated during construction of buildings or infrastructure and kept for later use.

soil regeneration.text: Creating new soil and restoring soil health by minimizing topsoil loss, retaining more carbon than is lost, boosting biodiversity and keeping water and nutrient cycles working.

soil health testing.text: Assessing soil health by measuring the ecosystem services a soil provides against benchmarks, combining physical, chemical and biological analyses.

ecosystem service.text: The many benefits that people derive from ecosystems, such as clean water, food, decomposition of wastes and flood control.

environmental soil science.text: The study of how humans interact with the pedosphere and with key parts of the biosphere, lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere.

interpretations of soil health.text: The differing ways users define soil health, understood as a soil's condition at a defined place and scale against benchmarks of healthy functioning.

soil quality indicators.text: The chemical, physical and biological measurements used to judge soil quality, since soil function itself cannot easily be measured directly.

forms of soil degradation.text: The four general ways soil declines in condition under poor management: erosion, and physical, chemical and biological degradation.

soil health gap.text: A concept, introduced by Maharjan and colleagues in 2020, that uses native land in a region as the benchmark for measuring how far managed soils fall short in health.

soil health versus soil quality.text: The relation between two overlapping terms: soil quality, a soil's fitness for a given purpose, and soil health, a holistic view of soil as a self-sustaining living system.

permaculture.text: An approach to land management and settlement design that copies arrangements seen in flourishing natural ecosystems.

regenerative soil practices.text: Farming and management methods, many from conservation agriculture, that regenerate soil and improve its quality.

soil resilience.text: The ability of a soil to resist destabilising influences or recover its healthy state after them.

soil governance.text: The policies, strategies and decision-making processes that nation states and local governments apply to the use of soil.

land rehabilitation.text: Returning damaged land to some degree of its former state after industry, natural disasters or other harm.

agricultural soil carbon loss.text: The release of soil carbon to the atmosphere through farming and fossil fuel use, which regenerative practices aim to reverse.

soil bioengineering.text: The use of living plant materials, such as seeds, plants and plant communities, to perform engineering functions like stabilizing slopes and controlling erosion.

septic drain field.text: A subsurface wastewater disposal facility, also called a leach field, that removes contaminants from the liquid leaving a septic tank after anaerobic digestion.

mine reclamation.text: Modifying mined land to restore it to an ecologically functional or economically usable state.

mapping soil functions.text: Mapping soil properties as interpretations for particular functions, such as food production, environmental protection or civil engineering.

soil as a filter and buffer.term: Soil as a filter and buffer
soil as a filter and buffer.text: The soil's role in regulating water and in filtering, buffering and transforming materials that move between the atmosphere, plant cover and water table.

septic tank.text: An underground concrete, fibreglass or plastic chamber where household sewage settles and is anaerobically digested as primary treatment.

drain field site assessment.text: Judging whether a soil can receive septic tank effluent, by a percolation test or by reading the soil's morphology.

onsite sewage facility.text: A wastewater system that treats and disposes of effluent on the property that produces it, where there is no public sewer.

soil health card scheme.text: An Indian government scheme, launched on 19 February 2015, that gives farmers soil cards with crop-wise nutrient and fertiliser recommendations based on soil tests.

eu soil policy.text: The European Union's approach to soil, which it treats as a non-renewable resource while leaving its governance largely to member states.

soil contamination.text: The presence in soil of human-made chemicals or other changes to the natural soil environment, a form of land degradation; also called soil or land pollution.

nonpoint source pollution.text: Diffuse pollution of water or air that does not come from a single, discrete source.

global soil partnership.text: A partnership set up by the FAO and its members in December 2012 to improve governance of the planet's limited soil resources for food security and ecosystem services.

soil governance in india.text: India's policies on soil, shaped by the weight of agriculture in its economy and by widespread farmland degradation.

urban and industrial soil governance.text: Governing soils in cities and industrial areas, where industrialization and urbanization are emerging as major causes of soil degradation, especially in the developing world.

nutrient pollution.text: Water pollution caused by too many nutrients, usually nitrogen or phosphorus, entering water bodies.

soil remediation.text: Cleaning up contaminated soil by removing, treating or containing its pollutants, to restore the soil's functions and values.

bioremediation.text: Using organisms, living or dead, typically bacteria, microalgae, fungi or plants, to remove pollutants from soil, water, air and other media.

heavy metals in soil.text: Metals such as lead, mercury, zinc and cadmium that resist breakdown and are among the commonest soil contaminants.

phytoremediation.text: Using living plants to clean up soil, air and water contaminated with pollutants; a type of bioremediation.

mycoremediation.text: A form of bioremediation that uses fungi to decontaminate the environment.

pesticide.text: A chemical or biological agent used to deter, incapacitate or kill pests, including herbicides, insecticides, nematicides and fungicides.

polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon.text: An organic compound made of several fused aromatic rings, formed mostly by incomplete burning of organic matter.

eutrophication.text: The build-up of nutrients in a body of water, boosting the growth of algae and other organisms that may then use up its oxygen.

ecological effects of soil contamination.text: The damage soil contaminants do to ecosystems, beginning with changes to soil chemistry and to the organisms living in the soil.

exposure pathways of soil contaminants.text: The routes by which soil contaminants reach people: swallowing soil or dust, eating food grown in it, skin contact, and breathing its vapours or dust.

pesticides in soil.text: Chemical or biological agents used to kill pests such as weeds, insects and fungi, and a major class of soil contaminant.

sources of soil contamination.text: The activities and materials that put contaminants into soil, such as mining and heavy industry, spills, leaking underground storage tanks, agrochemicals and waste disposal.

persistent organic pollutant.text: Organic compounds that resist chemical, biological and light-driven breakdown, are toxic, and persist in the environment.

ddt.text: A cheap, potent and persistent organochlorine insecticide, used on a massive scale from the 1930s.

soil vapor extraction.text: A physical, in situ treatment that removes volatile contaminants from unsaturated (vadose zone) soil by drawing them out as gas.

pfas.text: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances: synthetic chemicals with many fluorine atoms on a carbon chain, so stable they are called 'forever chemicals'.

environmental remediation.text: The cleanup of hazardous substances by removing, treating or containing contaminants in soil, groundwater, sediment and other environmental media.

biomagnification.text: The rise in a substance's concentration in the tissues of organisms at each higher level of a food chain.

agricultural nonpoint source pollution.text: Diffuse pollution of water by nutrients, agrochemicals and sediment washed or carried off farmland.

microplastics in soil.text: Insoluble synthetic plastic particles between 1 micrometre and 5 millimetres across, which pollute soil as well as water and air.

biostimulation.text: Modifying the environment, chiefly by adding nutrients or electron acceptors or donors, to stimulate bacteria already present that can carry out bioremediation.

groundwater pollution.text: The contamination of groundwater by pollutants released to the ground, or by unwanted natural constituents, that make their way into aquifers.

contaminant effects on soil functions.text: The disruption of soil functions, such as the cycling of carbon and nitrogen, when heavy metals and other contaminants alter the activity, mix and numbers of soil microorganisms.

health effects of soil contamination.text: The harm that exposure to soil contaminants does to people, which varies with the pollutant, the route of exposure and how vulnerable the exposed people are.

war-related soil contamination.text: Soil contamination left by munitions, chemical agents and other agents of war.

phytoextraction.text: Using plants whose roots absorb contaminants from soil or water and concentrate them in harvestable above-ground biomass.

brownfield land.text: Previously developed land, abandoned or underused, that may carry pollution or a risk of it from past industrial use.

agricultural pollution.text: The biotic and abiotic byproducts of farming that contaminate or degrade the environment and ecosystems or harm people and their interests.

metal toxicity.text: Harm to plants, animals or people caused by excessive concentrations of metals.

gis in environmental contamination.text: Using geographic information system software to map and analyse contaminants in soil, water and air.

electrokinetic remediation.text: Using direct electric current passed through the ground to draw organic, inorganic and heavy-metal contaminants out of soil.

anaerobic bioremediation.text: Bioremediation without oxygen, in which an added electron donor drives the reduction of oxidized pollutants such as chlorinated solvents, explosives and nitrate.

biopiles and windrows.text: Ex situ treatments in which excavated soil is heaped and aerated, by pumps in biopiles or by regular turning in windrows, to speed microbial breakdown of pollutants.

biosparging.text: Groundwater remediation by injecting oxygen, and possibly nutrients, into saturated contaminated zones so that indigenous bacteria degrade pollutants faster.

bioventing.text: Raising the flow of air or oxygen into the unsaturated zone of soil to speed the natural in situ breakdown of hydrocarbon contaminants.

genetically engineered bioremediation.text: The use of genetic engineering to design organisms for bioremediation, still at the stage of preliminary research.

limitations of bioremediation.text: The drawbacks that keep bioremediation rarely used: slow rates, pollutants that cannot biodegrade, and highly specific microbial needs.

pesticide bioremediation.text: Using microbes to break down pesticide residues in contaminated soil, seen as more promising than other ways of dealing with pesticide contamination.

in situ thermal desorption.text: A soil remediation technology that heats contaminated soil in place, sometimes under vacuum, to drive off or destroy pollutants; also called thermal conduction heating.

biodegradation.text: The breakdown of organic matter by microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi.

groundwater remediation.text: The treatment of polluted groundwater by removing pollutants or converting them into harmless products.

pathogens in runoff.text: Disease-causing bacteria and viruses carried in polluted runoff, a danger chiefly when they reach public drinking water.

phytodegradation.text: The use of plants to degrade organic pollutants, also called phytotransformation.

phytoscreening.text: Using plants as biosensors of subsurface contamination, to map contaminant plumes from what they take up.

phytostabilization.text: Using plants to contain pollutants for the long term by lowering their mobility in soil, holding them near the roots rather than in plant tissue.

phytostimulation.text: Boosting soil microbes' breakdown of organic contaminants in the rhizosphere, the soil around roots; also called rhizodegradation.

phytovolatilization.text: Removing substances from soil or water through plants that turn them into more volatile, often less polluting forms and release them into the air.

point source pollution.text: Pollution from a single identifiable source, such as one factory outfall or smokestack.

nutrient source apportionment.text: Estimating how much of the nutrient load reaching a water body comes from each sector, after attenuation or treatment.

nutrient trading.text: A market-based form of water quality trading in which polluters exchange credits for reducing nutrient pollution.

radioactive contamination.text: The unintended presence of radioactive substances on surfaces or within solids, liquids or gases, hazardous because their decay emits ionizing radiation.

natural attenuation.text: The natural breakdown of contaminants by a site's own microbes, with no human intervention, though the site must still be monitored.

landfarming.text: An ex situ treatment in which contaminated soil, sediment or sludge is mixed into the surface soil and periodically tilled so that microbes degrade the contaminants.

surfactant leaching.text: Decontaminating water or soil by mixing it with surfactants and then leaching out the emulsified contaminants.

bioaugmentation.text: A type of bioremediation that adds specialized microbial cultures to boost the breakdown of pollutants.

ecotoxicology.text: The study of how toxic chemicals affect organisms, populations and ecosystems, joining toxicology and ecology.

fungal biosorption of metals.text: The capture of metals by fungi, which bind them on their cell surfaces and concentrate them in their fruiting bodies for later removal.

fungal degradation of organic pollutants.text: The breakdown of organic pollutants by fungi, especially white rot fungi, using the enzymes and acids they secrete to digest lignin and cellulose.

mycorrhizoremediation.text: The removal of soil contaminants by mycorrhizal fungi, used to strengthen phytoremediation.

permeable reactive barrier.text: An in situ treatment zone set across a contaminant plume that removes or breaks down contaminants as groundwater flows through it.

arsenic contamination of groundwater.text: Groundwater pollution, often natural, caused by high concentrations of arsenic in deeper aquifer water.

dense non-aqueous phase liquid.text: A contaminant liquid that is denser than water and does not dissolve in it, such as a chlorinated solvent.

in situ chemical reduction.text: A soil and groundwater remediation technique that lowers contaminant concentrations by injecting chemical reductants, or placing them in a plume's path, at the site itself.

phytotoxicity.text: Any harmful effect of a chemical substance on plant growth, physiology or metabolism.

drastic aquifer vulnerability index.text: A score, often mapped with GIS, that rates how prone an aquifer is to contamination under its hydrological conditions.

contaminated land risk assessment.text: The staged evaluation of whether a site's contaminants pose unacceptable risk, moving from a qualitative conceptual site model to generic and then detailed quantitative assessment.

sve off-gas treatment.text: Treating the contaminated vapour drawn out by soil vapor extraction before release, most often by thermal oxidation or activated carbon adsorption.

air sparging.text: An in situ technique that injects clean air or gas into contaminated saturated soil and groundwater so that volatile organic compounds change from dissolved to vapor form.

hexavalent chromium.text: Any compound of chromium in the +6 oxidation state, a carcinogenic form produced mainly by industry.

metallophyte.text: A plant able to survive in metal-rich soil, classed as a metal indicator, excluder or hyperaccumulator.

hyperaccumulator.text: A metallophyte plant that grows in metal-rich soil or water, absorbing metals through its roots and storing them in its leaves.

pesticide degradation.text: The transformation of a pesticide into a benign substance compatible with the environment where it was applied.

in situ bioremediation.text: Bioremediation carried out at the contaminated site itself, without moving the polluted material.

phytomining.text: Extracting heavy metals from soil with hyperaccumulating plants, then collecting and refining the metals from the harvested biomass; also called agromining.

entomoremediation.text: A form of bioremediation in which insects, such as fly larvae, beetles, ants and termites, decontaminate soils.

nanoremediation.text: The use of nano-sized reactive agents to degrade or immobilize contaminants in soil or groundwater.

pump and treat.text: A remediation method that pumps contaminated groundwater to the surface and purifies it, typically by passing it through vessels of adsorbent such as activated carbon.

solidification and stabilization.text: A treatment that mixes a binder into contaminated soil to stop or reduce the mobility of contaminants.

surfactant enhanced aquifer remediation.text: The removal of non-aqueous phase liquids from aquifers by pumping a surfactant solution through the contaminated zone from injection to extraction wells.

aquifer vulnerability mapping.text: The mapping of an aquifer's intrinsic vulnerability to pollution by overlaying maps of the physical factors that control it.

geogenic groundwater contamination.text: Groundwater contamination that arises naturally from geological processes rather than human activity.

pathogen removal below on-site sanitatio.text: The die-off and adsorption of pathogens in liquid leaching from pit latrines and septic tanks as it passes through the unsaturated soil to groundwater.

acid mine drainage treatment.text: The neutralization of acidic mine outflow and removal of its dissolved metals, using limestone, lime, calcium silicate, ion exchange, wetlands or sulfide precipitation.

yellow boy.text: The yellow-orange iron(III) hydroxide that precipitates when the pH of acid mine drainage rises above 3.

thermal desorption.text: A remediation technology that heats contaminated soil or other solids so that contaminants volatilize and can be separated, then collected or destroyed.

light non-aqueous phase liquid.text: A hydrocarbon groundwater contaminant that does not dissolve in water and is less dense than it, so it forms a separate floating phase.

biosorption.text: A passive physicochemical process by which certain biomass concentrates and binds contaminants such as heavy metals onto its cell structure.

pesticide leaching.text: The movement of dissolved pesticides through the soil to sites beyond their target, a major source of groundwater pollution.

remediation of metal-contaminated soil.text: The cleanup of soils contaminated by heavy metals through isolation, immobilization, toxicity reduction, physical separation or extraction.

cadmium poisoning.text: Poisoning by cadmium, a naturally occurring toxic metal met in industry, in plant soils and in tobacco smoke.

bioslurping.text: A technique combining bioventing with vacuum pumping of floating free product (LNAPL) to recover it from groundwater and soil and bioremediate the soil.

dual-phase vacuum extraction.text: A high-vacuum technology, also called multi-phase extraction, that removes both contaminated groundwater and soil vapor through one well.

rhizofiltration.text: Phytoremediation that filters contaminated groundwater, surface water or wastewater through a mass of roots to remove toxic substances or excess nutrients.

pneumatic fracturing.text: A remediation method that injects gas into contaminated ground at a pressure above that of the gases already there, cracking the subsurface.

total petroleum hydrocarbon.text: A measure of the total amount of the mixture of hydrocarbons found in crude oil present at a site.

electrical resistance heating.text: An intensive in situ remediation method that passes alternating current through soil and groundwater between buried electrodes, heating them until contaminants evaporate.

microbial biodegradation.text: The harnessing of microbes' natural ability to degrade, transform or accumulate pollutants such as oil, PCBs, PAHs, pharmaceuticals, radionuclides and metals.

ecotoxicity testing.text: Standardized acute and chronic toxicity tests on terrestrial and aquatic organisms, including earthworms, used to rate a chemical's ecological hazard.

pesticide transformation products.text: The compounds a pesticide breaks down into, which may keep or even exceed the parent's harmful activity.

hydrocarbon biodegradation in soil.text: The breakdown of petroleum hydrocarbons by native soil microbes that use them for energy and carbon.

raymond process.text: An accelerated in situ bioremediation method, developed by Richard Raymond, that adds nutrients and electron acceptors to contaminated groundwater.

bioremediation of pcbs.text: The use of microorganisms, working in sequence, to degrade polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) at contaminated sites.

geochemical background.text: The natural levels of elements and other substances in soil, water and air, set by processes such as weathering, against which contamination is judged.

contaminants of emerging concern.text: Pollutants found in environmental monitoring that may harm ecosystems or health and are usually not yet regulated.

bioremediation of radioactive waste.text: The use of bacteria, plants and fungi to catalyze reactions that decontaminate soil, water and sediment affected by radionuclides.

bioreduction of radionuclides.text: The enzymatic reduction of radionuclides by bacteria to lower oxidation states, changing their solubility, mobility and radiotoxicity.

phytoextraction of radionuclides.text: The removal of radionuclides from soil by plants that carry them from the roots into their shoots.

sustainable remediation.text: An approach to cleaning up contaminated land that weighs a remedy's environmental, economic and social effects and seeks to minimize the footprint of the cleanup itself.

vapor intrusion.text: The migration of volatile chemicals, usually VOCs, from contaminated soil or groundwater into the indoor air of buildings above or nearby.

medical geology.text: The interdisciplinary science of how natural geological factors affect the health of people and animals.

itai-itai disease.text: The mass cadmium poisoning in Toyama Prefecture, Japan, from about 1912, named for the severe spine and joint pain it caused.

coccidioidomycosis.text: Valley fever: a fungal disease of mammals caused by inhaling spores of the soil fungi Coccidioides immitis or C. posadasii.

iodine deficiency.text: A lack of the essential dietary trace element iodine, which the thyroid hormones need.

selenium deficiency.text: A shortage of selenium, a critical nutrient, below the levels an organism requires.

melioidosis.text: An infectious disease caused by the soil-dwelling bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei, caught by contact with contaminated soil or water.

geophagia.text: The deliberate eating of earth or earth-like substances such as clay, chalk or termite-mound soil, by animals and people.

soil-transmitted helminthiasis.text: Infection with roundworms spread through soil contaminated with human faeces: ascariasis, hookworm and whipworm.

prion.text: A misfolded protein that makes normal copies of the same protein misfold, causing fatal, transmissible neurodegenerative diseases.

podoconiosis.text: A disease of the lymphatic vessels of the lower legs, also called nonfilarial elephantiasis, caused by long-term barefoot contact with irritant soils.

keshan disease.text: A congestive cardiomyopathy caused by dietary selenium deficiency together with a mutated strain of Coxsackievirus, named after Keshan County in China.

one health.text: An integrated approach that seeks to balance and optimize the health of people, animals, plants and ecosystems together.

chronic wasting disease.text: A fatal transmissible spongiform encephalopathy caused by prions that naturally affects deer, elk, moose and their relatives.

mycobacterium vaccae.text: A nonpathogenic bacterium of the Mycobacteriaceae that lives naturally in soil.

jinzū river soil restoration.text: The cleanup of cadmium-polluted farmland along Japan's Jinzū River after the itai-itai disease lawsuit.

avian geophagy.text: The eating of clay-rich soil by birds, notably South American parrots at clay licks.

soil ingestion by livestock.text: The swallowing of soil by grazing animals such as cattle and sheep, pressed onto pasture plants by their hooves.

biofortification.text: Breeding crops, conventionally or by genetic engineering, so that they contain more nutrients as they grow.

hygiene hypothesis.text: The idea that early-childhood exposure to certain microorganisms protects against allergies by properly tuning the immune system.

geochronology.text: The science of finding the age of rocks, fossils and sediments from signatures held in the materials themselves.

radiocarbon dating.text: A method of finding the age of material containing organic carbon from how much of its radioactive carbon-14 is left.

luminescence dating.text: A group of methods that find how long ago mineral grains were last exposed to sunlight or strong heating.

palynology.text: The study of acid-resistant microscopic organic remains, such as pollen and spores, found in sediments and sedimentary rocks.

cosmogenic nuclide.text: A rare isotope created when a high-energy cosmic ray strikes an atom's nucleus in the Solar System and knocks out protons and neutrons.

δ13c.text: A normalized ratio of the stable carbon isotopes carbon-13 and carbon-12, reported in parts per thousand (per mille, ‰).

optically stimulated luminescence.text: A method of measuring the radiation dose a mineral has absorbed from the light it emits when stimulated, used to date sediments.

tephrochronology.text: Dating and correlating sequences and events by their position between layers of volcanic ash (tephra) of known date.

thermoluminescence dating.text: Dating by the accumulated radiation dose of the time since crystalline material was last heated, as in lava or ceramics, or exposed to sunlight, as in sediments.

radiocarbon calibration.text: The use of a calibration curve of past atmospheric carbon-14 to convert a sample's radiocarbon measurement into an estimated calendar age.

radiocarbon dating of soil and peat.term: Radiocarbon dating of soil and peat
radiocarbon dating of soil and peat.text: Radiocarbon dating of the organic matter in soils and peat, which is hard to do reliably because younger humic acid tends to contaminate it.

surface exposure dating.text: A set of techniques for estimating how long a rock has been exposed at or near Earth's surface.

beryllium-10 as a soil tracer.text: The use of beryllium-10, a cosmogenic isotope with a half-life of 1.387 million years formed in the atmosphere, to trace soil formation and erosion.

bomb pulse.text: The sudden rise of carbon-14 in Earth's atmosphere caused by above-ground nuclear tests from 1945 until the 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty.

lead-210 dating.text: The use of lead-210, a radioactive isotope in the uranium-238 decay chain with a half-life of 22.20 years, to date recent sediments and trace soil movement.

rhizolith.text: An organosedimentary structure formed by plant roots in soils or fossil soils (paleosols).

silurian-devonian terrestrial revolution.text: The rapid spread and diversification of land plants and fungi between 428 and 359 million years ago, in the Silurian and Devonian periods.

geoarchaeology.text: A multidisciplinary field that applies the theories and techniques of the geosciences to archaeology.

taphonomy.text: The study of how organisms decay and become fossilized or preserved.

environmental dna.text: DNA collected from environmental samples such as soil, sediment, water, snow or air rather than from an individual organism.

soil mark.text: A difference in soil colour caused by archaeological features beneath it.

midden.text: An old dump for domestic waste.

stratigraphy (archaeology).text: The study of a site's sequence of superimposed units, or contexts, to learn when and how its deposits formed.

forensic geology.text: The study of earth materials as evidence to answer questions raised by the legal system.

forensic soil comparison.text: The comparison of a questioned soil sample of unknown origin with control samples, such as soil from the crime scene, to find similarities or differences.

law of superposition.text: The principle that in undeformed layered sequences the oldest layers lie at the bottom and newer material stacks on top.

celtic field.text: An old name for traces of prehistoric field systems in north-west Europe.

ridge and furrow.text: A pattern of ridges and troughs left by a ploughing system used in medieval Europe, typical of the open-field system.

forensic palynology.text: The use of pollen, spores and other palynomorphs to prove or disprove a link between objects, people and places in criminal and civil cases.

forensic archaeology.text: The branch of forensic anthropology that uses archaeological methods in legal cases, such as finding overlooked graves and processing mass graves.

geotaphonomy.text: The study of how a decomposing body and its burial affect the surrounding environment.

magnetic susceptibility analysis.text: Measurement of how readily a material becomes magnetised in an external magnetic field, used on soils and sediments.

geophysical survey (archaeology).text: Ground-based physical sensing techniques used to image or map buried archaeological features.

soil phosphate survey.text: Measuring and mapping phosphate in soil, which comes from people, their animals, rubbish and bones, to find former activity areas and sites.

cropmark.text: A pattern in growing crops, visible from the air or high ground, that reveals buried archaeological, natural or recent features.

raised field.text: A large cultivated mound, usually bounded by water-filled ditches, used to control moisture, frost damage and flooding.

history of soil science.text: How ideas about soil developed, starting from concepts built on Justus von Liebig's chemistry and refined by agricultural scientists in laboratories, greenhouses and small field plots.

the formation of vegetable mould through.term: The Formation of Vegetable Mould Through the Action of Worms
the formation of vegetable mould through.text: Charles Darwin's 1881 book on earthworms, their habits and their part in forming and moving the soil.

world congress of soil science.text: The International Union of Soil Sciences' conference, held every four years apart from a break for World War II.

world soil museum.text: A museum in Wageningen, the Netherlands, that displays soil profile monoliths representing the world's major soil types.

international year of soils.text: The year 2015, declared by the United Nations General Assembly on 20 December 2013 to raise worldwide awareness of soils.

development of soil taxonomy.text: The move from the qualitative soil classifications of Marbut and of 1938 to the quantitative Soil Taxonomy built under Guy D. Smith.

russian school of soil science.text: The school led by V. V. Dokuchaev and N. M. Sibirtsev from 1870, which treated soils as independent natural bodies with their own properties.

agricultural chemistry.text: The chemistry, especially organic chemistry and biochemistry, of agriculture.

australian society of soil science incor.term: Australian Society of Soil Science Incorporated
australian society of soil science incor.text: Australia's not-for-profit professional association for soil scientists and others concerned with managing the country's soils, publicly known as Soil Science Australia.
