soil and water conservation society.text: A professional and scientific membership society that fosters the science and art of managing natural resources sustainably.

marbut's soil profile concept.text: The American adaptation of the Russian soil concept, led by C. F. Marbut, which put the individual soil profile ahead of external soil features and surface geology.

park grass experiment.text: A long-term field study at Rothamsted set up to test how fertilizers and manures affect hay yields.

german soil science society.text: Germany's non-profit society of soil science experts and others interested in the field, the Deutsche Bodenkundliche Gesellschaft (DBG).

world soil day.text: An annual day, 5 December, that celebrates the importance of soil in people's lives.

long-term agricultural experiments.text: Field experiments run for decades, some for more than 100 years, to test the sustainability of farming practices from yield trends.

v.v. dokuchaev central museum of soil.term: V.V. Dokuchaev Central Museum of Soil
v.v. dokuchaev central museum of soil.text: A soil museum in Saint Petersburg, founded in 1902 by Vasily Dokuchaev.

burial of objects by earthworms.text: The slow sinking of surface objects, from stones to Roman ruins, as earthworms bring up earth from below and leave it as castings.

on the formation of mould.text: Darwin's 1837 paper to the Geological Society of London on the role of earthworms in forming soil.

history of bioturbation research.text: The study of how burrowing and mixing by living things shapes soil, from Darwin's earthworm work to its re-evaluation by soil geomorphologists from the 1980s.

modern study of soil formation.text: The shift, from about 1940, to treating soil formation as many interrelated physical, chemical and biological processes open to quantitative study.

rethinking soil organic matter.text: The recognition, in the 21st century, that soil organic matter differs from what soil science long taught about it.

soil surveys for nonfarm uses.text: The broadening of soil survey after 1950 from farming, ranching and forestry to information on how soils affect nonfarm uses.

broadbalk experiment.text: A long-running field experiment at Rothamsted Research, sown with winter wheat every year since 1843.

humus theory.text: The once-prevalent view that decayed plant matter, humus, was plants' main source of carbon.

soil map of the world.text: The world soil map published by FAO and UNESCO from 1971 to 1981 in 10 volumes at a scale of 1:5 million.

virgin lands campaign.text: Nikita Khrushchev's 1953 plan to boost Soviet farm output by ploughing new land in southern Western Siberia and northern Kazakhstan.

vasily dokuchaev.text: Russian geologist and geographer (1846–1903) credited with laying the foundations of soil science.

justus von liebig.text: German chemist (1803–1873), a principal founder of organic chemistry, who made major contributions to agricultural and biological chemistry.

hans jenny (pedologist).text: Swiss-born soil scientist (1899–1992) and expert in pedology, above all in the processes of soil formation.

sergei winogradsky.text: Ukrainian and Russian microbiologist, ecologist and soil scientist (1856–1953) who pioneered the cycle-of-life concept.

martinus beijerinck.text: Dutch microbiologist and botanist (1851–1931), one of the founders of virology and environmental microbiology.

friedrich albert fallou.text: German lawyer and land tax assessor (1794–1877) considered one of the founders of modern soil science.

konstantin glinka.text: Russian soil scientist (1867–1927), a student of Dokuchaev who carried the Russian school's ideas to the wider world.

eugene w. hilgard.text: German-American expert on pedology (1833–1916), considered the father of modern soil science in the United States.

curtis f. marbut.text: American soil scientist (1863–1935) who directed the Soil Survey Division of the US Department of Agriculture from 1913 until his death.

lorenzo a. richards.text: American soil physicist (1904–1993), one of the most influential figures in 20th-century soil physics.

mineral theory of plant nutrition.text: The theory, synthesized and promoted by Liebig, that plants draw essential nutrients as inorganic minerals from the soil, and carbon and hydrogen from air and water.

john bennet lawes.text: English entrepreneur and agricultural scientist (1814–1900) who founded the experimental farm that became Rothamsted Research.

guy d. smith.text: American soil scientist (1907–1981) who originally developed the USDA soil classification system, Soil Taxonomy.

rattan lal.text: Indian-American soil scientist (born 1944), a pioneer of soil-centred farm management for food security and climate-resilient agriculture.

hugh hammond bennett.text: Pioneer of soil conservation in the United States (1881–1960) and head of the federal soil erosion agency now called the Natural Resources Conservation Service.

edmund ruffin.text: American planter, politician and scientist (1794–1865), known for pioneering methods to preserve and improve soil productivity.

franklin hiram king.text: American agricultural scientist (1848–1911) who has been called the father of soil physics in the United States.

jean-baptiste boussingault.text: French chemist (1801–1887) who made major contributions to agricultural science.

edgar buckingham.text: American physicist (1867–1940) who worked as a soil physicist at the USDA Bureau of Soils from 1902 to 1906.

carl sprengel.text: German botanist and agricultural scientist (1787–1859) who first stated the law of the minimum.

liebig's nitrogen debate.text: The long dispute over Liebig's claim that plants feed on nitrogen compounds from the air, and over whether crops need nitrogen fertilizer.

selman waksman.text: Russian-born American biochemist and microbiologist (1888–1973) whose research on the decomposition of soil organisms enabled the discovery of streptomycin and other antibiotics.

joseph henry gilbert.text: English chemist (1817–1901) who spent a long career improving the methods of practical agriculture.

konstantin gedroits.text: Russian soil scientist (1872–1932) of Lithuanian origin, founder of colloidal soil chemistry in Russia.

peter erasmus müller (forester).text: Danish forester and naturalist (1840–1926) whose studies of forest soils laid early foundations for the study of humus forms.

discovery of chemosynthesis.text: Winogradsky's discovery of chemoautotrophy, popularly called chemosynthesis: organisms drawing energy from inorganic compounds and carbon from carbon dioxide.

charles darwin.text: English naturalist, geologist and biologist (1809–1882), best known for his contributions to evolutionary biology.

nicolas-théodore de saussure.text: Swiss chemist and plant physiologist (1767–1845), a major pioneer in the study of photosynthesis.

albrecht thaer.text: German agronomist (1752–1828) and supporter of the humus theory of plant nutrition.

albert bernhard frank.text: German botanist, plant pathologist and mycologist (1839–1900) who coined the term mycorrhiza.

albert atterberg.text: Swedish chemist and agricultural scientist (1846–1916) who created the Atterberg limits still used by geotechnical engineers.

lorenz hiltner.text: German agronomist and microbiologist (1862–1923) who developed the concept of the rhizosphere and helped found microbial ecology.

francis d. hole.text: American pedologist, educator and musician (1913–2002), known for mapping Wisconsin's soils and for popularizing soil science.

cyril g. hopkins.text: American agricultural chemist (1866–1919) at the University of Illinois, noted for his research and writing on Illinois soils.

roy w. simonson.text: American soil scientist (1908–2008) who studied soils across the United States and on islands of the Western Pacific.

thomas lyttleton lyon.text: American soil scientist (1869–1938) who wrote on the nitrogen cycle.

enrichment culture.text: A fundamental method of culturing microbes taken from the environment so that they can be studied.

farmers of forty centuries.text: Franklin Hiram King's book on the long-sustained traditional farming of China, Korea and Japan, now regarded as a classic of organic farming.

milton whitney.text: The first chief of the US Division of Agricultural Soil, forerunner of the federal soil survey.

nikolai sibirtsev.text: Russian soil scientist (1860–1900) who led the Russian school of soil science with Dokuchaev.

russian chernozem.text: Vasily Dokuchaev's 1883 book, his most famous work, a complete study of the chernozem soils of European Russia.

winogradsky column.text: A technique devised by Sergei Winogradsky for studying the microbes of sediments.

soil science society of america.text: The largest soil-specific scientific society in the United States, formed in 1936.

natural resources conservation service.text: An agency of the United States Department of Agriculture, formerly the Soil Conservation Service, that gives technical help to farmers and other private landowners and managers.

rothamsted research.text: One of the oldest agricultural research institutions in the world, founded in 1843 at Harpenden, England, and formerly the Rothamsted Experimental Station.

national cooperative soil survey.text: A nationwide US partnership of federal, regional, state and local agencies and institutions that investigates, inventories, classifies and interprets the nation's soils and publishes the results.

international union of soil sciences.text: The international scientific union of soil scientists, founded in 1924 as the International Society of Soil Science and a member of the International Science Council.

international soil reference and informa.term: International Soil Reference and Information Centre
international soil reference and informa.text: ISRIC, an independent, science-based foundation that provides quality-assessed soil information to address global environmental and societal challenges.

pochvovedenie.text: A Russian journal of soil science, published in English translation as Eurasian Soil Science.

soil science society of poland.text: The scientific and professional society of Polish soil scientists (Polskie Towarzystwo Gleboznawcze).

early united states soil survey.text: The beginnings of systematic soil survey in the United States, from the first field mapping in 1899 to the consolidation of all USDA survey work in 1952.

international humic substances society.text: A scientific society devoted to research on natural organic matter in soil and water.

soil science society of america journal.term: Soil Science Society of America Journal
soil science society of america journal.text: A bimonthly peer-reviewed journal publishing research on all aspects of soil science.

journal of soil and water conservation.term: Journal of Soil and Water Conservation
journal of soil and water conservation.text: A bimonthly peer-reviewed journal of conservation science, practice and policy.

international committee on anthropogenic.text: ICOMANTH, a committee active from 1995 to 2013 that worked on classifying soils derived from human activity.

european soil bureau network.text: A network of national soil science institutions, created in 1996 at the European Commission's Joint Research Centre in Ispra, that collects and harmonises soil information for Europe.

lunar regolith.text: The unconsolidated material covering the surface of the Moon, whose finer fraction is called lunar soil.

martian regolith.text: The fine blanket of loose, varied surface deposits covering Mars, whose finer fraction is called Martian soil.

lunar regolith simulant.text: An Earth material made to approximate the chemical, mechanical, engineering, mineralogical or particle-size properties of lunar regolith.

space weathering.text: The weathering of any object exposed to the harsh environment of outer space.

astropedology.text: The study of very ancient paleosols and meteorites relevant to the origin of life, and of soil systems on other planets.

perchlorates in martian soil.text: The chlorine-bearing perchlorate salts whose relatively high concentrations make Martian regolith toxic.

lunar dust hazards.text: The harm that fine, easily disturbed lunar dust can do to equipment and to the health of crews.

lunar sample return.text: The bringing of lunar rock and regolith back to Earth by space missions, beginning with Apollo.

lunar soil formation.text: The making and continual alteration of lunar regolith by impacts and space radiation, known as space weathering.

in situ resource utilization.text: The collection, processing and use of materials found on other bodies, such as the Moon or Mars, in place of materials brought from Earth.

extraterrestrial soil definition.text: The unsettled question of what counts as soil on other planetary bodies, where the usual Earth definition, which includes organic content, may not fit.

martian dust.text: The finest fraction of Martian regolith, under 30 micrometres across, much of it carried into the atmosphere.

lunarcrete.text: A proposed concrete-like building material made from lunar regolith to cut the cost of building on the Moon.

martian regolith simulant.text: An Earth material used to mimic the chemical and mechanical properties of Martian regolith for research and prototype testing.

impact gardening.text: The stirring of the outer crust of airless moons and other bodies by impacts, called lunar gardening on the Moon.

archean paleosols.text: Soils preserved from early Earth's Archean eon, which give circumstantial evidence of life in soils 3.42 to 3.46 billion years ago.

growing plants on the moon and mars.term: Growing plants on the Moon and Mars
growing plants on the moon and mars.text: Research into whether lunar and Martian soils, or simulants of them, can support the growth of plants.

martian paleosols.text: Ancient soils on Mars, recognised from rover analyses and orbital remote sensing of the Martian surface.

viking lander biological experiments.text: Four biological experiments carried to the surface of Mars by the two Viking landers in 1976 to look for signs of microbial life.

origin of life in soil.text: The idea that life evolved in soil, where water held between clay grains forms countless microscopic reaction chambers.

mars sample-return mission.text: A proposed mission to collect rock and dust samples on Mars and bring them to Earth.

plants in space.text: The growing of plants in outer space, mostly in pressurized, weightless space gardens in low Earth orbit.

labeled release experiment.text: A Viking life-detection test in which Martian soil was dosed with a dilute nutrient solution tagged with radioactive carbon-14 and the air above monitored for labelled gas.
